GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
IRA WINN COBU RN
GRAND MASTER OCTOBER 12, 1962 • OCTOBER 18, 1963
The formal records identify our Ninety- Seventh Grand Master as
given above. To all of his intimate friends and his host of devoted
admirers he is, with sincere affection, thought of as "Bud." This is a
most natural situation for while he displays that degree of dignity
and devotion so appropr iate to his ability in leadership, he possesses
the charming faculty of intimacy and comradeship which endear him
to all who have had the pleasur e of close association with him. And
so, in this account of a truly remarkable career there is no impropriety in using the latter designation.
Bud is, by heritage, well fitted for the responsibilities of leadership and of being a master builder. Into these responsibilities he progressed as natll1'ally as a hand fits itself into its glove.
Born in San Francis co on January 4, 1901, the son of Ira and
August a Schroed er Coburn , he was educate d in Lick-W ilmerdi ng
High School, the Univers ity of Californ ia at Berkeley, and the environment of his father's exampl e as a capable and successful builder who
was also a devoted particip ant in civic and Masoni c leadership. His
prepara tory schooling was made the more effective by his particip ation in athletics. He is a member of Delta Kappa Epsilon and his
election to four honor societies was the result of his campus activities.
On graduat ion in 1925, Bud immediately became part ·of his
father's general contrac ting organization, assuming charge thereof
following the death of Ira, Sr., in October , 1938.
The Masoni c career which led to his election as Grand Master
32 years later commenced with receiving the three degrees in Doric
Lodge No. 216 on April 14, May 12 and June 23, 1930, respectively,
his prompt selection as an officer of that Lodge and his service as its
Master in 1939.
The next step in Masoni c activity came with his appoint ment as
Inspect or of District 48B on January 1, 1941.
The outbrea k of war brough t a change from one type of leadersh ip
to another . Enlisting in the U. S. Army Enginee rs, he served his
country in the type of activity to which he was accustomed in civil
life. Most of that service was in the South Pacific and culminated in
his dischar ge at war's end with the rank of Lieuten ant Colonel.
Sevente en years later, following his visit to Hawaii as Grand Master, Bud vi·sited the Grand Lodge of the Philippines and through their
courtes y was able to revisit the locations of his wartime activity.
Upon his return to San Francis co after the war Ira's life was
enriche d by his marriag e to Alma Haaker , who so fully shared his
many activities until her death in April of this year.

Brother Coburn's active leadership in Doric Lodge has continued
through service as Treasurer .
Resumption of participation in our jurisdictional program came with
his appointme nt in October, 1948, to the Committee on Reconstruction
of the Columbia Temple. Appointm ent on this Committee was repeated
each year through 1953. Each of these reappointm ents included the
responsibility of being Chairman of the Committee.
Then followed three years of assignmen t to the Committe e on
Policy and General Purposes, interrupte d by being Grand Marshal
during 1955.
Combined with the flnal assignmen t on the Policy Committee there
was added assignmen t as Trustee on the committee to operate the new
California Masonic Memorial Temple. The following year the Committee on Dedicatio n Arrangem ents was appointed with Brother Coburn
designated as Vice-Cha irman.
Of the ·six years of service as a T'rustee of the Tempie, the flrst
three were by appointme nt. Election as Junior Grand Warden came in
1959 so from then until his election as Grand Master in 1962 there
followed three years of ex-officio membership on two of our most
important Constituti onal Boards-T he Trustees of the Masonic Homes
and the Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple. His
activity on the latter Board included being its President during 1960-61.
Thus we complete the details of a most impressive career which led
to election to Masonry' s highest office. The available space does not
permit adding, here, the even more impressive account of Bud's year
as Grand Master. The full story of that is supplemented by the edicts,
decisions and recommendations which he issued, as covered in his
message printed in thios same volume. In reading that material there
comes a full realization why to know him is to like him, to work with
him leads to admiration and to assign him a responsibility is to assure
the success of the project.

Lincoln knew the facts of the Bible, but this didn't mean

Then Lincoln turne d to the Lord with anoth er proble

where in our public life we do not have justice with

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

looked to us for understanding and help. Our American ideal. from the
beginning, has been freedom and justice, with generosity, and that holds
for American individuals dealing with one another here at home, and
for our nation, in its dealings with people throughout the world.
The fourth building on the edge of the village green was, of course,
the church. Not only the teachings of Masonry. but the work of Masonry undergirds all four institutions. I believe these institutions have
made America g<reat in the past, and make her great today.
Masonry undergirds the Church. It lays the foundation for the
Church in a man's life. It is a friend of the Church. However, we believe
in the separation of Church and State. We do not want the State to do
the work of any Church, and we do not want any Church to
have special privileges beyond the rest. We want the churches to be
free, here in America, but we maintain as the Masons in colonial days
maintained, that absolute power belongs to God alone. "In God we
trust, and Him only." Now, there are several ways of looking at this
statement.
I was scheduled to speak in Berkeley at Commencemen t time, and
registered at a motel as an Episcopal Bishop, dressed in the Bishop's
street garb. I had on my clerical collar, purple vest, Bishop's ring and
pectoral cross. As I registered, the man behind the counter didn't say
anything until he saw my Masonic ring, and then he said, "Well, I guess
I won't have to worry about being paid for this room!" And I was glad
that at least the Masons have a reputation for honesty!
The tale is told of a settler in the days when the west was won. He
got mad at the thirty-five or forty other people living in the crossroads community, and decided to leave. He was saddling his horse when
another settler came up and said, "Don't go, John-there is nothing
wrong here that a little water and some good people won't help." John
turned his head and said. "You can say the same thing about Hell, too!"
Yes, Hell would be helped by water if it is the fire and brimstone
Hell. And if a few good people got into Hell, it would not be Hell any
more, because there would be hope. Good people make the difference.
They bring hope to hopeless situations.
On the other hand - suppose you had all of the water you need,
all of the rich soil and wealth in the world-all of the blessings you could
possibly think of-you would still be in Hell If there were no good people
around you, and if you, yourself, were not good, and felt cut off from
God.
Goodness makes the difference--even more difference than water in
a desert land.
Masonry catches a man as it finds him, anywhere, perhaps as a carefree pagan, and turns his attention towards God, and turns his face
towards the light, more light, as God gives him to see the light.
Alexander Whyte made a sociological study of the Organization

Man a few years ago. One out of five families in America move every
year, from one commuity to another. They leave the old friends, and
must find new friends wherever they go. Dr. Whyte said that what these
people who move about so much need, is instant fellowship. They are
also looking for instant solutions to their problem•s.
We live in a day of automation and large cities and we need to be
reminded that every individual counts. Masonry makes this point in a
very effective way. Consider how the elaborate courtesy of our ritual
reminds us that every individual is important, and has something to contribute to the benefit of all.
The Mason can find instant fellowship wherever he goes in America,
because he is a Mason. The solution to problems cannot be found in a
moment-but only as the Mason becomes a man of God, a Godly man,
can he begin to deal with his problems in the creative way that will bring
about a right solution, no matter what the problems may be. For hundreds of years Masonry has known what the experts know-that no
man has ever climbed up hill from moral degradation without faith in
God.
The man of faith receives from his religion the qualities that high
religion has always built into the lives of the faithful-love, joy, peace,
kindness, goodness, humility and self control. These qualities are what
makes us call a man a good man. And this man also is, we believe, the
kind of man who can find the answers to the problems facing America
today.
The man of faith knows that the Liberty Bell was rung on the Fourth
of July in Philadelphia, not that everyone who heard it might run home
and hide; the bell was rung in 1776 that everybody who loved freedom
might rally 'round and cooperate and sacrifice and even fight, to make
freedom possible.

14

The Godly man puts his final trust in God. He receives his dignity
from the relationship he has with God. He has the right to freedom
because he is God's child, made in God's image. And this man, and this
man only, is to be trusted with solving the problems of America, and the
problems of people in the world.
"Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly,
nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
But his delight is in the law of the Lord and in His law doth he meditate
day and night.
"The Lord knoweth the way of the righteous, but the way of the
ungodly shall perish."
And from what I know of Masonry, not one of us should want anything more--or anything less-than that!

CUBA

On May 10, 1963, I issued an edict, the purpose of which was to
permit Cuban Masonic brethren residing in California the opportuni ty
to hold Masonic communication, and visit Lodges in this jurisdiction. The
edict set forth a procedure by which members of Cuban Lodges and the
Grand Lodge of Cuba could pay their dues to our Grand Secretary, and,
after proof of membership by examination, visit any of our constituen t
Lodges. All such dues so collected are being held in trust in our Grand
Lodge office until such time as the Cuban Lodges, and the Grand Lodge
of Cuba, are again able to function, without outside influence, as the
Supreme Masonic authority in that jurisdiction.

CENTENNIALS

California Masonry is well into its second century of activity. Consequently, many of our older Lodges have been, or soon will be, conducting their "centennial" programs, especially in those parts of the
state, such as the older mining areas, the Mother Lode area, etc., where
Lodges were established in the mid-19th century. These original Lodges
give proof of Masonry's basic strength, stabililly, and vigor. As time
passes, and economic conditions change, some of these areas do not
have the population they once enjoyed. Nonetheless, the Lodges, so
long established, have their roots deep in the Masonic soil of their
communities. Their areas may not provide for present membership
increase, and in some of them the officers may have served repeatedly.

NECROLOGY

As the detailed report of our Necrology Committee will show, our
hearts have been saddened this year through the loss of many fine
Masons and members of Grand Lodge. The passing of every one of
these brethren is a distinct loss and brings sorrow to our Fraternity.
the cause of Masonry, and to the members of their immediate families,
to whom we extend our sympathy.
The Grand Master has no thought of minimizing the passage of any
brother who has passed on this year. As Tennyson put it so beautifully,
"God's finger touched them, and they slept." We have also been particularly saddened at the taking from among us of some of the most
devoted special workers of our Craft. Appropriate eulogies will be given
these departed brethren on Wednesday morning. Included in that group
will be a eulogy for one of our officers, our Assistant Grand Lecturer
Ralph W. Collins, whose talents, courage, ritualistic ability and devotion to the work of Grand Lodge and its causes earned him a place that
will be hard to fill; to him I want to pay this special tribute.
I can say of all these departed brethren that many were dear friends
and co-workers whom I will always remember with deep affection.

MEMORIAL TEMPLE

Although we did not achieve our complete goal to make the Memorial
Temple "Debt-Free in '63," the debt has been reduced to a figure les'5
than $900,000.00. Under the new Building Manager, Brother George D.
Gavin, numerous improvements are being made in facilities; increased
use is being made of the auditorium and exhibit hall, resulting in a consistent increased garage service.
More good news with respect to the Memorial Temple Corporation
is the U.S. Internal Revenue Service ruling exempting the corporation
as an organization from federal income tax. Contributio ns made to the
Temple are deductible by donors: and "bequests, legacies, devises, transfers or gifts for J'emple use are deductible for Federal estate and gift tax
purposes under provisions of Sections 2055, 2106 and 2522 of the Code."
Our construction of the Memorial Temple has been more and more
justified with the continuing passage of time. It is an outstanding
Masonic symbol. impressing its beauties upon a constantly increasing
number of visitors every year. Its complete public acceptance confirms
the sound business judgment of our committee which originally recommended that it be built.

SOJOURNERS

This is a subject of vital concern to me. Frankly, it also seems to
have been one on which there has been much general talk with little
action or specific results despite the ex•cellent work of the committee. In
my travels I have been appalled to learn of the many Masons who do
not know that they can invite sojourners to enjoy Masonic associations
with them.
I wish to quote from the comments of Past Grand Master John R.
Moore on the ~ubject:
"On the journey westward the pioneers brought with them the
public school, the church and the Masonic Lodge. The lodge hall became
the focal point of community affairs, such as social, economic and other
activities. As Masons from other jurisdictions arrived they sought membership in the local Lodge and participated actively in fraternal, church
and community affairs. As a result Masonry flourished and contributed
so much to the growth and well-being of community, county and state.
"Masonry is still flourishing but members who change their residences are not bringing their Masonry with them, that is, they are not
dimitting to local Lodges in appreciable numbers. . . . The situation
might be rectified if the members of the local Lodge would seek out the
sojourners and invite their attendance and membership. To any great
degree this is manifestly impossible for the address of the sojourner is
unknown, even his name is not known.
"The solution then rests with the sojourner himself for it is a simple
matter for him to locate a local Lodge and its officers, but fewer and
fewer are doing this as the years go by. The suggestion then must be
that the Grand Lodge (from which the •sojourner came) instruct its offi-

29

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

cers to urge its members, wh0 change their permanent address, to seek
membership in a local Lodge in ti1e area of their new residence.... "
There has been some sojourner criticism of our required $25 Homes
payment as a membership requisite. I recommend that the requirement
be continued: I feel that it is little enough for a man to pay for the
privilege of membership in a California Lodge and for what Masonry in
California has to offer. It also establishes his eligibility for admission to
the Home should he or his widow find themselves in financial need.
I urge the Grand Lodge of California to do everything possible in
co-operation with our committees to bring the sojourner "into our fold."
I further recommend that the complete co~operation of Grand Lodge be
given to the conduct of campaigns by individual Lodges to attract sojourners to attend California Masonic meetings, and take part in our
activities, to the mutual benefit of all.

COMMERCIALISM

It has been the policy of your Grand Master to work closely with
the Committee on Commercialism, and I have enjoyed the Committee's
loyal and active co~operation. Our code sets forth the rules and regulations on commercialism so clearly that there have been very few misinterpretations. During the year, there have been some instances where
an interpretation has been requested. Our policy has been to extend the
helping hand to all, to "whisper good counsel." Usually a note from the
Grand Master to the Committee Chairman completes the matter satis~
factorily. Rather than make a commitment, we urge that inquiry be made
first, to save any embarrassment's. All those submitting inquiries during
the year have been most ·co-operative; all show that they respect the
Grand Lodge position. In some instances inquiries have been made when
they were not required: however, the answer is always gladly given.
When in doubt. make the inquiry: it's "better to be safe than sorry."

CONSTITUTIONAL OBSERVANCE

I am much pleased to report that I find a greatly renewed interest in
the work of this committee throughout the state. I believe that the
American people are becoming much concerned with some of the inter~
pretations being placed on portions of their National Constitution. I also
believe that this concern is a salutary and healthy condition. I therefore
recommend that the work of this committee be greatly expanded, with
more programs and added adivity. As an example of such possible
activities, I cite my May 10, 1963 proclamation urging all California
Masons to encourage and take part in July 4th community "Bell Ring·
ing" Independence Day observances. This proclamation produced an
excellent response, a most gratifying activity on such short notice, and
further proof of the average Mason's inherent patriotism and love of
country. Many Masons now serve on their Lodges' committees because
of their Masonic principles and their interest in the continuation of our
constitutional form of government.

LODGE FINANCING

This committee also has done an outstanding job during the year.
Their counsel and advice has been requested by many Lodges, to their
great benefit. The best evidence of this is that all of our Lodges are
not only solvent, but are in the best financial condition in California
Masonic history. I want to emphasize that this committee was established to be of assistance to the Lodges, not to investigate their finances
or interior activities. As an example, I cite the case of one of our Lodges

Although I realize that the authority under Section 203 C.M.C.

FINANCE

It is well to remember that we are and will continue to be in an era
of rising costs. The work of this committee, too, has been outstanding
- to keep in bounds, yet not restrict, the Grand Lodge activities and
program. We must be prepared to face 'continued rising costs.
Many years ago in the early days of our nation, Patrick Henriy, a
great American patriot said: "No free government or the blessings of
liberty can be preserved to any people but by a firm adherence to justice,
moderation, temperance, frugality and virtue, and by a £requent recurrence to fundamental principles." I think this applies equally to the free
institution of government, and to our Masonry. I feel that it is reflected
in the policy of your Finance Committee. That policy, briefly stated, is
to be prudent, yet not restrictive; and for this policy and its work the
committee is to be commended.
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

DEMOLAY

CORRESPONDENCE COMMITTEE, CALIFORNIA FREEMASON

Much has been done by California Masonry in assisting and training
the young leaders of tomorrow by precept and example. Much remains
to be done. Nothing is of more importance than the guiding and training
of our youth. A great step forward was taken in that direction by this
Grand Lodge when in 1956 it officially recorded its approval of the
ideals, aims and purposes of the Order of DeMolay. I refer specifically
to the note under the old Section 333f C.M.C. for a full statement of
this policy.
luiplementing this policy is the job of adult leadership from within
the AJiks of our Lodges. DeMolay Chapters reaching their maturity in
the family of DeMolay, based upon my observation, is the result of men
dedicated to ideals of DeMolay. I urge that each of our Lodge officers
re-appraise the structure of their DeMolay programs. In our Masonic
teachings we promise to stretch forth a helping hand. The challenge for
today is an honest answer to the question: When did I last stretch forth
my helping hand to the boys of DeMolay?
Although I have discussed the work of only some of our committees,
I cannot close this portion of the report without expressing my sincere
thanks to the chairmen and members of all committees. They are all
devoted servants to the cause of Masonry; to them is due the appreciation of all California Masons.

I cannot let the opportunity pass to compliment the work of the
Correspondence Committee and its Chairman-Editor, Brother Newcomb
Condee, for the remarkable job done with the California Freemason. It
is well edited, informative and provides many of our members with news
of current, past and forthcoming Masonic events in California.
I feel strongly that the Freemason should be placed in the hands of
every California Mason. It is somewhat singular that our "house organ"

A study of our overall committee structure should be carefully reviewed. At the present time the record shows that we have fifteen standing committees and sixteen special committees. In discussing objectives
with committee chairmen, it is my considered opinion that there is
presently a considerable overlapping of duties and responsibilities.

I have already referred to the increasing number of requests for
Masonic participation in, or conduct of, public cornerstone or dedication
ceremonies. I think this increase is due to two reasons: First, the activity
of our local Lodge members stimulating interest in our public schools;
and secondly, our general activities, resulting in an improved public
image. Local programs for the observance of Public Schools Week in
California, established so many years ago by our Past Grand Master
Charles Albert Adams, have played an important part in the formation
and development of our public image. However, I ,sense a slowing down
of the momentum of past years in local Public Schools Week observance
programs. I feel that we must vigorously reorganize our whole concept
of our Public Schools Week, to follow more closely the original ideas of
Brother Adams. Also the Masters of the Lodges must vigorously pursue
this most important Grand Lodge activity. We must remain ever-vigilant
with relation to the entire concept of our public schools. In our Lodges
the members are closer to the individual teachers. They can be very
helpful in the formation of ideas, and in developing public information
on the teachers' role and value as youth character builders in their
formative years.

Throughout this year many qualified members of Grand Lodge have
indicated a desire to serve Masonry but are being deprived of this opportunity. In the recommendation I am about to make I am mindful of the
quality of leadership and sound judgment in the present membership of
all our committees. Experience and mature judgment is important - but
if this Grand Lodge is to continue in its growth, and if it is to maintain
its high standard of leadership, that experience and maturity should be
more equitably distributed.
I therefore recommend that a special committee be appointed by the
incoming Grand Master to make a thorough study of our present overall
committee structure, their duties. activities, objectives, etc., with the
objective of consolidation where possible and the elimination of overlapping responsibilities.
No. 1
was questioned by the CommitClub
The Paradise Park Masonic
tee on Commercialism as to its right to use the word "Masonic" in the
Club's name.
Facts: Paradise Park Masonic Club was organized and formed
in 1921. Its location is in Santa Cruz, California. It has a total
membership of 399. 318 of whom are Master Masons and 81
Eastern Star members. It is strictly a Masonic Club for Masonic
fellowship and is in no way engaged in a commercial enterprise.
Its membership is limited to Masons and their families. An investigation disclosed no violation of Masonic law.
The answer is "Yes." Where the word "Masonic" in connection
with an association or club is not used for the purpose of advertising
a business or inducing the public to believe that a business is being
conducted under the auspices of the Masonic fraternity and whereas
here the Club is composed of Masons and is organized for Masonic
purposes and to further the aim and purpose of Masonry and is conducted by Masons and for the use and benefit of Masons then it may
use the word "Masonic."

PROCEEDING S OF THE
COMMISSION ON MASONIC PRACTICES

At the outset of this Masonic Year I expressed to the Craft my deep
conviction that the time had come when the Fraternity in this Grand
Jurisdiction should subject its Masonic practices to a process of thorough
self-analysi s and self-evaluation in order that the objectives of Freemasonry might be attained in the best possible manner. This was not
to say that either those objectives, or the ancient landmarks which safeguard them, were the subject of concern, for their validity and worth
stand unchallenge d just as they have through the centuries. Rather, it
was a belief - largely based upon countless expressions of individual
Masons made to me, and supported by my own observation s - that
many current difficulties which are being experienced by the Fraternity
in this, as well as in other Grand Judsdictions , could be lessened or
eliminated by improving the practices now being used in the pursuit of
our objectives.
Acting upon my conviction, I therefore created a special Commission
on Masonic Practices and delegated to it the power and charged it with
the duty to inquire in my behalf into the Masonic Practices being followed in this Jurisdiction: the problems - if any- related to these
practices and the views of the Craft as well as any conclusion which
might be drawn by the Commission as to possible improvements which
might be made in our practices.
This has been, in fact, one of my main objectives for this Masonic
year. I repeated it in my message to the Craft in the summer, 1963, issue
of the California Freemason, from which I now quote again:
"Since the beginning of time, man has constantly undergone change.
Each succeeding generation changes. The works of man are progressive
because of this continuing change. Yesterday is not the same as today.
"Thomas Jefferson, one of our greatest Americans, said of change:
'I am not an advocate for frequent changes in laws and constitutions,
but laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the
human mind - as that becomes more developed, more enlightened. As
new discoveries are made, new truths revealed, as manners and opinions
change with the change of circumstances, institutions must advance in
order to keep pace with the times.'
" 'For civilized society, or even segments of society, to remain stagnant is to remain "under the regimen of their barbarous ancestors." A
pool becomes stagnant because no fresh water enters in. Finally it becomes dogged with its own algae, and dries up, and is no longer a pool.
It is this stagnation which we should guard against - and the inevitable drying up which follows.'
"Masonry has oSuffered through many wars and much bloodshed:
through plague and poverty: through degradation and even oblivion,
but it has always risen to greet another sunrise! Can our generation do

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

35

less t~a~ ou.r forbears? Can we, through apathy, permit stagnation
when it is within our power to open the floodgates and loose a rush of
clear water to revitalize the pool?"
This Commission, together with its associates and with the assistance
of large numbers of the Craft, has worked with great diligence during
t~e past year. In that time it has received and analyzed some 8,000 individual. resp~nses to questionnair es and has conducted over 2,500 per~onal intervie~s with Masons throughout the entire jurisdiction, including many soioumers.
Its firs~ Repo.rt has now been made and delivered to me. It constitutes a trail-blazing study made in some depth and to a degree which I
believe to be unique. I regard this Report as of such stature and importa.nce th~t I a~prove and adopt it in its entirety, and have ordered
that it be printed in full and made available today to every constituent
Lodge.
The~e are two basic matters relating to this Report which I wish to
emphasize.

The .first is .that the Report does not attempt to prescribe any quick
and easy solution for those areas of Masonic practice with which the
Rep~rt deals. In. fact, the Report neither prescribes nor recommends any
specific change in our practices. The whole approach and philosophiy
of ~he Report has been - on the contrary - to identify and define a
s~ries. of Masonic practices which apparently need more enthusiastic
direction on the local level.
. The Commission's own statement on the nature of its Report makes
this very clear. It ·s ays:
"Th~ obje~ti~~ of the Commission in this present Report is in reality
to submit an initial set of facts and opinions concerning the state of
Freemasonr y in this Jurisdiction, to the end that full discussion and
further <Study may assist in formulating measures which will commend
themselves to the Craft for general acceptance. ''
. In my opinion, the Commission has succeeded superlatively in achievin~ this announced objective, and has produced what I am sure the Craft
will recognize as an objective and highly thought-pro voking work.
This leads me to the second basic comment which I wish to make on
the Commission's Report.
This comment is to call attention to the fact that it is now up to the
Craft, up. to every officer and up to every member, to familiarize themselves with the c~ntents of this Report, to discuss freely its many
references to possible courses of remedial action, and then to act with
courage and .imagination in experimenting with the uoSe of various
courses of actl?n a~ fits their own local conditions. Very few of these
courses of action involve any need for legislation by Grand Lodge,

36

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

almost all of them being of the nature which any Lodge can put into
operation by action of its Master, Officers and its members.
And lest there be any hesitancy in putting into immediate operation,
at least on an experimental basis, any or all of the courses of action
described in the Commission's Report which do not involve legislation,
I strongly urge that every Lodge in this Grand Jurisdiction feel both
free and obligated to ascertain by actual trial which of the various
courses of action may prove most effective. After all, the acid test of
any study is to subject it to experimental operation. Only then can we
find those measures which by their fruits will have proved their validity.
Given a year of such experimentation, the Craft may well be in a position next year to come to conclusions which might then be applied profitably throughout the entire Jurisdiction.
Finally, I express my earnest hope that the work of this Special
Commission will be continued, both to collaborate with the Lodges
throughout a year of experimental action in many directions, an~ to
develop and present to the Fraternity a fudher report upon areas of
Masonic practices in respect to which it has already gathered much
material.
To my Commissioners I express my deep gratitude for their unstinting devotion and distinguished service. They have done well the
extremely difficult task to which they were assigned.
And so, brethren, I close this accounting of my stewardship for this
past year, as your Grand Master, a year whose memories, thanks to all
of you, I shall always hold close to my heart.

PROCLAMATION- DEMOLAY WEEK
March 17-24, 1963
Roger Babson is quoted as having said: "The real safeguard of the
world's treasure is the character now being implanted in the young men
and women who will ·soon become its custodians - or despoilers." Many
forces are competing today for the minds and energies of our youth.
For California Masoncy, the Order of DeMolay offers a golden opportunity and a constructive plan to guide our youth along the road to
good citizenship and useful lives, and to become clear-thinking men
of good character.
DeMolay is founded on Masonic principles, and teaches love of
parents, belief in our Supreme Being and fidelity. In addition it promotes
comradeship. courtesy, dean living, patriotism and championship of our
public school system. The intrinsic value of DeMolay training is evidenced by the high percentage of former DeMolays who occupy positions of leadership - not only in Masonry, but in business and public
life.
Our Grand Lodge has adopted a policy of encouraging the development of this youth organization - indeed many of our Lodges now
sponsor and SUJ>port DeMolay Chapters in their communities. To those
Lodges desiring to have a part in building for the future, I suggest this
worthwhile opportunity : that of working with our vibrant young people.
Surely few opportunitie s are more rewarding! Individual members of
our Lodges can encourage DeMolay by assisting in the formation of new
Chapters when the need exists, and by supporting the whole program.
Therefore, to aid this most worthy activity, I hereby proclaim the
week of March 17-24, 1963, as DeMolay Week in this Jurisdiction, and
each Lodge is directed to give due notice of this Proclamation in its
March bulletin. I further direct that this Proclamatio n be read at the
February and March Stated Meetings.
Dated: January 22, 1963
Fraternally youm,
IRA w. COBURN
Grand Master
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

PROCLAMATION

PROCLAMATJON

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH

FORTY-FOURTH ANNUAL PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

"Blessed is the man who seeth his brother's need and supplieth it."
Our Masonic Homes Endowment Fund translates this thought into
positive action by the care of our cherished ones in the Home for
Children at Covina, and the Home for the Aged at Union City._ Through
our contributions to the Fund we are living our Masonic teachmgs. Our
love and concern reflect our thinking as Masons.
With living costs continuing to rise, and with the population of our
Homes increasing, the need is greater than it has ever been. A const~nt
growth of our Homes Endowment Fund will help in assuring our meeting
these growing needs as they develop.
Let each of us as Masons remember the many blessings we have received and enjoy. Let each of us strive to do more this year than ever
before. Let each of us show by his generous contribution that because
of these blessings we have "an understanding heart."
It is directed that this Proclamation be read at the April and May
Stated Meetings, and I urge that a copy hereof be sent to each of your
members.
Dated: February 1, 1963
Fraternally yours,
IRA w. COBURN
Grand Master
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

Alexander Pope wrote: "'Tis education forms the common mind;
as the twig is bent, the tree's inclined."
Generations ago our forefathers recognized the importance of a
free public schools system. Through the years our splendid system of
American public schools has grown in almost unbelievable fashion. It
has developed millions of boys and girls in the fundamentals of good
citizenship, love of freedom and pride of country.
The week of April 22-26, 1963, has been designated as "Public
Schools Week," and our theme for this forty-fourth annual event is:
"OUR PUBLIC SCHOOLS - SYMBOLS OF FREEDOM."
As individual Masons, and as citizens, we can and should occupy
ourselves with the perpetuation of this system. We should indeed consider ourselves as guardians of a sacred trust - remaining ever vigilant
- lest this heritage of our children be lost to those who have threatened
to "bury us."
In California, School Boards are practically autonomous. They
employ the adJDinistrators who employ the teachers who, in turn, directly affect our youth. We have a never-ending interest, therefore, in the
composition of these Boards. Let us take an active part in our respective
communities by electing those whose interests are compatible with our
historical freedoms, and let none of their actions go unobserved! Let us
interest ourselves, as citizens, in the year-round activity of our schools
and, as Masons, publicly display our concern by taking active parts
in our local observance of Public Schools Week.
I direct that only Stated Meetings or those for Public Schools Week
observance be held during Public Schools Week.
This proclamation is to be read at the Stated Meetings held in the
months of March and April, 1963.
Dated: February 15, 1963
Fraternally yom:~.
IRA W. COBURN
Grand Master

The United States Constituti on is one of the unique contributions
the American people have made to the art of government. In a profound
distrust of tyranny, it grants power hut also limits power. It will live
through the ages as our great charter of freedom. Born out of hardship
and sacrifice, it is the finest instrumen t of human liberty ever conceived.
This memorable document, the work of the Fathers of our Country,
was signed by thirty~nine rare and gifted men, twenty~three of whom
were known or believed to he Masons. It became the law of our land
on September 17, 1787 - just one hundred seventy~six years ago this
September. Today, when our great accomplishments as a Nation and
our system of governme nt are under world~wide scrutiny, the written
Constitution stirs the patriotism of every loyal American and fires the
imagination of the world.

Lodges or Districts, in conjunctio n with service clubs or other public
organizations. It is important that the Constituti on Observan ce be a
community event, under ·Masonic sponsor>Ship, with the public invited.

"IN QUESTI ONS OF POWER, LET NO MORE BE

EDICT

To the Constituent Lodges of the Grand Jurisdiction of California,
Free and Accepted Masons
In order to provide Cuban Masonic Brethren residing in California
with the opportunity to hold Masonic communication and visit Lodges
of this Grand Jurisdiction, I have directed the Grand Secretary to make
provision for these Brethren to pay their dues to him. This money will
be held in trust until such time as the Cuban Lodges and the Grand
Lodge of Cuba are again able to function, without outside in8uence,
as the Supreme Masonic authority in that jurisdiction, possessing all
the attributes of sovereignty and government - legislative, executive
and judicial - and limited only by a strict adherence to the Ancient
Landmarks of the Order and by the provisions of its own Constitution
and Regulations.
To qualify for payment of dues the Brother must:
1. Fill out a form, to be furnished on request by the Grand Secretary, entitled "Request for Acceptance of Dues in Trust for
The Most Worshipful Grand Logia de Cuba, A. F. & A. M."
2. Attach to this form his last dues receipt and present in person
to the Grand Secretary at 1111 California St., San Francisco 8.
3. Pay a sufficient amount, based on dues formerly collected by his
Lodge, to place him in good standing to the end of the current
calendar year (December 31, 1963).
4. In return he will receive a letter of acknowledgment signed by
the Grand Master, attested to by the Grand Secretary, stating
that his dues are paid to December 31, 1963. The original dues
receipt will be returned to the applicant.
In addition to the aforesaid requirements, any applicant desiring
recognition, admission to or affiliation with a California Lodge shall
also be subject to a complete, careful and thorough Masonic examination by a special committee of not less than three ( 3) members, said
committee to be appointed by the Master of such Lodge. It is pointed out
that an applicant must prove he is a Mason before he can visit a Lodge.
Hence, it is up to the examining committee to satisfy itself that the
applicant is qualified.
Should an applicant wish to pay Ms dues to a local Lodge, due to
the distance from San Francisco, he must:

49

a. Tender his last dues receipt and cash as outlined in steps 1 through
3 above to the Secretary of the local Lodge.
b. The Secretary will send it to the Grand Secretary, certifying that
he personally witnessed the signature on the application referred
to in step 1.
c. The Grand Secretary will make the proper record and return the
original dues receipt of the applicant with the letter of acknowledgment listed in step 4 above.
This Edict is to be read at the next Stated Meeting of all Constituent
Lodges in the Grand Jurisdiction of California after receipt hereof.
Dated: Maiy 10, 1963
Fraternally yours,
IRA W. COBURN

Grand Master
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

SUMMARY REMARKS BY ROBERT B. WATTS,
CHAIRMAN OF GRAND MASTER'S SPECIAL
COMMISSION ON MASONIC PRACTICES
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Past Grand Masters, Distinguished
Guests, and Members of the Grand Lodge:
In response to the invitation and direction of the Most Worshipful,
there are a few brief comments which I should like to make in behalf of
the Grand Master'·s Special Commission on Masonic Practices.
First of all is the expression of the Commission's deep gratitude for
the unive11sal enthusiasm and assistance which has been extended by the
entire Craft throughout the past year. To a considerable degree, the
Commission has been operating in uncharted areas of Masonic inquiry.
and has therefore particularly benefitted from your wise guidance and
cooperation.
Next, I should like to point out that the Commission's flrst report which has heretofore been flled and will be in your hands today - is not
a presentation of the theories or proposals of the Commission, but is, to
the best of our ability to make it so, an accurate reflection of facts relating
tu Masonic practices as California Masons see them - and a presenta-

50

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

tioo of multiple possible courses of action which, in the opinion of various
members of the Craft, would serve to improve those practices and
strengthen our beloved Fraternity.
One inevitable result of this characteristic of the Commission's report
is, therefore, that it will present no startling and heretofore unheard-of
suggestions. It is distinctly not a magic formula which, taken painlessly
after meals, will cure all or any of the current problems which beset our
Order. On the other hand, we believe that it does eliminate much guesswork and former speculation, and does lay out, in respect to a series of
important Masonic problems, speciflc alternative means of attacking
each problem, each of which alternatives has sufficiently commended
itself to many of our members to result in its inclusion in the Commission's report.
The Commission makes no selections among these proposals. It submits them for thought, for discussion and above all for actual experimentation by the various Lodges as they may choose. It believes that
this method of proof by trial is the surest means of flnding those new
approaches which by their success may then result in their general
adoption. Almost none of the proposed lines of remedial action require
legislation. Most of them may be put in operation at will by the officers
of Lodges or by simple action of the Lodges themselves. In short, the
Commission presents the leaders of the Craft with tools suggested by
their fellows - and leaves to them the selection and use of those tools
in their own Masonic labors.
Finally, the Commission wishes to say that its consultive services are
at the disposal of the Craft - both during this session, at Committee
Room No. 8 on the Registration Floor, and throughout the coming year
at your call. It is eager to see the freest possible experimentation by the
Lodges and equally eager to aid in such endeavors.
Most Worshipful, for myself and my fellow Commissioners, let me
thank you most sincerely for the wonderful opportunity and experience
which you have given us by having selected us for our task and by
having supported us as you have. We only hope that our performance
may reflect in some small measure the magniflcent vision and courage
with which you laid down the design upon the trestle-board, and that
the work which you have begun will long continue to the beneflt of
every Master Mason.

REPORT OF GRAND MASTER'S
SPECIAL COMMISSION ON MASONIC PRACTICES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
In his flrst message to the Craft, Grand Master Ira W. Coburn
sounded a tocsin which has electrifled the entire membership of the
Grand Jurisdiction of California. He said, "Freemasonry may be
likened to a reposing titan - a large body having a g·reat potential, but
not making full use of its inherent power. . . . How do we transform
this potential strength into a vigorous, positive, constructive and dynamic
fol"ce for good?" He then implemented his observation and question by
establishing directly under himself a Special Commission, charging
it with its mission in the following stirring words: "Now we must
take action. We must be alert and call to our assistance every Freemason - so that the real facts may be discovered which we hope will
make a valuable contribution to our future prosperity and growth." 1
Here was a bold design, drawn in sweeping strokes of great simplicity upon the trestleboard by a Master Craftsman who has implicit faith
in the capacity and readiness of his Masonic brethren to follow that
design in strengthening and further adorning the structure of Freemasonry.
And to this design, ever most careful always to remain inquirers and
not advocates nor partisans, the Special Commission on Masonic Practices has devoted itself continuously since its formation last October.
No written words can possibly convey adequately the extent to
which the Commission is indebted to the Craft for the magniflcent and
hearty cooperation which it has received in its largely unprecedented
search for facts, opinions and suggestions. From the most newly raised
Master Mason to the most experienced and distinguished Grand officer
and Past Grand officer, few indeed have been the brethren who have
failed to respond most willingly to aniy inquiry or request directed to
them by the Commission.
The Grand Secretary and his entire staff have been unceasing and
unstinting in making available to the Commission, often at real
sacriflce because of their own heavy burdens, the full resources of the
Grand Secretary's office, with its accumulated wisdom and experience
of many years.
Finally, but only that the last in mention may be the flrst in honor,
the Commission most gratefully acknowledges the enthusiastic support,
without which its task would have been hopeless, of the Grand Lecturer,
the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the corps of Inspectors.
With the aid of those mentioned, and with the active participation
Note 1. See Appendix "A" for details on the composition of the Special Commission.

52

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master and the Grand
Wardens, the Commission has undertaken to use every practical means
to ascertain what the entire Craft feels about the basic problems presented. There has never been put in question the soundness of Freemasonry;
the inquiry has been exclusively as to its practice in this Grand Jurisdiction.
In an attempt to secure otherwise unavailable statistics as well as the
opinions and suggestions of every present Master, the Commission pcepared a special questionnaire which went to everiy Master. And to
spot-check all other members, another and more general questionnaire
was prepared and distributed to ten persons (officers, members or
sojourners) in each Lodge. The tabulation and compilation of this huge
mass of material has been accomplished on a selective item basis for
purposes of the present report. 2 Further use of this data as it relates
to subject matters not discussed in this report will be made later.
Next, and in order to double-check on spot questionnaire results, the
Commissioners and their Associates have personally travelled all over
their Divisions, including Hawaii, and have conducted private interviews with members of a great many Lodges. While always confidential,
these interviews have at times been attended by officers of the Lodges
involved - a fact which has brought about concrete results which
will be discussed later. The information secured from these interviews,
supplemented by the contents of many letters sent to the Commission,
has been integrated with questionnaire results for the purpose of this
report. The Commission is of the opinion that the resulting combined
data presents a fair cross-section of the present thinking of the Craft. 8
The objective of the Commission in this present report is in reality
to submit an initial set of facts and opinions concerning the state of Freemasonry in this jurisdiction, to the end that full discussion and further
study may assist in formulating measures which will commend themselves to the Craft for general acceptance. The Commission therefore
makes no specific recommendations in this report for immediate action,

even though it believes that the facts which it is reporting may be highly
persuasive of experimental action on the part of many of the constituent
Lodges or of the Grand Lodge itself.
Nothing in its report is intended by the Commission as a personal
criticism of any individual or part of the Fraternity. To the extent that
critical comments are reflected, the reflection is the result of serious and
unbiased research and careful reporting and is offered as the starting
point for remedial action. The Commission most earnestly warns that
in its opinion there is no one sovereign remedy for such lack of Masonic
vigor as may now appear. The conditions which it will present are
relatively easy of identification but generally complex in contributing
causes and hence often complex in the remedial action required.
The Commission is delighted to report certain concrete results of
the Grand Master's program which have come about as the Commission
has proceeded with its work. The first and most thrilling is that practically the entire membership of the Fraternity in this jurisdiction is now
thinking and talking about their Masonic practices with tremendous
interest. This enthusiasm and quick response from the heart to the
Grand Master's call to bestir the sleeping giant is in itself convincing
proof of an aroused vitality which proves the basic soundness and
power of our Masonry.
Secondly, the Commission notes with the greatest satisfaction that
the Grand Master's challenge is being met with a surge of enthusiasm
and special activity on the part of Grand Lodge officers and Grand
Lodge Committees, all seeking means by which their several functions
can better serve the needs of the Craft. 4
Perhaps of even greater significance is the fact that without awaiting either the making of this report or the occurence of any formal
action resulting from it, many of the constituent Lodges are already
putting into operation various ideas with which they have come in
contact while working with the Commission. 5 Here again is proof of
the inherent strength of the Craft once it is aroused to the existence

The Commission is, however, convinced that the trends shown are accurate.

Moving on from this basic membership data, the Commission now
reports upon the major streams of opinions and suggestions of the
Craft which it has recorded. Actually. of course, problem areas and
suggested remedies do not exist in separate compartments without
interrelation. One problem area overlaps another, and both causes and
possible means of correction weave in and out of one and all. Yet for
convenience in study and discussion, a general presentation by categories
will be followed.
One keenly perceptive comment which perhaps might suggest a
tentative keynote to this presentation was voiced by one of our beloved
Past Grand Masters. He wrote that in his opinion the Craft "suffers from
some fraternal hardening of the arteries." And his views have been
repeated in one form or another wherever the Commission has gone.
Emerging from scores of Masonic practices complained of by the
Craft, and towering above many specific problems which it has engendered, is our practically universally recognized need of better leadership of the constituent Lodges.
A check of specific short-comings in our practices as reported by
both members and sojourners will show that a substantial number
actually require no legislative action to achieve remedies, but lie within
the power and practice of the Lodges and hence call for dynamic,
dedicated and experienced leadership on the part of Worshipful Masters.

56

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Under our Masonic law, the Master is the sole executive officer of the
Lodge. From him must come the constant energy, the active imagination
and the skillful administration which will put in motion the basic remedies
which the Craft seeks and has suggested. Given such leadership, the
Commission has seen dramatic instances of recovery and resurgence
of Lodges within a single year.
But the unpleasant fact is that in far too many cases the Fraternity
is no longer obtaining leaders of this caliber. No longer is our typical
Master a trained executive or outstanding professional man. All too
often he fails to command the recognition and respect of the community
as the local personification of Masonry. And in instance after instance
his woeful failure to sense and to respond to the needs of his members
and visitors stands at the root of apathy, atrophy and absenteeism.
The Commission has diligently sought to ascertain the reason for
this situation, and in general has found a dual response. The first, although perhaps the lesser, is the all too frequent casual selection of
junior officers - followed by an inertia which allows the passing years to
float such casual selectees into the East possessed only of the requisite
certificates of ritualistic proficiency. Clearly it would appear that our
practice should change from such inertia to active selection and repeated
evaluation. The best means of accomplishing this result would appear
to be insi-stence upon a procedure (now the rule but often ignored) of
single year tenure in appointive office, at least up to that of Junior
Deacon. Coupled with such clearly established and understood single
year tenure there is also room for liberal use of lower officers or sideliners to fill positions on a temporary and experimental basis. Given such
procedure, not only could more members participate in our ritual but
from the performances given a much more intelligent selection of junior
appointive officers could be made.
The second and clearly the more pronounced reason for failing to
secure good leadership (assuming it to exist within the membership)
is the unwillingness of the most capable leaders, typically hard-pressed
for time as successful men, to devote the number of years required to
move through all of the chairs. (The non-membership of such men in
the Fraternity will be discussed separately). Three remedial courses
to meet this objection have been suggested, one involving legislation,
the others not. Their common factor involves asking of a capable leader
fewer years of continuous service, and sharply lessening the demands
upon his time during such service.
The first is to shorten the "progressive line" to five years by simply
following the practice of regarding it as beginning with the Junior
Deacon. Thus an outstanding man could be assured that the over-all
time span of active service asked of him as a prospective leader of the
Lodge would be five years. And where such a man was not available
in a particular year, the selective and evaluative proceslS of choosing

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

57

junior officers would clearly indicate the best material for Junior Deacon
and the "progressive line." The Commission finds heavy sentiment
in support of this suggestion.
Significant support is also evidenced for the second suggestion. This
is that the present time demands upon the senior officers be sharply
curtailed. In part, these time demands arise from excessive degree loads.
To the extent that this is the case. one effective remedy (to be discussed
separately later in this report) appears to lie in the reduction of the sizes
of Lodges. In part, excessive time demands appear to stem from participation in collateral activities related to the Lodge (such as Temple
Associations) and in customary appearances and visitations with other
bodies - much of which could apparently be avoided by taking turns
in making really necessary appearances. And in large part, so far as the
tremendous present time demands on the Master are concerned, there
appear to be available such effective remedies as his virtual relief from
ritual by the device of "moving up" the line at the -start instead of at
the latter part of his year, and his ability to delegate substantial
administrative burdens by appointment of an assistant who could
supervise all committee activities.
The third suggestion which has been advanced comes from more
limited sources and would involve legislation. Briefly, it would constitute the "progressive line" as ritualistic specialists, and create the
new offices of Executive Officer and Deputy Executive Officer to handle
all matters of the Lodge other than ritual, except the opening and dos~
ing of stated meetings. 8 The proposal is, of course, designed to attract
highly capable executive leaders who would serve for only two years,
and perhaps also be made Past Masters upon the completion of their
management of the Lodge.
The Commission urges the most -serious study of proposals such as
these, for it is convinced that one of the most important things which the
Craft can do is to adopt new practices which will produce better and
better leaders.
The next universally recognized problem area, which in addition
to its own characteristics is closely related to our lack of adequate
leadership, emerges from the statistical information, for it consists of our
membership problem. In short, by what Masonic practices are we to
attract good (with emphasis upon the "good") and younger peti~
tioners for our degrees?
Opinion among the Craft is crystal clear at this point that we are
failing dismally and disastrously to inform the public of today what
Masonry is and what it stands for. Far worse than opposition, we face
wide ignorance of the very existence of our Fraternity.
Note 8. This is really not at all a new idea or device, but is regularly used in essence
in other Masonic organizations, including both the York and Scottish Rites.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

On every side, the Commission is reminded with deep regret that
our present restrictions are such as to cause us to shun meaningful
Masonic participation in the life of the communities in which our Lodges
are located. Participation as Masons in most public events is barred.
67 per cent of those whom we have contacted believe that this restriction
is a mistake and should be dropped. The public display of regalia is in
general forbidden. (Yet who has not been aware of the deep impact
made upon those few and fortunate communities where literally tens
of hundreds of Masons wearing aprons have paraded before the Grand
Lodge officers in full regalia en route to a cornerstone laying!) Again,
wherever the Commission has gone it has heard bitter complaints that
the Fraternity is both unreasonably fettered and still further isolated
from the public by the current rigid limitations against local fundraising by ordinary and generally accepted breakfasts and similar
lawful public affairs. Moreover, what are regarded widely as the now
somewhat hackneyed traditional State-wide observances are put in
question as having long since lost most of their public attraction. In
short, the belief is general that the public knows very little and hence
cares very little about the Fraternity and its aims and activities.
This leads naturally into the question of what can be done about this
public ignorance and apathy. And the equally obvious answer would
appear to lie in a concentrated and continued effort to tell non-Masons
about the things for which our Fraternity stands. An overwhelming
number of our members, 82 per cent of those queried. urgently request
such a campaign.

Commission inquiries as to why many of our members waited so long
before petitioning. Man after man reported that for yea11s he had wanted
to be a Mason, but had waited in vain for an invitation. 0 Many reported
that even when they had asked "what it took" to become a Mason they
had been brushed off because they had not in so maniy words said
that they wanted to petition for membership!
Obviously, these grievous misconceptions in the minds of Masons
can and should be dispelled by alert Lodge leadership. And almost
without exception the members contacted strongly urge that this be
done at once. Related to the removing of these misconceptions is the
matter of arousing the Lodges to a realization that their representatives,
as members of the Grand Lodge, can by appropriate resolution and
the exercise ~f ~heir heavy voting power, either eliminate or modify many
present restrictions which conflict with the opinions of the members of
the Craft.
Othe11s urge supplemental methods of improving the public appraisal
of the Fraternity. Many report with shame on ill-kept Lodge exteriors
and dirty and unkempt Lodge interiors and their resolution to correct
these c?nditions. Many urge the production by the Grand ·Lodge of a
professionally done color moving picture which might be widely shown
pub~icly to tell. the st~ry of Freemasonry. Many suggest the use of professional pubhc relations employees to aid in securing recognition in
n~ws .media. And others urge regular appearance of the Grand Lodge,
with its best orators, on television and personally in all parts of the
jurisdiction for major public programs without regard to ritualistic
procedures such as dedications or corner-stone ceremonies. All of these
areas of sugge!tion are, of course, directed to making the public aware
of the Fraternity, sympathetic with its objectives and desirous of participation in achieving those objectives.
The problem of attracti~g younger men, insofar as not covered by
the general approaches reviewed above, has occasioned much discussion. Proposals to lower the age limits of petitioners, while supported
by many, do not now appear to enjoy the support of more than 33% of
those contacted by the Commission. On the other hand, 91 % of those
queri~d. are strongly in favor of broadening and expanding the present
permissive areas for the financial assistance of both boys' and girls'
youth gro.ups. And many members sincerely offer the suggestion that
the llnanoal burden of petitioning (especially where young men are involve.d ). should be eased either by xeducing the fee for degrees or by
=:ittmg payment for the degrees in three or four installments, or by

58

One Past Grand Master expresses the point with great clarity. He
writes: "I know of nothing in the landmarks that, in my opinion, prohibits any of us from really boasting about Masonry to our friends
who are not Masons - telling them about what Masons have done
in the past for our country, and for other countries which have attained
freedom: what Masonry has done by way of Masonic charity: what
the teachings of Masonry are; what the relation of Masonry is to religion
- of our teaching of reverence for the Deity, our teachings of morality
for every man, and the many other things we may take pride in. I think
I can do all these things without violating the landmark on solicitation."
But the Commission has been startled to discover the extent to which
many of our members are firmly convinced that it is absolutely improper
and forbidden to discuss any aspect of Freemasonry with non-members,
including interested non-members who have requested basic information
as a preliminary to petitioning for membership.
An even more revealing and distressing current belief among large
numbers of the Craft is that they are likewise forbidden to inform nonMasons, even when asked directly, that Masonry invites and solicits
no members but requires the voluntary application of the potential

We come next to that which appears to be at once a major problem
and equally perhaps our greatest undeveloped asset - the sojourner.
There is, of course, no existing means by which any accurate count can
be made of sojourning Masons who have moved into this Grand Jurisdiction. Indeed, therein lies one large facet of the problem which
consists of locating them. The Commission believes it to be sufficient
and still valid to quote on this subject from P.G.M. Harold Anderson's
1957 message: "Even the most conservative Mason's estimate would
give California a Masonic population of sojourneM from other jurisdictions equal at least to the membership in our constituent Lodges, and
every passing day adds to that figure."
We are singularly fortunate that the tide of population flow has
for some time been in our direction and has brought vast numbers of
these brethren to our communities. And the energizing effect which
would result from bringing substantial numbers of them back into
active Masonry with us almost defies the imagination.
What, then, does the Commission find about our efforts to welcome
these sojourners and make them members of our Lodges? Bright spots
are found, but the general picture as of the time of this report is dismal.
An almost unbelievable 84 % of our Lodges report that they have no
organized program whatever to interest and recruit sojourners. Member
after member, in mounting scores, admit that they have never in their
Masonic career even invited a sojourner to affiliate with their Lodge.
And again, to the astonishment of the Commission, a widespread conviction has been found that it is unmasonic to even suggest to a sojourner
that he join a Lodge in his new home community!
When the Commission asked sojourners themselves, frank responses
were made as to why they had not affiliated in this jurisdiction. All too
many reported that they found our Lodges cold and apparently uninterested in them as individuals. Many were examined on a first visit and
then left without anyone with whom to talk. 10 And others were subjected
to such embarrassment in the course of examination that they were left
with deep resentment. Many of our members believe that the $25
required donation has kept sojourners contacted by them from affiliating,
and they would abolish the requirement. And many sojourners frankly
said that theior dues elsewhere were much lower than in this jurisdiction
and they saw no reason to increase their expenses by affiliating.
Such appear to be the present obstacles to obtaining greater numb~s
of affiliations, but such are the obvious potentials for growth and greatly
increased 1Masonic activity from such affiliations that the Commission
urges the most serious efforts of every officer and member to overcome
these difficulties and harmful practices.

The final major area upon which the Commission now presents the
results of its inquiries is that which may be generally described as the
problem of non-attendance. As was the case with other areas, neither
the causes nor the suggested remedial mea.sures are unrelated to the
over-all problem. Here again is to be seen the need for far better leadership; here again are found many of the results of our membership problems and pracHces.
Based upon statistics (unfortunately not wholly complete) .furnished
by Masters, as taken from Tilers' 1'egisters, the Commission has encountered a strange and thought-provoking phenomenon. This is that
average attendance in the constituent Lodges averages 39 at stated
meetings and 31 at degree meetings: and that by and large, attendance
varies little from these figures regardless of the size of the Lodge. In
other words, attendance is definitely not proportional to the size of the
Lodge.
What, then, lies behind this patent apathy? The Commission's findings in this acea are multiple.
To begin with, the sheer frequency of meetings in itself discourages·
regularly of attendance, especially where there is a high factor of
repetition of activity.
Secondly, the sincere desire of Master Masons to be a real part of
their Masonic group is all too often frustrated . .Men seek that warm
companionship which comes from being with others who are truly not
only .friends but brothers. They yearn to stretch and expand the circle
of their intimates. Yet very substantial numbers of members have told
the Commission that the sheer size of their Lodge makes these things
so impossible of achievement that they give up and stay home. Nor is
this feeling conifined to sideliners. More than one Past Master has conceded that there are large numbeM of his Lodge brethren whom he
doesn't even know by sight!
Asked for remedial suggestions, a strong majority of 72% urges
the limitation of the size of Lodges - the upper limit usuaUy suggested
being 500. It is hoped by most of those supporting this view that competent Grand Lodge authority might so endorse and support this
proposal as to bring about widespread voluntary action by the constituent Lodges in splitting off their excess membership and assisting
in the formation of new Lodges by them. If voluntary limitation were
not forthcoming, legislation on the subject is proposed.
Several distinct benefits are foreseen from such reduction in Lodge
size.
With fewer members, more peMonal friendship would follow. And
with a smaller Lodge, there might reasonably be expected a lessening
of the frequency of meetings - thereby lessening the burden on officers and em:oucaging better leadership.
Moreover, if such a limit of approximately 500 were placed upon

Note 10. Some Lodges report excellent results in overcoming failures to fraternize by
issuing large type name badges to all those present, including both members
and sojourners.

62

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

our present Lodge structure (ignoring some 55 Lodges which are
slightly over that figure) spectacular results would follow. There would,
for example, spring into existence some 102 new Lodges! (Presumably,
Masonic charity would relieve the Grand Master from the usual
requirements as to their institution and constitution). These new Lodges
would immediately create some 1224 officer opportunities, and at least
an equal number of new committee opportunities for non-officers. And
if general experience in other fields is equally valid in Masonry, it is
reasonable to expect a pick-up of new petitions and applications for
affiliations in each of the newly created Lodges. Obviously there are
policy and procedural problems involved, such as equitable divisions of
surplus funds and utilization of existing Temples, but these are matters
quite susceptible of solution if the basic suggestion commends itself to
the Craft.
Further to combat absenteeism, widely supported pleas have been
received for more social activity in and related to our Lodges. They ask
for more family dinners, dances, picnics and other "fun" times which
will provide a Masonic focus for their family life. They clearly evidence
a ·realization that the day of the traditional "men's house" has passed
and that those organizations (whether religious, fraternal or otherwise)
which reach out and interest the entire family group are the ones which
are strong and vigorous in our modern society.
Another, though doubtless lesser, reported cause of absenteeism is
said to be lack of adequate notice. Members say that a routine monthly
announcement is not enough. Many have wished that there might be
newspaper announcement of scheduled meetings, and for some reason
considerable members have the belief that such publication of the mere
time, place, and degree or stated meeting involved is violative of
Masonic law! Others urge Masonic bulletins at the entrances to communities, advising the traveler (and reminding the member) of the
time and place of Masonic meetings. There has appeared strong belief
that the names of candidates should appear in trestleboards, as per#
mitted in other jurisdictions, thereby encouraging .friends to attend.
And there is complaint that under our present system no effort is usually
made (even when previously specifically requested) to discover Masonic
friends of the candidate and advise them when he is to receive his
various degrees.
We come next to the deadly effect of poorly planned and awkwardly
conducted meetings. Member after member has explained his absence
from a Lodge which fails to start its meetings on time, which wallows
without control or direction through masses of inconsequential or un#
necessary trivia, which permits rambling and repetitive discussion by a
few brethren who insist upon continuous harangues, and which close
far too late. Apparently there is almost nothing so effective in driving
away members.
As its final - and perhaps most meaningful finding, the Commis#

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

63

sion reports that basically those queried are not really concerned with
such "competitive" factors as television, the theater, sports or ~e
'°mplexities of modern life as the causes of poor attendance ~t Masonic
meetings. Instead, their voices rise in a steady and most smcere plea
that their deep hunger for flesh and blood teaching of the great Masonry
truths be fed. The brethren know instinctively that lying beneath and
beyond all Masonic form, ceremony and symbol there are the universal
truths and the age#old wisdom which will give answers to the riddles
of life. They know that that which has attracted their predecessors and
forefathers to Masonry is a true means of understanding themselves
and their relationship to their Creator. They know that here they can
banish fear by acquiring unshakable faith. As one unknown author has
written, "Masonry redirects the attention of any thoughtful man to
the fundamental questions of his being and his destiny. Surely, he is
dull of soul whose spirit is not quickened by this experience, and whose
heart is not warmed by this great fellowship."
Yet today the brethren feel these teachings lacking. They miss
them. They yearn for them. And almost to a man, when asked what
their reaction would be if a regular but brief exposition of these matters
were presented at their Lodge, they reply that nothing could then keep
them from being present.
These truths which the brethren seek, Masonry possesses. These
truths it has taught through the centuries. And if we would reclaim
our heritage and regain the "vigorous, positive, constructive and dynamic
force for good" for which the Grand Master calls, we must find the
means by which to teach these truths again.
With these presentations of our Masonic practices and what
the Craft is seeking, we conclude the present recital of our findings.
If what we have been able to report throws light upon the path which we
seek, we rejoice. If it stimulates discussion and experimentation, we
applaud. And if, as we believe, it evidences the need for continued
inquiry and proposals and a search for the way by which to revitalize
Masonry's teachings, we await further instructions from the Grand
East.
Respectfully submitted,

PERMIT GRAND LODGE TO INVEST FUNDS WITH
INSURED SAVINGS & LOAN ASSN.

(3)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the constituent Lodges of California are allowed to
invest their funds in Insured Savings and Loan Associations, and
WHEREAS, the Investment Committee of Grand Lodge is deprived
of this privilege, and
WHEREAS, it is to the advantage of Grand Lodge to be allowed to
have the same privilege as the constituent Lodges and be allowed to invest the monies of Grand Lodge where they can earn higher dividends
than that now earned in banks, and
WHEREAS, we are constantly striving for conformity in our Ritual
and Law, and
WHEREAS our ordinances are not consistent concerning the consituent Lodges and Grand Lodge:
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that Article 246 of the California Masonic Code, Section 3, be amended by adding the following
sub-sections to be known as "C" as follows:
Savings Accounts in and Investment Certificates issued by a Building
and Loan Association or a Savings and Loan Association organized and
exi,sting under the laws of the State of California or of the State of
Hawaii, which is an Insured Institution as defined by Title IV of the
National Housing Act, and Shares issued by any such Association which
issued no Investment Certificates and which is an Insured Institution as
defined by Title IV, and Savings Accounts in and Shares issued by any
Federal Savings and Loan Association; but in the case of each Association onl.y to the extent that such accounts, Investment Certificates or
Shares, are insured by the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation.
Respectfully submitted,
CECIL M. PRIOR, Past Master, Lodge No. 673
WILLIAM C. KuNz, Past Master, Lodge No. 673
