CONTRIBUTIONS LEVIED UPON LODGE~
REVOLVING BUILDING FUND
(4)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, most Masonic Lodges, at their inception, are hampered
in their struggle for a Temple because the financial burden falls on a
few, and
WHEREAS, there are many older Temples in the State of California
which need remodeling or reconstructing and which are eyesores and
indeed a discredit to the Fraternity, and
WHEREAS, all Masonic Lodges are obliged to borrow from private
loaning institutions, thereby making their financial dealings known to
outsiders, and
WHEREAS, there would be more charters requested and granted
and established Lodges would flourish if it were not for the lack of
financial assistance, and
WHEREAS, Masonry in California is not growing at the rate at
which it should, and
WHEREAS, there are approximately 250,000 Masons in the State
of California who have obligated themselves to aid and assist each
other, and
WHEREAS, there has long been an ever-increasing need for the
establishment of a fund controlled by Grand Lodge whereby loans could
be made to qualif,ying Lodges for the purpose of Temple construction or
remodeling, now
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that each Lodge, whether
chartered or under dispensation, shall pay with its annual returns a contribution; in the form of a per capita tax, the sum of one dollar ( $1.00)
for each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of June 30th. That such
monies be set aside in the form of a California Masonic Lodge Temple
Building Fund to be administered by the Grand ·Lodge Committee on
Lodge Finance. That loans be made out of said Building Fund to the
various requesting Lodges at the discretion and at the arrangement of
said Committee.
It is our considered opinion that this Resolution, if adopted, will stimulate a healthy and rapid growth of Masonry in California.
Respectfully submitted,
ALBERT F. TOPHAM, Junior Warden, Lodge No. 788
JOHN EsTERAH, Master, Lodge No. 788
F. LEE RABY, Master, Lodge No. 24
ROBERT D. LAKE, Master, Lodge No. 689
THAINE McKrn, Past Master, Lodge No. 788
GUILFORD J. WHITEHEAD, Senior Warden,
Lodge No. 788
Ref erred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purposes, on Finance, and on Lodge Financing.

IN CONSOLID ATION CONFER TITLE PAST MASTER
(14)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, Section 490 of the California Masonic Code provides
that the title of Past Master applies to one " ... who has been regularly
elected or na~d in a charter and installed and has served a term as
Master ... ". And as further provided in paragraph "d": "A Master
must serve to the end of his term to be a Past Master ... ", and
WHEREAS, there is provision for this title to apply to a duly qualified Master, elected in mid-year, and completing his term, ( 490e). and
WHEREAS, there is further proviision for this title to apply to a
Master who dies in office without completing his term, ( 490 - 1962
Supp.), and
WHEREAS, 490d further provides that, "If he resigns during his
term he loses that title.", and
WHEREAS, there is no definition in the California Masonic Code
of the word "term" in connection with tenure of offi.ce terminated by the
consolidation of Lodges, and
WHEREAS, in connection with the consolidation of Lodges one
Master may not be reelected, since his "term" has been completed by
the extinction of his Lodge, but
WHEREAS, the Master, reelected, will qualify under Section 490e,
and
WHEREAS, delay of consolidation to the end of the normal end of
year, and term, in order to protect the rights of the non-surviving Master, deprives the Lodges in this degree of the financial economies and
other benefits inherent in the consolidation,
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that Section 490 of the California Masonic Code be amended as follows: "The un-reelected Master
of a consolidated Lodge shall become a Past Master of the consolidated
Lodge, providing he has served more than half of the term for which he
was originally elected."
Respectfully submitted,
W. F. POYNTER. Past Master, Lodge No. 640
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the custom of refusing admission to a physically imperfect applicant came to be developed during the old days of operative
Masonry, when the work on the erection of stone edifices was both
arduous and hazardous, and a physically impaired workman constituted
a danger to himself and to his fellow workers, and liable to become a
burden to his Lodge or Guild, and
WHEREAS, we no longer work in operative Masonry but speculative only, these physical requirements are now obsolete, and
WHEREAS, there are many worthy and well qualified men who
have been wounded, maimed, or otherwise physically disabled in the defenise of our country in its wars, and others similarly worthy and well
qualified who, through misfortune or tragedy have also become physically disabled or maimed, and who are literally unable to comply with
the physical requirements of our laws and are therefore denied participation in our privileges, and
WHEREAS, numerous Masonic jurisdictions around the world,
with whom we are in Fraternal accord, have seen fit to modify or entirely eliminate this old operative principle from their present speculative
practices, without detriment to the Craft, and without incurring the displeasure of the rest of the Masonic world, and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of California has never officially
taken into its Masonic Law the twenty-five principles that Albert G.
Mackey tried to establish as "The Landmarks" (pages 342 and 343
CMC). nor has it established any specific set of Landmarks of its own,
and this question of the physical qualifications is therefore not affected
by the possible question of "The Landmarks," and
WHEREAS, it is now one of our basic and universally accepted
teachings and precepts that it is the internal and not the external qualifications that recommend a man to be made a Mason,
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 511 (not including sub-paragraph s a to q inclusive) of the California Masonic Code be
rescinded and the following substituted therefor:
"511. Moral and physical qualifications. An applicant for the degrees of Masonry must be a man; no woman nor eunuch: free born,
being neither a slave nor the son of a bond woman: a believer in God
and a future existence; of good moral character, capable of reading,
writing, learning the arts, and able to conform, with assistance or demonstration if indicated, to what the several degrees respectively require
of him. In the event that a candidate is unable to physically execute or
perform acts prescribed in the various degrees, the conferring Lodge is
vested with the power and authority to assist the candidate, either actu-

78

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ally, by demonst ration, or other appropri ate means, to perform or
execute those physical requirem ents which his disability prevents him
from performi ng or executin g without such assistanc e or demonst ration.
Any prosthes es usually worn, carried, or used by a candidat e, for his
safety, comfort, physical improvem ent, well being, or necessity , shall be
permitte d to be worn, carried, or used during the conferrin g of the
degrees. "
BE IT FURTH ER RESOL VED. that Section 512 and all subparagrap hs thereof, of the Californ ia Masonic Code be rescinde d and
the following substitut ed therefor:
"512. Sound discretio n required . The question as to the applican t's
ability to conform, in accordan ce with Section 511, to what the several
degrees respectiv ely require of him, shall be left to the sound discretio n
of the Lodge and the Lodge only."
BE IT FURTH ER RESOL VED, that all other reference s to physical sufficiency or physical qualifica tions for the degrees, containe d in
our laws, rules, regulatio ns, edicts, decisions , or any other matter on this
subject, written or unwritte n, having the force of law, be rescinded .

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Ordinance 545 of the California Masonic Code stipu~
lates that, "Such examination shall be held in front of the East.", and
WHEREAS, " ... in front of the East," can only be 'interpretated
to mean between the Altar and the Worshipful Master, and
WHEREAS. when examining candidates in this location, it is diffi~
cult to hear candidates' responses in the West, especially with cooling
and heating equipment in operation, now therefore
BE IT RESOLVED, that the last sentence of Ordinance 545, to
wjt: "Such examination shall be held in front of the East," be changed
to read: "Such examination shall be held with the candidate facing the
East." This would allow locating the candidate between the Altar and
the Senior Warden.
Respectfully submitted,

NOTICE TO DELINQUENT MEMBER
(20)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section No. 579 C.M.C. requires the Secretary to
notify any member who has refused or neglected to pay his regular dues
during a period of twelve months, and
WHEREAS, this section requires that the notice be sent either by
certified or registered letter to the last known address and deliverable to
addressee only, and
WHEREAS, in the majority of cases the member is not at home and
the letter cannot be delivered, thus resulting in it finally being returned
to the sender, now therefore
BE IT RESOLVED, that Section No. 579 C.M.C. be amended by
striking out the word "only" in line four ( 4) which follows that part of
sentence reading "deliverable to addressee" and adding thereto the
words "or his representative." This line will then appear as follows,

in the U. S. Post Office."

WEARING OF MASONIC CLOTHING (21)

FUNERAL

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 328c of the California Masonic Code directs
that at meetings the officers should wear aprons indicating their rank or
office, and
WHEREAS. Section 605 of the California Masonic Code directs
that the Master may call the members of his Lodge together at a place
designated for a funeral and there put on the proper regalia and conduct the funeral. and
WHEREAS, Section 605f of the California Masonic Code, in conflict with Section 328c and the wording "proper regalia" of Section 605,
indicates that officers at a funeral can only wear white aprons and not
aprons or jewels indicating their rank or office, and
WHEREAS, funeral services are considered a legitimate activity of
our Lodges and for which a proper ceremonial is provided it is only
fitting that these services be conducted in the best Masonic manner possible by the wearing of aprons and jewels indicative of the officers conducting the funeral services, and
WHEREAS, other organizations, fraternal and otherwise, always
make use of their proper regalia to the edification and inspiration of
members and non-members alike, we as Masons should likewise be
proud of our regalia and proud to display it when the proper occasion
presents itself,
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED. that Section 605f of the California Masonic Code be rescinded and that our Funeral Ceremonial be
changed to instruct the Master, Chaplain and Marshal to wear their
proper jewels and aprons indicating their offices while conducting funeral services for a deceased Brother.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM C. KuNz, Past Master, Lodge No. 673
CEaL M. PRIOR, Past Master, Lodge No. 673
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purposes, and on Ritual.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Ledge F. & A. M. of California:
WHERAS. California Masonic Bodies and Organizations are permitted to identify the buildings housing such organizations by use of
appropriate Masonic emblems, or names, and
WHEREAS, ownership and custody of these buildings are permitted to change hands, and
WHEREAS. such future use may not be compatible with Masonic
teachings, principles, and .gtandai'ds, and
WHEREAS. the Grand Master of Masons for the State of California is responsible for the action. conduct and impressions given by all
Masons under his jurisdiction,
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED. that it shall be the
duty of the Grand Lodge of Masons for the State of California, under
the direction of the Grand Master or his duly appointed assistant. to see
that all identifying names, insignia, and emblems are removed or obliterated from such buildings before ownership or custody is permitted to
pass from the Masonic Body responsible, and be it
FURTHER RESOLVED. that every effort be exerted by the
Grand Lodge to obtain permission from the owners of buildings now
displaying such emblems or identifying marks and no longer housing
Masonic Bodies to remove same at the expense of the Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,

CHARITA BLE FUND BOARD OF CONTRO L
(32)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
RESOLVE D, that there is hereby established a separate fund of
this Grand Lodge, which fund shall be known as "Boards of Relief
Charitable Fund," and which is hereby created, and shall be operated
exclusively for charitable purposes. and which may be allocated among
the several Boards of Relief organized and operating for charitable purposes pursuant to the California Masonic Code, but which funds shall
be kept separate and apart fa-om the other funds of this Grand Lodge.
RESOLVE D FURTHER . that this Grand Lodge will accept, hold
and administer any gift, grant, devise, or bequest made to said fund,
subject to the terms and conditions of this resolution;
RESOLVE D FURTHER . that said fund, and the proceeds and
income therefrom, shall be administere d and distributed by the Grand
Master and Treasurer of this Grand Lodge, subject to the direction and
control of this Grand Lodge. pursuant to the terms and conditions of
this resolution;
RESOLVE D FURTHER . that the Grand Master and Treasurer of
the Grand Lodge shall maintain separate books and accounts for said
fund: that no part of the net earnings of said fund shall be used for the
benefit of any officer, trustee, member of, or individual associated with
this Grand Lodge; that no part of said fund shall be used for carrying
on propaganda or otherwise attempting to influence legislation or for
participation or intervention, directly or indirectly. in any political campaign on behalf of any candidate for public office;
RESOLVE D FURTHER . that this Grand Lodge shall have the
power, with respect to the assets of said fund or any part thereof, and
upon such terms and in such manner as it may deem advisable, to retain
in the fund, for such time as it may deem advisable, any property received by it; to manage, operate, control. sell, convey, exchange, partition, divide, subdivide, improve, repair: to grant options and to sell upon
deferred payments; to invest and reinvest the principal. and income if
accumulated, and to purchase or acquire therewith every kind of prop-

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

erty, real. personal or mined, and every kind of investment it may deem
advisable; and to compromise or otherwise adjust any claims against or
in favor of the fund; to commence or defend such litigation with respect
to the fond or any property of the fund, at the expense of the fund; to
borrow and lend money for any fund purpose, to encumber of hypothecate by mortgage, deed of trust, pledge, or otherwise, and with respect
to securities held in the fund, to vote, give proxies, and pay assessments
or other ,c harges, to participate in foreclosures, reorganizations, consolidations, mergers, and liquidations, and incident thereto, to deposit securities with and transfer title to any protective or other committee upon
such terms as this Grand Lodge may deem advisable, and to exercise or
sell stock subscription or conversion rights; and the Grand Lodge shall
have such additional powers as may now or hereafter be conferred upon
it by law or as may be necessary to enable it to administer this fund in
accordance with the provisions of this resolution and subject to any
limitations thereof that may be provided for herein;
RESOLVED FURTHER. that distribution and application of the
income of said fund and of such portions of the principal thereof as may
from time to time be available for such distribution and application, shall
be made from time to time exclusively to or for the benefit of relieving
the distress of visiting Masons, their widows and orphans, by the
Boards of Relief of constituent Lodges of said Grand Lodge which, pursuant to the California Masonic Code, thus administer and pay the
expenses of the said charitable activities, subject to the direction and
control of the Grand Lodge; that no part of the assets of said fund shall
be expended, upon dissolution or otherwise, in payment of the general
obligations or expenses of this Grand Lodge; and that the property of
said fund shall be and is hereby forevocably dedicated to charitable purposes, and upon the liquidation, dissolution, or abandonment of the
fund, shall not inure to the benefit of this Grand Lodge or any private
person, but upon such liquidation, dissolution, or abandonment, all the
property of the fund shall be transferred to the Endowment Fund of
Masonic Homes of California, or its successor, organized and operated
exclusively for charitable purposes, and if there be no successor, then to
a fund, foundation or corporation organized and operated for charitable
purposes.
Respectfully submitted,
ARTHUR DvoRIN, Past Master, Lodge No. 639

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Herewith is my Third Annual Report as Grand Treasurer.
Attached will be found all of the financial reports and audits of the
Grand Lodge, Masonic Homes of California and the California Memorial Temple.
To fully appreciate the ever increasing size of the financial operations
of the Grand Lodge and its components, I urge the membership to give
strict attention to the material contained in the various schedules.
APPROPRIATIONS AND DISBURSEMENTS
All appropriations and disbursements have been carefully reviewed
by the professional auditors Lybrand, Ross Bros. and Montgomery,
C.P.A.'s as provided in Section l 94CMC.
Detailed records and vouchers are on file in the office of the Grand
Secretary.
SUPPLEMENTAL APPROPRIATIONS
. Last year the Finance Committee presented what they termed a
tight budget and the various Boards and Commissions are to be commended for their strict compliance with its provisions. The Grand Secretary has done an outstanding job in getting full measure for every
dollar expended and his careful attention to detail has saved a sizeable
sum for the Grand Lodge.
A number of items were most difficult to estimate and as a result
nine supplemental appropriations were approved by the Grand Master'.
They are listed below for reference.

CovELO LODGE No. 231
On October 31, 1962, Covelo Lodge No. 231 lost their Temple in
a fii'e which destroyed most of the Lodge records and other possessions.
This is the third time that the Lodge lost its hall and records - once
shortly after it was organized, in 1873, again in 1903 and in 1962.
It was necessary to replace the charter for the third time. In the
absence of a photostatic copy of the charter of Covelo Lodge the present form of charter was completed with the information available.
The Grand Master was Isaac Sutvene Titus and the Grand Secretary was Alex G. Abell.
An appeal was made in the Winter issue of the California Freemason for furniture and equipment. The response was overwhelming and Covelo Lodge had offers of far more than they could use.
The Chairman of the Charters Committee was advised of extra paraphernalia and equipment available for possible use by new Lodges.

98

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The basis for limiting the remission of dues to those cases where
such action is really justified lies, again, in following a program of more
careful investigation of each case. Avoid all those instance~ where
remission is voted, year after year, simply because the brother mvolved
was the basis for ,such action in the previous year. The Lodge cannot
afford to sacrifice dues income simply because a precedent has been
previously voted.
. .
.
.
The type of remission which is more subject to un~u~ttfi~d action ts
that taken under special provisions of Section 577-re~1ss1on •? advance.
While this section allows the Lodge authority to remit dues m advance
in two types of cases, members who have belonged in this jurisdiction
for forty or more years and members who have reached the . a~~ _of
seventy-five and have rendered special service to the ~dge •. ehg~b1hty
for such type of remission is still limited by the condition cited m the
first paragraph of the section: "those of its members who are unable to
pay."
This limiting factor is frequendy misunderstood. Its impoi:t ~as
clearly stated in a 1955 decision approved at the Annual Commumcatton
and set forth in annotation "h" of Section 577:
"It is a violation of our law to relieve a Mason of the duty to pay
dues merely because a certain number of years has been satisfied. The
provisions relating to 40-year Masons and 75-Y_ear old ~asons were
intended for distinguished service and to be applied only m thos~ ma~­
ginal cases where there may be ability to pay but where a hardship still
would be worked. A man should consider it a high privilege to help
bear the cost of his own Lodge and of the Grand Lodge, and thus make
his contribution toward the onward march of Masonry."
It should be borne in mind that the basis for any remission should
be the financial situation of the member and that the remission of such
dues in advance only constitutes an additional court~sy_ to a .m~m~er
who has satisfied the conditions of forty year membership m the JUrtsd1ction or of having attained the age of seventy-five.

Financial Aspects
.
. .
The comments made with reference to Suspension and Rem1ss1ons
have been presented from the standpoint of numbers involved a_nd
remedial steps available. An additional consideration is the results which
affect the entire membership of each Lodge involved.
Each case of an unwarranted suspension or remission places an
additional financial burden on the Lodge itself and on its dues parying
members. While it is true that the Lodge does not pay per capita on
the members who were suspended, or whose dues were remitted under
the qualifying conditions, this amount is small as compared with the
income the Lodge would have received from a brother who was continued as a dues paying member.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

99

For the jurisdiction as a whole the average dues specified in the
By-Laws is approximately sixteen dollars. After deducting from this
amount of specified dues the amount saved in per capita, we find that
the net loss to the average Lodge in each case of unjusti'fied action
amounts to approximately twelve dollars and a half.
Last year the net loss by suspension was 1060 and the number for
whom dues were remitted was 3515, a total of 4575. If we are conservative and assume that two-thirds of these cases represent justified action
we still find a total net income to the Lodges of nineteen thousand
dollars which could have been realized with proper understanding of
the regulations, proper investigation and limiting action to justifiable
cases. Without doubt there are cases where following proper procedure
would have avoided the necessity for the Lodge increasing the amount
of its annual dues.

Forfeiture of Fees and Contributions
This is another area in which there seems to be a degree of indifference. Such indifference is the basis for not attaining the number of new
members which would become potential if our candidates were fully
dedicated to the principles which Masonry emphasizes. The new method
of enabling the coaches to more effectively explain Masonry to the
candidates will undoubtedly result in decreasing the number of forfeitures. The Grand Lecturer and the other members of the Ritual
Committee have provided a very effective toll for accomplishing this end.
We are continuing the survey of candidates which was referred to
in my report last year. The required forms have been sent to all the
Lodges. The completion of the task will depend upon the promptness
with which the answers are returned to our office.
From the information developed bry this survey it appears that over
four thousand men who have been elected to receive the degrees, and
who have had one or two of the degrees conferred upon them, are now
subject to the procedure leading to forfeiture. Picture the beneficial
results, both as to increased membership and increased dues income,
which could result from a program of instilling in half of those indifferent candidates the same enthusiasm which led them to present their
original applications for the degrees.
Here, as in the handling of suspensions and remission of dues,
personal interviews with the men involved could well provide constructive answers as to the future of Masonry in this jurisdiction.

CONCLUSION

Since submitting the editorial portion of this ·report for printing. two
matteM have come to my attention which I feel should be reported to
Gr~nd Lodge.
.
.
In accordance with the Grand Masters Edict of May 10, 1963, rela~
tive to Cuban Masonic Brethren, the Grand Secretary has now accepted
dues from three members of Cuban Lodges. The funds are held in trust,
and the money is placed in a savings account. I am happy to report that
one of these members has now affiliated with a California Lodge.
On October I. 1963, Grand Master Ira W. Coburn approved the
consolidation of Jonathan Lodge No. 545 and Veritas Lodge No. 640.
All requirement s of the law respecting consolidation does not become
effective until December 1, 1963.

Grand Secretary
Ref erred to Committee on Distribution.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTUR ER
To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
As this report was in preparatio n, the Grand Lodge lost, through
death, one of its ablest and most dedicated members, Worshipf ul Ralph
W. Collins, who passed away July 23, 1963. Honor will be done him on
Wednesd ay morning during the Necrology service. The Grand Master
has appointed Worship Robert A. Crigler, a Past Master of John
Marshall Lodge No. 636, and Inspector of District No. 5.90, as the
successor Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division V.
This has been a year of advance in the practice of Masonry in this
jurisdiction. Advance in the perfection of the ritual is important, for
without it, we would have no foundation in Masonry. I can report to
you that, with few exceptions, the ritual as portrayed by our lodges, is
the envy of other jurisdictions. This comes about by reason of the
system of lodges in districts, districts in divisions, and, over it all, a
spirit and desire on the part of you Masters and Wardens to excel. The
total of schools held by Inspectors for the lodges numbers many hundreds and the number of divisional schools held by the Assistant Grand
Lecturers will number several dozen. Each of the Assistant Grand
Lecturers. at the annual conferenc e of his division, then reviews the
work under the eye of the entire Ritual Committee and, finally, on
Saturday, October 12, the Grand Lecturer, with all Inspectors present,
holds his annual school.
Divisional Conferenc es were held on the dates and at the lodges
shown. M,y thanks to the brethren of these lodges for making their
facilities available.

The fact that this is a lodge and district program with great flexibility is now very apparent. Reaction has ranged from apparent apathy
to great enthusiasm. Apathy is apparent in those lodges and those districts where leadership is lacking. Neither geography , nor age, nor the
size of a lodge need be a factor. Leadership and enthusiasm go together.
But, let the districts speak for themselves. The enthusiasm shows in the
following reports from a cross-section of districts up and down the
State. The leadership is apparent in each case.

GENERAL REVIEW

Ten days after the close of the Grand Lodge Communication last
year, the sad news went out from our Grand Secretary's office that the
Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes had lost its one remaining
emeritus member, Most Worshipful Charles M. Wollenberg. Grand
Master in 1929. With the passing of this venerable brother at age 89,
California Masons lost one of their most devoted and loyal servants who
had served our Homes Board .for over a half century. 39 years as its
President. Our Necrology Committee will pay him due homage in their
report later in this communication. but we of the Board of Trustees want
to express our appreciation not only for his years of service, but for the

125

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

solid foundation which was laid during his leadership, upon which we
are still building. We shall always revere his name and his memory.
On February 14, 1963, the resignation of Trustee George D. Gavin
was received in order that he might continue to serve the craft in a new
capacity as Manager of this California Masonic Memorial Temple.
While his service on the Homes Board was relatively brief, we miss his
devoted activity. As of the same date the Grand Master appointed Past
Grand Master Alf red F. Breslauer to fill the vacancy and the Board
welcomed this talented brother who had been serving as our legal
advisor.
We wish to thank the several Board of Relief Managers who have
made preliminary investigations for us in connection with applications of
children of out of state Lodges. This is no easy task and these busy
brethren have cheerfully complied with out requests for assistance, and
their excellent services have been vei;y much appreciated.
We should like to again stress the importance of the preliminary
investigations required of the Lodges before filing a formal application
for admission to either Home. While we do not ask the Lodge committee
to pre-judge the case, the decision of course resting with the Trustees,
yet at the same time we feel that too many applications are filed which
obviously do not meet our entrance requirements of a financial need, and
in the case of oldsters - the requirement of being in satisfactory physical
condition and being ambulatory. Many miles are traveled by our two
Social Workers in making some of the investigations and this entails a
substantial expense which oftentimes could be saved by a proper preliminary investigation by the Lodge, together with a more complete understanding of our rules for admission. Your careful cooperation in this
respect will save the Homes Board both time and money.
We also remind you again that when your Lodge has the continuing
burden of helping to support a brother or his family who are not eligible
for admission to our Homes, an application for outside relief is always in
order. By outside relief is meant monthly financial assistance to the
Lodge by the Homes Board, where the Lodge is obligated beyond its
means in the care of a brother or his family. These cases, however,
should be just as carefully investigated by the Lodge as an application
for admission, and our investigation also will be just as thorough, including a check-up on the finances of the applying Lodge. You may be
interested to know that at present we are assisting 21 Lodges in their
permanent relief cases outside the Homes.

lovely young ladies were all interviewed by the entire Board of Trustees
and where needed and when requested were given scholarship assistance
for their further education.
You may recall that two years ago legislation was adopted to permit
the Trustees in their judgment to admit to our home Masonically affiliated children of other jurisdictions under proper circumstances and
limitations. You may be interested to know that since the approval of
these new regulations six such children have been admitted.
As some of you old-timers may remember, we at one time owned a
site on Balboa Island which was used as a permanent summer camp for
our Covina children. Since the disposal of this site many years ago, we
have been hoping that we could at some time acquire another location
for summer camp purposes. Your Trustees have made trips to see
various suggested locations at both the beach and the mountains but
until now without success. We are happy to say, however, that we are
now in negotiation with a wealthy gentleman - a non-Mason incidentally - who has a very well located mountain camp which he desires to
give us, and we have been told by his attorney that we can fully expect
to be in possession of the property in the very near future.
In our reports to you for the past two years we have also indicated
our desire eventually to acquire a new site for our Children's Home and
you have by the unqualified acceptance of our reports agreed that the
Board had the authority with the concurrence of the elected Grand
Lodge officers to do whatever was necessary to accomplish this end.
After investigating numerous ,sites we are now carrying on negotiations
which we feel hold great promise and if consumated will provide us with
an ideal location for a modern and flexible facility for our youngsters.

COVINA

Whereas in 1961 we reported a population in our Children's Home
of 38, and in 1962 a total of 49, this year has been an active one and as
of the end of our fiscal year, June 30, 1963, we have 55 children as our
guests after graduating four of our high school senior girls. These four

UNION

CITY

Last year is was reported to you and those of you who went to our
oldsters' home in Union City saw, that we had started construction on
three new buildings, two dormitories for our male employees and another
containing apartments for our employed married couples. We are glad
to report that these new accommodations have been in use since early
spring and have added greatly to the contentment of our employees and
materially reduced our labor turnover.
We can report demolition of the old employees' quarters. The ground
will be used to enlarge our parking area. The old hospital or infirmary,
which since the building of our new hospital has been condemned for
use by our guests, has also been demolished and there is now appearing
on the site a new dormitory to be called the Charles Albert Adams Hall
in memory of our late lamented and beloved "Charlie." This building
will be used to house our married guests and also to provide additional
rooms for those who may require some supervisory attention.
We are most grateful to have as the Vice President of this Board

126

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Past Grand Master "Pete" Anderson, who by profession is an engineer.
With all of the building activity that we have been engaged in during
the past several years as well as that contemplated in the future, his
dedicated services to this Board have been invaluable. His personal
interest in and supervision of every aspect of our building program is
something that cannot be purchased with money, and to him we are all
very grateful.

FINANCES

While our guest population in Union City is near its all-time peak,
we have at the moment a number of vacant rooms for both men and
women. The chief reason for this is that our permanent hospital population is at an all-time high. Our hospital of course was built for the
need of those guests who after some years of residence in the Home come
to that point where hospital confinement seems necessary. Our admission requirements to the Home still require that the applicant be ambulatory and in reasonably good physical condition, but we have had many
cases in the past year where the favorable condition of the applicant, as
reported in the application, was not supported in fact. upon aorrival at
the Home. In a number of cases the guest was taken right into the hospital although there was nothing in the application to indicate any
untoward physical condition. This has caused us to overflow our new
hospital on several occasions although it was contemplated that its
capacity would not be taxed for several years at least. It has also increased our hospital costs out of all proportion.
For these reasons we must now require in ·some instances that the
applicant be required to be examined by a physician of our designation
so that we may have a complete and unbiased report. upon which to base
our decision for acceptance or denial.
Another problem confronting us has to do with application from
couples. It appears that since we announced a new dormitory for
couples. we have had a great inc·r ease in couple applications. We have
processed these applications in the usual manner and have acted upon
some of them, and presently five couples are waiting for accommodation s,
and we have quite a number of additional couple applications pending.
In one or two cases, due to the long wait for an apartment, one of the
couple became physically ineligible before a vacancy occurred, and this
was upsetting to everyone concerned. We must now announce that
applicants will only be investigated at the time we have accommodation s
for them.
To complicate the problem the Board has approved two marriages
between our guests during the past year and of course these folks anticipate an apartment also.
We hope of course that our new dormitory now under construction
will make it possible for us to eliminate all waiting lists.

127

It is an old story but one that we must repeat again. The cost of the
operation of our Homes is increasing. This is due to many factors
beyond our control, among which are increased labor costs, number of
guests, number of hospital patients. obsolescence, repairs, etc .. to say
nothing of general inflation.
To offset this in a great measure we have several factors working in
our favor. First of all we have our Homes Endowment Board which
each year raises more and more money for our Permanent Endowment
Fund. Their record this year of over $740,000 is a new high and the
income from this sum replaces to a great extent the loss of income from
our reserve funds which we are now using for building purposes. To
every member of the Board - our profound thanks for your valuable
service to the fraternity.
The Investment Committee under the direction of our most capable
Assistant Grand Ti'easurer also makes an invaluable contribution to our
welfare in keeping our funds soundly invested and frequently realizing
capital gains in addition to an excellent over-all interest return.
And last but by no means the least, we express our gratitude to the
dozens of brethren who named the Masonic Homes in their wills to
receive substantial amounts - oftentimes their entire estate. These gifts
are allotted, unless otherwise devised, to our various reserves which make
possible our building program.
· As you know, the balance of our funds come from two sources, the
$25 fees paid by each new applicant and affiliate and the per capita tax
on the Lodges. New applications are not coming in as fast as formerly
and the total membeI'Ship statewide is almost at a standstill, so that these
sources of funds are not keeping up with the inflationary trend. The
time may come when we might suggest raising the $25 fee to $30, and
the per capita on the Lodges may soon have to be increased. Your Board
of Trustees. however. is most anxious to defer action on both of these
matters as long as possible, and we therefore recommend a continuation
of the $1.00 per capita tax for the use and benefit of the Masonic Homes
of California for the next fiscal year, the same amount as has been in
effect since 1960.
CONCLUSION

The management of each of our Homes is literally a 24-hour-a-day
job and one that requires not only ability in many lines but also a world
of tact. understanding and patience in dealing with many types of
people with greatly varying backgrounds.
Our fraternity may count itself most fortunate to have as the Superintendent of each of our Homes a Past Master of this jurisdiction. Each of
them is ideally suited to his position and gives unstintingly of his time
and effort, assisted in each case by an understanding wife. to maintain

128

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

our Homes on the high standard to which we have all become accustomed; and to these dedicated brothers the Board expresses its deep
appreciation. Their respective reports appended to this report will give
at least some indication of their manifold activities.
We wish, too, that we could pass on to you some of the intimate
letters we receive from guests and their families expressing appreciation
for the care and attention given to both our youngsters and our oldsters.
They are heartwarming to say the least and indeed compensate your
Board for the hours of time devoted to this great charity of ours. Each
of you has a part in it, and we hope that this report will bring to you the
glow of satisfaction which always accompanies a job well done.

ADDENDUM
Since June 30th we have come into possession of figures and information which were not available to us when this report was prepared.
We are adhering to the $1.00 per capita tax request for this year but
stating unequivocally that our request next year will have to be substantially increased. We make this statement at this time so that you
may be prepared for the inevitable. As late as yesterday the Board
seriously debated requesting a substantial upward revision in our per
capita request this year.
Respectfully submitted,
EDGAR V. STEWART, JR., President

REPORT OF SUPERINTEND ENT-MASONIC HOME
AT UNION CITY (Decoto)
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
We have just completed another year as of June 30, 1963, and it is
my pleasure and duty to submit to you my Seventh Annual Report.
The population of the Home on July 1, 1962, was 151 men and 225
women; this included 20 married couples. The overall average age was
81.65 years.
During the year 23 men, average age of 78.69 years and 25 women,
average age of 79.08 years entered the Home. We laid to rest 25 men,
average age of 84.95 years, and 27 women, average age 81.85 years.
As of June 30, 1963 our population was 372, which consisted of 149
men and 223 women, including 22 couples. The average age of the 372
residents is 81.70 years.

Of the 372 total, 119 were in the hospital, of which 102 are permanent.
In addition, 39 women are confined to the 4th floor North and East
Wings, who are receiving nursing care and under the supervision of the
hospital staff.
Our hospital has a capacity of 131, and on several occasions we had
many more than this number because of colds and other acute illnesses.
We have been very .fortunate to continue having the services of Mrs.
Eleanor Farris as our Hospital Supervisor. She has fulfilled her duties
most efficiently at all times, and it has been difficult, with the hospital
over-crowded and with shortage of help.
Our medical care program is under the direction of the Palo Alto
Medical Clinic, and our visiting doctors are Dr. Joseph Carson and Dr.
John Eckert; our dentist is Dr. Ken Lee from Fremont. Dr. Wayne
Collins is the podiatrist; Dr. Roger Wilson the optometrist; Dr. Frank
Siead the chiropractor, all of Hayward. We are using the services of
the local laboratory. In addition to our medical program, those who
prefer may have the service of a Christian Science Practitioner of their
choice within a radius of 50 miles.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The residents are quite happy with the entire medical plan at the
Home.
There have been several changes in the staff the past year. Brother
Hugh Herring came with us in September 1962, replacing Brother L. L.
Cain as Assistant to the Superintendent. Brother Hugh has taken a very
active part in the affairs of the Home and the residents. He is well-liked
by everyone. He is Junior Warden of Mount Diablo Lodge No. 448.
The position of Matron is now held by Mrs. Harriette Olson, who
came to us on June 5, 1963.
Mr. Al Soderholm has taken over as Chef. The residents seem to be
quite satisfied with the results. The new dishes are very pleasing.
Mrs. Eleanor Herring has taken the position of Office Manager and
doing very well. The Rev. Elliott Paulsen is filling the position as Home
Chaplain. Both Mr. Paul Reichert in Purchasing and Stock Control and
Mrs. Velma Huckabee as Recreation Coordinator are doing a fine job.
The residents enjoy the bus rides which were approved several
years ago. We endeavor to get a group out once a month. Some of the
places we have visited are: Ball Games, Ice Follies, Cinerama, Golden
Gate Park, Marin County, Carmel. and many points of interest.
Some of the visitations during the year that have caused enthusiasm
among the residents are: the visitation by our Most Worshipful Grand
Master and the reception .for him; the annual visitation of the Board of
Trustees for their quarterly meeting. It is always a pleaslli'e to welcome
both our Grand Master and members of the Board. It is also a great boost
for the residents.
During the year several of the Trustees visited on many occasions
to view the Home and the buildings that were under construction and
completed the latter par.t of January. These were quarters for employees,
both married couples and single men. This was a grand addition and the
turnover of single male help has diminished a great deal.
In addition, there were two other large and outstanding days. "Grand
Lodge Day" was held Wednesday, October 10, 1962. Approximately
1450 Grand Lodge representatives and their families enjoyed a box lunch
and a visitation of the Home. On August 18, 1962 The East Bay Past
Matrons Association held their annual "Jam and Jelly Day" and reception for their Grand Matron. There were approximately 800 in attendance for the day, and they brought with them a full year's supply of
jams and jellies and other goodies. We enjoyed having these groups
visit the Home, and on behalf of the residents we extend to them our
most sincere thanks and appreciation.
In addition, we want to acknowledge some of the outstanding contributions to the Home this past year. We apologize for not mentioning
all the gifts, but space won't permit.
We acknowledge with pleasure a beautiful color TV from Belmont

Shore Lodge delivered on December 24, 1962. We express our thanks
and appreciation on behalf of the residents who have enjoyed it very
much.
Our thanks and appreciation go to all the Lodges, groups and
individuals that sent Christmas contributions for the entertainment fund,
that the residents might have a very merry Christmas.
To all the organizations, individuals and groups who have contributed a large variety of items, such as TV's, wheel chairs, clothing,
foods, books, dressings, gowns, etc., we extend our sincere thanks and
appreciation for their thoughtfulness and generosity.
We are indebted to all the groups that brought all the fine entertainment to the Home for the benefit of the residents. This includes the
booking companies from which we received our movies. Our heartfelt
thanks to them and may they continue to entertain our people.
During the last year there has been much activity with new building
at the Home - as previously mentioned, the dormitories for single males
and apartments for married employees - then on May 20, 1963 the
contractors started demolition on the old hospital building, where there
will be erected a new three-story building. This will house about 60
ambulatory people plus some 35 semi-ambulatory patients who need
nursing care.
During the year there were 4,465 visitors that signed the register,
representing 495 Lodges in Californnia, 73 foreign jurisdictions and 8
foreign countries.
To the residents, on behalf of the staff and myself I wish to express
our sincere thanks for their cooperation and assistance in helping to
make this a home.
To all the personnel, my thanks for your cooperation, your interest
and untiring efforts in caring for our large family.
My thanks to the Board of Trustees for their confidence in me and
their interest and dedication to the Home and the cesidents. It has been
an extreme pleasure to serve both the Board and the Fraternity.
Respectfully submitted,
GAIL H. DAVID, Superintendent

Grade placemen t of our Home Family is as follows: twenty-o ne
children in high school, nine in junior high. twenty~three in grade 'school.
one in kinderga rten, and one in pre-school. One of the graduate s, Diana
Werner. will reside at the Home while she attends classes at Mt. San
Antonio Junior College.
In order to foster a healthy mind in a healthy body, an athletic and
recreational program has been pursued. Home boys have participa ted at
the school. in Little League, and in the sports contests with other Homes
in the southern Californi a area. The Home is a member of a League
comprise d of Children 's Homes in the San Gabriel Valley. While it is
difficult to enter teams in all sports because of the number of boys
required in a special age group, the Home free-lanc es many activities.
Swimming is an attainme nt required of all the children , not only in
connection with their participa tion at summer camp but also as an important preparat ion for life. To this end, Red Cross instructio ns for
junior and senior lifeguard s were conducte d once again this spring. at
the close of which training five senior certificates and eight junior certificates were issued. Again this season there was the Swim for Distance
competition between the various Dorms, won this time by the Senior
Boys who swam a total of 31.75 miles, which bettered the record of the
group that won last year. Bob Warrick won the high individua l honor
by covering 8.16 miles in 4 1/ 6 hours. The combined total for the Home
was 136.75 miles.
All of the groups enjoyed a vacation period at the Coronad o Youth
Camp and at Mission Bay during the summer, where they participa ted
in surfing, bathing. boating, fishing, and sailing activities. This proved
to be one of the most popular camps ever conducte d for the children.
As part of the Easter holidays, the Senior and the Intermed iate groups
were able to ·spend a few days at Lake Mohave. Horseba ck riding !es~
sons have been arranged with the help of Mr. Smithson in the Farm
Departm ent.
Our 4-H Club. the Masonic Pioneers , has been reported on in detail
in previous years. The activity of the Club and its success has continued this past year. The value of this phase of our program takes on
increased meaning when one is fully aware of its therapeu tic significance.

This year, also, there has been a Sewing Project for 4-H under the
supervision of Mrs. Young, and many of the girls have made great
strides in this womanly art.
We have members of Job's Daughters, Bethel No. 98, of George
Washington Chapter of De Mclay; children in Scouting and Brownies,
as well as other youth activitie-s. The children receive weekly piano and
voice lessons whenever talent, aptitude, or interest expresses itself.
The Home Tutor has assisted on all levels of education, with special
emphasis on remediel and accelerated work. Speed and remedial reading were offered during the past summer.
We have been fortuna te in having been able to continue the everpopular Movie Nights with films delivered to the Home courtesy of Mr.
Bliss and his delivery service. Participating distributors are Columbia
Pictures Corpora tion, Metro-Goldwyn-M ayer. Twentieth Century Fox,
Universal Films, Warner Brothers, and Allied Artists. Attendance at
these showings is open to guests of the children, too. Continuing activities which have become almost "institutions" are the Westerners' Scholastic Contest and Award Dinner, and the annual Monrovia Lodge
Christmas party now in its fortieth year. Another such event is the
annual trek to the Orange Show as guests of the San Bernardino Santa
Fe Masonic Club.
One of the most marked changes brought by fifteen years has been
the role of driving in the lives of the children. Not too many years ago,
the ability to drive was a nice accomplishment, nothing more; now it is
practically a "must" for the young people when they reach the required
age. In some areas, a car is almost an "essential" to enroll~ent .at col.le~e.
For this reason, the students are encouraged to take Drwers Training
and Behind the Wheel courses at high school. Only when they have
achieved sufficient proficiency to be licensed by the State, have been
further instructed by the Horne Staff in the proper handling of automobiles, and shown themselves to have a responsible attitude are they
permitted to drive the Home cars. A thorough knowledge of safe-drivin.g
methods is considered a prerequisite before they are launched in todays
world.
Licensed drivers are permitted to petition for the use of the "Date
Car" for specific events with approval of the Administration; otherwise
the Home provides the necessary transportation by means of the station
wagons or the Home bus. Those children permitted to use the "Date
Car" are responsible to see that it is maintained, thus providing them
with an additional opportunity for training.

V ISITATIONS

The opportunity to visit the Home on third Sunday of every month
exc:pt December continues to be popular with Lodges and concordant
bodies. A~ .nearly as possible, the Board policy of limiting the number
of these v1srt~rs. to a maximum of four hundred for a given Sunday is

to every second year. V1s1tors seem to enjoy both the chance to picnic

Requests are received as well from nursery schools, kindergarten
classes. and church groups to visit the farm area and the aviary.
THE ALUM N I

Each year, we are proud to say, the contact between the Home and
the Alumni appears to be strengthened. The office force make a concentrate.cl effort to keep a current mailing list of as many graduates as
possible. and encourages all the Alumni to aid in keeping this roster
up-to-date. One-half the subject matter of each Newsletter is contributed by .or devoted to the Alumni , who in addition to change of
address notices are asked to mail in reports pertaining to weddings,

128-H

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

births, deaths, graduations, special honors or awards. interesting occupations , and all such matters.

wise might never have come about. This is a unique and satisfyin
compensation in itself. I am grateful to have had this opportunity t~
serve. with the friendships, associations, and stimulating contacts which
it has made possible.
The fifteen years have brought many changes . Covina , itself, has
metamorphosed from a sleepy little village to a bustling "suburb" of
Greater Los Angeles. The Charter Oak Unified School District not only
came into being, but is quickly mushrooming into a giant in itself. The
surrounding orange groves have given way to tracts, residences, and
shopping areas. Through it all. the children and their problems have
remained much the same. and have continued to provide the joyful incentive which is peculiar to the field of Child Care.

The 1963 New sletter will be half again as large as that published
in 1962, and will contain over one hundred more letters from former
Home children than appeared in the 1962 volume. These letters come
from many points on the globe and represent a diversity of occupations
and endeavors.
Two Home graduates are with the Peace Corps. one in Thailand
serving as a medical technologist, the other in Ethiopia as a teacher.
Both individuals have submitted contributions which provide an interesting picture of life in the countries to which they have been assigned.
Another graduate of the Home has had the privilege and honor of
designing the insignia for the space ships of the astronauts, and her
personal accounts of the contacts with these national heroes are memorable, indeed. Recent graduate Bill Barraclough, an Engineering Major
at the University of Southern California, was awarded a four-year scholarship by the Proctor and Gamble Company. Bill was also the recipient
of the top award in the Westerners' Scholastic Contest last year. Jim
Hoard, a classmate of Bill's , is also at the University of Southern California , where he received the John L. Burt Engineering Scholarship.
Through these contacts we are able to follow the progress and
achievements of the Home Alumni. Again in 1962 there were four
official Reunions: a picnic at Sacramento in the spring, a picnic at the
Covina Home in the late summer, a dinner in San Francisco during
Grand Lodge Communication, and a fall Dinner Dance in Covina. All
four evoked enthusiastic response.
Copies of each Newsletter are sent to all the Alumni who write letters
or send in notices of vital statistics or changes of address; all those who
visit the Home personally; and all those who register at any of the
Reunions. It is the Home policy to send a copy of the Newsletter to each
Lodge currently sponsoring a child in the Home, to Grand Lodge officers , to all members of the Board of Trustees, the Past Grand Masters,
and all members of the Endowment Board. Thus, the interested crosssection of Masonry in California is in a position to obtain a valid
impression of activities at the Home for Children.
Recent graduates at Covina continue to return to the Home to visit
for brief periods. They are able to return to their "old haunts" just like
any child coming "home" for a visit. Everything is done to make these
young people feel that there is a place to which they may return for
advice, help, and companionship as well as a warm welcome.
May I say, personally, that the years have been rewarding and full
of interest. One of the joys of the Child Care field is that an individual
privileged to serve in my capacity is able to see tangible proof of his
efforts in the form of living testimonials and "Success Stories" that other-

PRINTED ITEMS OF PUBLICITY

During the past year, the Lodges ordered 1,400.000 printed items
from the Endowment Board, for sending to the members to "inform the
brethren" and to further encourage the brethren to make regular contributions to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund. This is in addition
to the countless thousands of letters and other items prepared by the
Lodges and sent to members, and many hundreds of articles written in
Lodge bulletins.
Obviously, a great amount of extra work was done by the Lodges
in sending these items to the members. Much of tha t extra work neces~
sarily falls to the Lodge Secretary and all such Secretarie.s a re to be
especially commended for their untiring efforts. The same applies to
the Masters . Wardens, Lodge Endowment Committeemen and all others
who contribute time and effort to this work.
Something new in printed items! This Christmas season, for the
first time. the Endowment Boa rd is offering a Christmas fold er. depicting the Christmas Party in our Children's Home in Covina, for mailing
to members. Also, a Holiday Season leaflet entitled "Have a Heart in
Your Holiday Season for Our H omes." These items should be appropriate and effective if sent to members in November and December,
during the season when most people are " thinking of others."
CHANGES IN ENDOWM ENT BOARD PERSONNEL

Fred Blanchard moved out of the area in which he was appointed to
serve and was replaced by Everett S. Todd. former Grand Standard
Bea rer. Howard L. Rose requested that he not be reappointed and was
replaced by Norman W. Shaw of Stockton . H enry G. Van Dyke requested that he not be reappointed, after serving the Board for three
years in the Long Beach area, and Myron E . Roudebush. fo rmer Inspector, was appointed to that area. Lester A. Price also requested that he
not be reappointed, a fter having served 16 years on the Board. and he
was replaced by R alph C. H ine of Santa Barbara, former Inspector and
Grand Orator. George C. Poloynis of Bakersfield, form er Senior Grand

135

Steward, was appointed to replace Harold R. De Tuncq, who resigned
the previous year.
To the brethren who left the Board, we say thanks so much for you r
devoted work, and we know you will continue to enthusiastically support
the Homes Endowm ent. The brethren who replaced these former
members of the Board have already demonstrated their ability and
devotion to the Homes Endowment progra m.
OuR APPRECIATION T O ALL

It would be impossible to na me the many hundreds of brethren who
have assisted in this work. but we do wish to especially thank the Grand
Master, M . W. Ira W. Coburn, fo r his devoted support, and the same
goes to all Grand Lodge Officers and Committeemen: to Don G. Campbell, Grand Lecturer. and his Assistant Grand Lecturers and Inspectors
who have been of tremendous assistance in this work; to the Grand
Secretary, Edward H . S iems, P.G.M., and Assista nt Grand Secretary,
Verne W . Hendrix, together with members of their staff who have a ll
been so willing to assist; to the Masters, Wardens, Secretaries, local
Lodge Endowment Committeemen , and all other Lodge Officers and
members who assisted in so many ways; to the more than 11 5,000 brethren who contributed of their means: and we would not forget the
devoted brethren who are me mbers of the Board of Trustees of the
Homes, together with the Superintenden ts of the H omes, their wives
and members of their staffs , who are more directl y concerned with the
daily needs o ~ those children and elderlies in our two Masonic Homes.
To all, we give our sincere thanks and appreciation.
I N CONCLUSION

The members of this Endowment Board take great pride in the fact
that our H omes Endowment is a voluntary program, rather than compul~
sory. and we hope it will always remain as such. H owever, the cost of
operating the Homes is constantly increasing and will increase more in
the near future. The number of residents is at an all-time high a nd will
increase decidedly at the D ecato Home when the new Charles Albert
Adams residential building, now under construction, is completed, because of the number of elderlies on the waiting list of applicants for
admission to the Home, and costs will increase accordingly.
.These added costs must be borne, either voluntarily or compulsorily.
Lets keep it voluntary by an all-out effort for the H omes Endowment
during the coming months. The Endowment Board has changed the
calendar! The "Endowment M onth of May" starts this week and con-

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

as to the purposes, functions and objectives of our Boards. A Board of
Rel ief is not an autonomous organization. each Lodge has equal representation in its government and operation.
BOARDS OP RELIEP

Within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California we maintain and operate nineteen Boards of Relief, five of which also operate
Employment Bureaus. The Boards are established to perform those
duties and obligations which have been so clearly defined by Grand
Lodge in the matter of relief to the distressed or needy worthy brother,
his widow and orphans. By custom and procedure in the matter of
charity they are endeavoring to create a virtual California Masonic
landmark.
The continued migration into California with its accompanied proportion of sojourning brethren has caused considerable increased activities in our Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus. Notwithstanding
the additional work that has been thrust upon them these devoted brethren and their employees continue to go far beyond the call of duty, on
foot and out of their way, in carrying out their work. No money can
buy that kind of devotion and dedication; Brethren, it can only be
acquired by the application of the tenets of Freemasonry to the hearts
,..,f men.
The Board of Control assun..; you that relief as administered in this
jurisdiction conforms in every detail to our ancient and honored custom.
Long practice in administration of relief has permitted us to develop
business-like methods without distracting from proper consideration,
understanding and courteous attitude in the granting of relief. Changing conditions of prosperity, depression, peace or war have not permitted them any de..,·iation from our established practices. A review of
the rulings will show that relief as administered within the jurisdiction
of California has kept to the spirit and intent which our ancient Brethren so wisely and carefully established.
After carefully analyzing the audited reports which have been submitted by our nineteen Boards of Relief. we ask your brief indulgence
in the following condensed statistics covering their operations during
the Masonic Year ended June 30, 1963:
Advanced for Relief--------·-· --------·············· .. ········-$30,723.43

The magnitude of these activities warrants for these heroic Masons
the undying gratitude of the entire Craft.

REIMBURSEMENTS TO MASONIC BOARDS OF RELIEF

REPORT OF TRUSTEES,
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE

It has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge that no worthy
sojourning brother, or his immediate family, shall suffer in our Jurisdiction for the necessities of life, or shall have other than a decent
burial upon his demise:, regardless of the willingness or ability of the
brother's own Lodge to make us whole. Grand Lodge undertakes and
has in the past reimbursed Boards of Relief for such unrecoverable
advances. We are mos t pleased to report that although more than
$30,700.00 have been advanced to sojourners and their dependents all
monies have been repaid, thereby obviating the need for reim bursements.
In closing may I leave you with this thought: "Where. my Brethren,
can the tangible evidence of Masonry practiced out of the Lodge be so
evident as in a Board of Relief?"
The Board of Control has received the utmost cooperation during
this past year from the Most Worshipful Grand Master, the Grand Secretary and the Assistant Grand Secretary, as well as from their officers
and associates. We are: most grateful for all of their assistance and their
kindnesses.
Respectfully submitted.

REPORT OF MANAGER
To the Trustees of California Masonic Memorial Temple
Brethren:
We have now entered upon the 6th year of operation of the California Masonic Memorial Temple. The past six months have developed
several changes in personnel which will result in revised policies and
operating procedures.
Alvin Horwege, who has served as Building M anager for the past
five years, retired effective February I, 1963. We congratulate him in
his retirement and hope that he will enjoy his well-earned rest. In August
of 1963 our Building Superintendent, Harry Haines, also retired and
we wish him success in his new endeavors.
IMPROVEMENTS

During the past year new fixed spot and follow lights have been
installed which aid materially in servicing our concerts. We believe our
acoustical problems have been met and we look for little trouble in this
regard.
MAINTENANCE

As our Temple becomes older, maintenance might be expected to
increase. Constant attention is being given to preservation of our
facilities in order to avoid, as much as possible, any major overhauls.
During the last year the cost of janitorial and other service~ . ~nd
supplies has increased. This affects our income from use of our facilities.
We are endeavoring to offset these increases with economies in our
operating procedures.
CONVENTION COMPETITION

San Francisco and the Bay Area continue to be favorable localities
for conventions and entertainment attractions. Competition for occupancy of facilities for conventions has grown during the past year.
The Fairmont Hotel completed its new tower and ballroom, the Mark
Hopkins is developing plans, the new Hilton Hotel is under construction, the Cow Palace anticipates a 3Yi million dollar improvement for
convention purposes. and the Civic Auditorium is nearing completion
of its 7!/i million dollar face-lifting.
OCCUPANCY

The occupancy of our Exhibit Hall and particularly our Audit~~i~m
has increased satisfactorily during the year. Income from these fac1ht1~s
was approximately I Oo/o ove r last year. We have been fortunat~ m
being able to book several high-type attractions w?ich included eight
Pops Concerts conducted by Arthur Fiedler and six performances ~y
the Ballet Folklorico of Mexico. Such stars as Ray Bolger, John Raitt.
Pearl Bailey, Mahalia Jackson. Joey Bi~hop . Phyllis Diller. the Lime•

163

lighters, the Kingston Trio, and three Hootenany Shows have appeared
this year on our stage. Chief Justice Earl W a rren, P.G.M., spoke to the
State Bar of California in the Aduitorium. We are booked heavily for
the balance of this year and have a good number of top-name performers signed for the spring season of 1964.
It was gratifying to have the General Electric use our facilities for
their las~ annual ~hareholders meeting. They are particularly adapted
for meetings of this type and we have had other inquiries in this regard.
TOURS

We have continued our policy of keeping the Temple open on
Saturday and Sunday from 12:00 to i:OO p.m. for visitors. We are
revitalizing our Visitor's Committee to assure the proper handling of tour
groups which are again making requests for dates.
GARAGE

With the increased occupancy of our Auditorium and Exhibit Hall.
and the added attractions at the hotels on Nob Hill, our garage has
benefited through greater usage. This fiscal year, ending June 30, 1963,
will find our rental income in excess of $60,000, which is an increase of
over $9.000 above the previous year. Our lessee has been most co~
operative and diligent. We have confidence that we can continue the
upward trend of revenue from the garage through continued activity
and occupancy in the Temple.
OUR IMAGE

Every effort is being made to build a favorable image of our Temple
in theatrical, convention, and civic circles through personal contacts and

correspondence. We have been appointed a Director of the San Francisco and Visitors Bureau to fill a vacancy on the Board. This will
continue to be a very valuable point of contact for our future activities.
Our Temp~e has great dignity, beauty, comfort, and prestige for
those ':"ho. use 1t. We expect with realignment of our personnel to effect
the Objectives planned. We are happy to play a part in the operation of
our California Masonic Memorial Temple, and are most appreciative
of the confidence which you as Trustees have placed in us. It is our
hope that we shall fulfill your expectations.
Respectfully submitted.
GEORGE D. GAVIN, Manager

To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In the report of this Commit tee a year ago, attentio n was called to
the provisio ns of Section 343 as amende d in 1961 . The detail involved
concern ed the situatio n for those Lodges whose designa ted date for
Stated Meeting could occur during the five days of the Annual Communicat ion and whose individu al By-Law s, as reflected in the records

168

PROCEED INGS OP THE

of the Grand Secretar y's Office, did not contain provision for an alternate meeting date. A survey was made covering all Lodges which
might be so involved.
The above survey brought to light the many instances in which the
records referred to did not contain a copy of the Uniform Code as
adopted and submitte d for approval .
To remedy both types of deficiency a_s involved in Lodges whose
designat ed date for Stated Meeting might occur within the period of
the Annual Commun ication, a letter was sent to each of these Lodges
suggestin g they adopt and submit the complete Uniform Code, including a specified alternate date.
The cooperat ive response of the Lodges has been very gratifyin g.
Of 86 Lodges to whom the letter was addresse d, 52 have promptly
complied with the request. Of the 34 Lodges which have not yet taken
the suggeste d action, only 6 have Stated Meeting dates which fall during the period of this Annual Commun ication. The large number of
Lodges so involved explains the high number of instances of adoption
of Uniform Code as included in this Report.
During the past year close contact has been maintain ed with the
office of the Grand Secretar y and all cases of action by a Lodge in
adopting or amendin g By-Laws have been reviewed promptly . We wish
to commend the care and effectiveness with which the staff of that
office have studied each item submitte d to them and have immedia tely
taken steps to correct any procedur e which failed to comply with the
requirem ents of the regulations. In the very few instances where an
error or misunde rstanding was subseque ntly discovered, the same type
of efficiency has been demonst rated by the staff in correspo nding with
the Lodge involved and bringing about correct understa nding and procedure.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History presents the following report:
The members of the Committee express their appreciation to the
Grand Lodge and especially to our Grand Master, Brother Ira W.
Coburn, for the privilege of serving.
Our Grand Master has been most friendly, cooperative, and understanding, so it has been a distinct pleasure to have served under him
during this past year.
The members of your Committee have attended numerous cornerstone layings and other Masonic events where history might be involved. The Colored Slide Lecture "Some Came by Land and Some by
Sea" has been presented to numerous Lodges and Masonic groups.
This lecture, though not a history of Masonry in California, does show
by means of color slides how some of our Lodges, one hund~ed or
more years old, were furnished, and makes one wonder how, with the
limited availability of furnishings of that period, such beautiful furnishings could have been obtained. This lecture is available to Masonic
groups by contacting one of the Committee members.
No new projects were formulated during the year, as it was felt
that Brother Wally Wohlgemuth, who was so ably following in the
footsteps of our one and only Mr. Masonic History . Past Gran~
Master Leon 0. Whitsell, would return to the Committee after his
special assignment this year. He had a number of projects in mind for
the Committee that would add to our historical data for presentation
to the brethren.
With his untimely passing we were unable to follow through with
this program.
We also regret the passing of Brother Frank Everett, who ser~ed
this Committee faithfully and well for many years, and who, like
Brother Wohlgemuth, was greatly loved and will be sorely missed by
all of us.
In order that the Committee can be reorganized, and definite programs can be set up for the coming years, we respectfu.lly request t~at
the ·sum of $500.00 be appropriated for our use durmg the <:ommg
Masonic year to cover expenses of meetings, stationery. and incidentals
required to effect these programs.
Respectfully submitted,
KENNETH H. DOWNS
LEON 0. WHITSELL
RALPH A. HERBOLD
KENNETH B. CONKLIN

REPORT OF COMMIT TEE ON COMMER CIALISM
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California :
Your Committee on Commercial ism is most pleased to report that
infractions of our laws, rules, and regulations continue to lessen in
scope. seriousness, and number.
.
.
There were no infractions called to our attention in connection with
constituent Lodge's activities. In a few instances. apparently t.~rough
inadvertenc e individual members of the Craft were found to be out of
line." By ha~ing them gently admonished corrections were made without hurt to anyone.
At the start of this Masonic Year, our greatest problem continued
to be with privately owned, out of state, so-called Masonic Magazines.
In the report made to last year's annual communicat ion particular mention was made of two such magazines; one published in the Mid-West
and the other in a nearby State. As to the Mid-West publication, which
as far as we know, is still being published. the format, name and
appearance are so changed that it is hard to recognize it a~ .t he. sa~e
publica tion. We have had no complaints nor reports of ~ohc1tahon tn
our jurisdiction since the first of th is year, and we believe that .our
troubles from this source are ended. As to the nearby State publication, it has been giving us less and less trouble. Solicitation in this
jurisdiction apparently has not "paid off" in recent months. Latest
information indicates that this publication has been re-sold and the new
owner does not intend to solicit advertising in this jurisdiction.
From time to time we hear rumors of a ctivities of other so-called
Masonic publications in our jurisdiction but we have not been able to
"pin any down" nor secure anything definite in regard to them or to
their activities.
We have had brought to our attention several infractions by a certain concordant organization which were immediately passed on to
their Grand Officers who quickly took corrective action.
Several violations by appendant groups. both adult and adolescent,
had to be called to the attention of their Grand Officials. In each
instance the fullest cooperation was extended and prompt corrective
action taken.
In our endeavor to bring about conformity with the California
Masonic Code, infractions brought to our attention are generally called
to the attention of the Master of the Lodge and/ or the Inspector when
a Lodge or a Brother is involved. When a prerequisite organization . is
involved we work with its Grand Officers. This we feel is most desirable. not alone for our purposes, but it gives the prer~quisite organization the opportunity to " put their own house in order . . We have found
this to be the most effective way to handle, thus leaving no hard feelings or fences to mend.

GRANO LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

173

More and more prerequisite groups are "asking before leaping" so
as to be certain that our law will not be violated. This is as it should
be and eliminates trouble all around.
In our report to last year's Communica tion, mention was made of a
cemetery in this State established by one of our Lodges some ninety
years ago for Masons. which gradually through the passing years lost
the Masonic characterist ics and Is now open to all Caucasians. Its name
has continued to carry the word "Masonic" in its corporate title. The
word "Masonic" is now in the process of being removed.
It is not the purpose of this committee to go on "witch hunts." Infractions which we investigate originate in complaints received by Grand
Lodge or are brought to the Committee's attention in various ways.
Once in a while an anonymous complaint is received, to such complaints
we seldom pay any attention. The complainant should either have the
intestinal fortitude to sign his name or not complain. As a matter of
fact our sources of complaint are considered confidential and are never
disclosed.
Let us repeat that continuous vigilance is most necessary if we are
to keep a check-rein on those who violate our law. whether it be through
ignorance. inadvertenc e or willfulness. Unfortunate ly there always
seem to be a few who are unable to conform and who, in order to
promote their own ideas try to find ways and means of circumventi ng
the intent and the spirit of our law instead of following the patterns of
Masonic behavior esta blished by the Grand Lodge.
In the work of this committee. we have at times found it necessary
to call on some of our Grand Lodge officers for counsel and guidance.
Our Grand Se~retary. Most Worshipful Edward H. S iems, several of
the Assistant Grand Lecturers and several Inspectors, when called on.
were most cooperative and gracious--o ur grateful thanks to them.
We particularly wish to express our sincere thanks and appreciation
to the Most Worshipful Ira W. Coburn, Grand Master, who has been
so very understandi ng of our problems and with whom we found it
necessary to counsel on occasions. His assistance and advice have been
exceedingly helpful. We feel highly honored to have served and worked
with him.
Respectfully submitted.
VINCENT P. McMuRoo
WILLARD A. BRAASCH
JACK L. BLAINE
HARVEY A. HARKNESS
ALBERT R. BENNISON
