(THIS AMENDMENT APPLIES ONLY TO CONSTITUENT LODGES AND DOES NOT APPLY TO
THE INVESTMENT OF GRAND LODGE FUNDS).
With respect to the authority to invest in Groups II and III , the
Ordinance reads as follows: "No such investments, however, shall be
made which at the time of purchase will result in the total market
values of the securities referred to in this section exceeding twenty per
cent (or sixty per cent) of the total market va lue of all the cash, bank
accounts and securities held," - the controlling point being that there
cannot be more than 20% or 60% invested in Groups II and III, at the
time of purchase. ( 100% may of course be invested in Group I.)
At the 1959 Communication certain amendments were passed with
respect to the percentages which could be invested in Groups I and III.
Group I was reduced to 20% and Group III was increased to 60 % . In
this connection. it is very important to call a ttention to the following,
which ls contained in the Reports of the Committee on Jurisprudence
and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
"Your Committee on Jurisprudence respectfully calls attention to
the fact that this proposed amendment is permissive only and is not a
directive. Great care should be exercised in making investments under
the authority granted by this proposed amendment."
"Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends the
adoption of Resolution D-7 but with this admonition to the Lodges:
"A) The authority granted is permissive only and is not suggested
as an investment guide under present economic conditions.
"B) That in making investments in Group III the Lodges be most
circumspect in taking advantage of this additional authority.
"C) And that they strictly comply with the provisions of the last
paragraph of Section 403 of our Ordinance-s, to consult with and heed
the advice of the professional investment advisors used by Grand Lodge,
and made available to the Constituent Lodges without charge to the
individual Lodge."
The above comments are included in the reports of the Committee
as they appear on page 282 of the 1959 Proceedings.
At the 1960 Communication Section 403 was amended. as follows:
"The provisions of this section requiring securities to be fully listed
and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Ex·
change Commission as a N ational Securities Exchange. shall not apply
to the Honolulu Stock Exchange. This exception is confined to Lodges
located in the State of Hawaii." (The H onolulu Stock Exchange is
not as yet a National Securities Exchange, as defined by the Securities
and Excha nge Commission.)
Since its formation the Investment Committee has met regularly
every three months. Between quarterly meetings the business of the
Committee is handled by correspondence or telephone.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

These evidences of debt or certificates are owned by the Masonic
Homes of _California. It would be appreciated if negotiations were undertaken by those Lodges or Temple Associations who could afford to
redeem these certificates. The Investment Committee would greatly
appreciate your consideration of this request. Just write to the Grand
Secretary for further information.
The entire portfolio is listed in the Auditor's Reports, and, therefore,
is not included herein. The securities are held in safekeeping for Grand
Lodge by the Trust Department of the Crocker Anglo National Bank,
at its One Montgomery Street Office, San Francisco.
The matter of stock dividends was discussed at the meeting on May
14, 1963. Whether or not stock dividends should be considered a part
of current income is a topic of discussion among financial institutions.
There is no uniform procedure as yet, although the majority apply stock
dividends to principal. It was the thought of the Committee that further
study should be made before any changes are recommended to Grand
Lodge. It was also suggested that an analysis be made of the value
of the stock dividends received by Grand Lodge. As a matter of
information, the stock dividends received by the various funds during
the past year had a value of approximately $68.500.00.
We have had excellent attendance at our Investment Committee
meetings. as has been the case in the past.
Again we come to that place in the Investment Committee report
when we try to summarize in few words the financial and investment
outlook as we see it.
We can again definitely state that we continue to pursue a conservative cour,se, with the objective of obtaining the greatest amount of
protection for our funds. under conditions as they exist.
The problems do not diminish, but we are prepared to meet them as
they arise. Fortunately, we can move swiftly, which we have done
when necessary.
We again repeat that our course of action can be quite different
from that of the individual for a variety of reasons. This statement is
made so as not to influence personal actions.
Our thanks to the Grand Secretary. the Assistant Grand Secretary,
and my thanks to the members of the Investment Committee for their
wholehearted and generous cooperation at all times.
Respectfully submitted on behalf of the Investment Committee -

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
OF THE MASONIC CLUB
UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA AT LOS ANGELES

JoHN M. GORDON

E. v. STEWART, JR.

PAULA. PFLUEGER, Chairman
Adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
A detailed explanation of the Club's social activities is not necessary
at this time as we gave a .fairly complete summary in our report last
year, and the same schedule is applicable now.
Our Masonic Club movie continues to stimulate interest. We are
constantly getting requests for it from Lodges in both Northern and
Southern California, and it is always well received.
The matter that gives us the most concern, however, and one that
seems to be of concern to most Lodges, is the falling off of membership
and poor attendance.
A brochure has been printed. and by the time this report is incor~
porated in the Proceedings of Grand Lodge. we hope all Lodges will
have received their copies for inclusion in a monthly mailing with the
Trestle Board. This brochure gives many interesting details regarding
both clubs and it is hoped that it will be of <Sufficient interest to the
entire California membership so that their sons and daughters will be
made aware of the Masonic Club facilities at both Berkeley and Los
Angeles, and that those attending both universities will avail themselves
of those facilities. It is only by constant publicity that we will be able
to increase our membership and extend those benefits to those eligible.
We, in Los Angeles. are faced with the very difficult task of finding
a replacement for our very efficient, exceptionally capable Director, Mrs.
Faith C. Sheldon. who will retire on a service pension December 31.
1964. She has had over twenty years of faithful and loyal service and
while she well deserves her retirement, we shall certainly view her
going with extreme reluctance. She has done a really outstanding job.
We regretfully report the passing. during the year, of our Brother,
John R. Klarquist, who served on our House Committee for so many
years. Brother Klarquist, in his business life, was a general contractor
and his guidance and advice in the operation of our Club were invaluable; he will certainly be sorely missed.
The Grand Master appointed as a replacement for Brother Klarquist, Brother Herbert H. Cooper. who returns to our Board after an
absence of one year.
Again, as before. your Board of Directors feels gratified at the
functioning of the Club during the past year. and are proud to have
served in this very important adjunct of Grand Lodge.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Club here at Berkeley are trying very hard to increase membership.
for all are aware that if only a limited number of new people join, the
work load for each member will be increased. This has, and will
continue to be detrimental to academic work, and I call for the understanding of the Masons should progress be slow at 11rst; I know,
however, that success is imminent. for we have a fine product to sell."
The augmented Board. increased from 9 to 15 members, has functioned harmoniously this past year. There has been excellent communication between the Board and the students as well as with the
hostesses. We continue to invite to Board Meetings the student
President and Social Chairman and on one occasion our Board met
jointly with the student council. with all the students being greatly
impressed by a talk by Brother A. Hopkins of the Publicity Committee directed to the important business of increasing their membership.
We adopted the Budget in conformity with the appropriation of
Grand Lodge; and the report of the auditor, copies of which have
been furnished to the Finance Committee. (See Exhibit B, page 7
thereof) indicates that we have fairly well lived within that Budget .
considering the figure of $3,777.40 representing our income under
(less than} expenditures for the year ended July 31. 1962 as an
addition to the General Working Fund. Grand Lodge appropriated
and gave us $1 9,100.00 of which we allocated $750.00 to our Insurance Fund, and the balance of $18,350.00 to said General W orking
Fund; this latter amount. added to said sum of $3,777.40, gave us a
total available of $22.127.40 in the General Working Fund. Actually,
we expended and charged to said Fund $22,021.29. leaving an excess
of income of only $106.11. However, it is important to note that our
building is 40 years old and during this past year we found it necessary, after some intensive investigation and work by the Building
Committee a nd Mrs. Janaice Kohl. to rebuild our furnace and expend
therefor $2,012.19. As further shown in said Exhibit B. page 7. the
bulk of our income from interest and dividends was allocated by us
to the Property R eplacement Fund, i.e. $2.172.93 and under Expenditures there was charged for Renovation and Replacement of Property items totalling $1.853.41, leaving a small excess of income over
expenditures in that field of $319.52.
With the appointment of certain new members to the Board has
come inspiration and drive - a challenge to approach the problems
of a Clubhouse with new ideas. This is manifested in a report published by the Publicity Committee of our Board and we feel that
the great effort and considered planning of this group should be
made known to the officers and members of the Grand Lodge. A few
quotations from this report will explain why we are asking for an
increase in the Budget. The Budget for the fiscal year ending July 31.
1964. adopted by the Board. and previously submitted to the Finance

" The whole purpose of this Club, of Grand Lodge's investment of the Board who are giving of their valuable time and efforts - is

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
An analysis of the report of the Committee on Lodge Financing for
the past year indicates a continuing increase in the interest and progress
in the construction, maintenance and operation of Masonic Temples
throughout the jurisdiction. A ·s tudy of the activities discloses definite
improvement in the administration and management of Temple financial
affairs. This improvement is reflected in a review of the annual financial
statements submitted by the Temple Associations concerning their financial transactions and other matters relating to Masonic Temple fiscal
processes and control. Due to continued educational information furnished by the Committee, resulting in increased interest and excellent
leadership, a great majority of Lodges throughout the jurisdiction are
being managed in a most excellent manner and, almost without exception, are in a very high degree of solvency. During the past year 262
Temple Associations and Lodges have submitted financial statements
and these statements reveal very intelligent and businesslike operation.
Each year more and more Lodges and Temple Associations are establishing necessary cash and depreciation reserves which are so important
for the repair, rehabilitation and replacement of the Temples as required
in the future. The increased and continued success of the financial operations of Masonic Temples gives cause for the Committee to again
recommend to the Lodges (who have not as yet done so) that they
form non-profit Temple Associations to carry on the business and
&nancial affairs of their Temples.

199

The past year has been a most successful one in the activities of
th~ Committee and this is largely due to the splendid cooperation received from th.e ?fficers and the brethren of the various Lodges and
Temple Associations. We especially desire to acknowledge our sincere appreciation to the full support and encouragement given by our
Grand Master, Ira W. Coburn, and his officers. Their wisdom in
difficult situations has safely carried us through any "rough seas"
encountered in our endeavors. We are equally grateful to the Grand
Secretar,y and the Assistant Grand Secretary for their counsel and
ad~ice. and also to their efficient and accommodating staff for the
assistance and cooperation given the Committee. Such advice and
assistance provided the Committee in its efforts on behalf of the
constituent Lodges has made our service on the Committee very
rewarding.
Masonry is on the move in California, and will continue onward
so long as its members have the determination and desire in their
hearts to build and to continue to build Temples creditable to the
c·r aft where they may gather together in unity and harmony to dedicate and re-dedicate themselves to work diligently, live creditably
and act honorably by all men.
In conclusion, it is the desire to include in this report a statement
of the Committee'·s high regard and esteem for John T. Bond, member of the Committee who passed away during the year.
In addition to the active, forthright and dedicated manner in which
he engaged in all his civic and Masonic endeavors, he was also recognized as a Senior Statesman in his business ability and success
and became kn'own throughout the country as Mr. Candy Man.
The memory of his good character and good works will live in
our hearts forever; these cannot be lost.
A life such as his does not need any footnotes. It is much better
that a man's good deeds should praise him rather than the words of
another person.
John Bond's life speaks for itself.
Respectfully submitted,
MARK A. GREEN

The Lodges now operating under this plan are:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The past Grand Lodge year marked the tenth that the Committee
has published the quarterly California Freemason. This has become its
principal function. although all proceedings of sister jurisdictions a re
carefully scanned and reviews are published in every issue. The present
format for the magazine was adopted in 1959.
The California Freemason is an official publication but its articles
do not necessarily present the opinion of Grand Lodge. It has attempted to maintain sound Masonic standards and to give our readers
Masonic information and inspiration, but it must always be understood
that its statements are not necessarily the official position of the Grand
Lodge of California. Articles are printed which have some Masonic
connection and which are educational, informative, stimulating and
even provocative. News of Grand Lodge activities is presented as well
as unusual and outstanding items about individual Lodges, but a
quarterly is not a news magazine and space is not available to mention
every local happening.
The publication of the California Freemason as a quarterly by
the Correspondence Committee was authorized by resolution adopted
in 1954. Section 203 was added to the California Masonic Code in
1957, and this is the present statutory provision for the publication.
The Section reads:
" In addition to its usual and customary duties. the Committee on
Correspondence shall publish and distribute the magazine California
Freemason . Said publication and distribution shall be made at least
once each quarter under the direction of the Grand Master."
This provision authorizes the Grand Master to determine the manner in which the magazine is distributed. The several Grand Mas ters
from time to time have set the subscription price at $1 a year. Sub~
scriptions paid in advance at the time the subscription for one year
is entered bea r a reduction of $.25 per year, which represents the
sa ving in sending expiration notices, etc. As the statutes now stand.
the Grand Master could direct that the magazine be delivered to all
members at the expense of Grand Lodge.
Section 411 of the Masonic Code . which sets out discretionary
expenditures permitted to individual Lodges, was amended in 1957
to provide that a Lodge may in its discretion purchase subscriptions
to California Freemason for its members. Thereafter, the Grand Master determined on what basis blanket subscriptions by Lodges could
be provided for. A number of Lodges now send the ma ga zine to their
entire membership. This pra ctice has more than paid for itself in
increased membership interest. The arrangement for blanket subscriptions is that if a Lodge adopts a resolution so to do, each member is

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
To recite to you the record and accomplishments of the ~ublic
Schools Committee is a lengthy chore, but after months of trying to
condense our story into fitting length and form we will try to limit
ourselves to the bare essentials without any particular form or order.
It has been for years the aim of this Grand Lodge to perpetuate
democracy's greatest tap root. the American Public School System.
It is easily recognized that this major aim c~n only be at~amed by
enlisting the interest of the voting public. An 1_nformed an_d interested
electorate will surely cure any weaknesses which now ~x~st. . . .
How well California Masonry has fulfilled its m1ss1on is md1cated by the ever-increas ing number of Public School cornerstone
ceremonies-by the nationwide spread of Public Schools Week-by
the many hours spent by devoted members of the craft, as well as the
dollars s pent-by the numbers of our fraternity who participate ~s
school board members. administrators and teachers-by the official
s tands taken by other bodies, particularly the York and Scotti~h Rites.
How far we have fallen short in our efforts to have an informed
and interested public may be measured by the poor attendance of o~r
own members at meetings designed to keep them informed on Public
School matters-by the number of school bond issues and tax override elections which are lost-by the small turnout of voters at most
school elections- by school "drop-outs," and by the uninformed comments you hear from day to day.
.
.
Much has been accomplished since 1919, but there 1s still so much
more to be done. To be effective. this work must be done at the
local level. because our Public Schools must be kept local and close
to the people. Individual Lodges and their members are the key to

This year your committee. well aware of the proud re~ord of ?ur
Grand Lodge in support of Masonic education, felt that 1t was time
to study what was being done elsewhere in this field in the hope. t~e
knowledge gained would offer an opportunity to improve Masonic
education in California. A questionnaire was prepared and letters were
sent by members of the committee to every Grand Lodge in the U.nit~d
States. As of the writing of this report 22 of the 48 Grand JurisdJCtions have replied. The questionnaire is made a part of this report.
Your committee wishes to express its appreciation to those Grand
Lodges which have provided so much of their time and publis~ed materials to assist this study. The committee proposes to continue the
study until it is completed and then to assemble the material for the
benefit and information of Masonry in general.
As a preliminary report. there are many interesting facts learned
from the replies received. Eight jurisdictions have Research Lodges,
one having two of them. The Grand Lodge of New Mexico has just
approved the formation of a Research Lodge.
.
As might be expected. the method of disseminating Masonic education is almost as varied as the number of jurisdictions. Texas and
Oklahoma have ta ken much of their plan from that of Arkansas.
Rhode Island has utilized much of Massachusetts and Indiana plans.
Some plans such as New York, New Mexico, Illinois and Ohio are
very elaborate. Virtually all plans are voluntary. The G~and. Lodge
of Arkansas publishes a handbook for Lodge Officers which is valuable. This plan establishes 15 zone Institutes throughout . the state.
These are somewhat like the all-day seminars of our committee. The
scope of this session in Arkansas may be seen from the cop~ of the
program attached. In some of the Grand Lodges. the ~asomc Ed~­
cation Committee has been responsible for the preparation of candidates' handbooks similar to the excellent Candidates' Coaches' Handbook prepared in California by our Grand Lecturer.
Many of the Masonic Education Committees are required to ~re­
pare and publish Grand Lodge magazines similar. though not supenor,
to our own California Freemason.
.
Several jurisdictions have adopted a so-called ment~r ~Ian. This
plan is perhaps most thoroughly exemplified by the Illin01s Intend.er
Handbook which acknowledges its indebtedness to Indiana and 0~10.
The Intender, to quote the Grand Lodge of Illinois handbook, den~es
from the old operative Lodges of Scotland. The Inten~er was. an important official in the Lodge in S cotland, entrusted with the instruction of new candidates. The Schaw Statutes of 1598 provided that an
Intender be chosen by each new Fellowcraft. The minutes of the Lodge
of Aitchison's Haven indicate that an Intender was provided for both
new Entered Apprentices and new Fellowcrafts.
.
The Grand Lodge of New York has a Committee on Masonic Edu-

207

cation and Lodge Service which has in addition to a Chairman, a fulltime, paid Director. All materials produced by this committee are
provi~ed t~e Lodges without charge. The brochure published by this
committee is perhaps the most complete of all educational systems. It
contains ma terial and suggestions for Lodge programs. instructions
f~r Masters: in~ormation on the use of the New Yark Grand Lodge
Library, which is one of the larges t. and is a circulating library. The
first page of the committee handbook reads as follows:

In the light of this study of Masonic education in the U nited
States, your committee has reviewed its own activities this year. E very
effort has beeq made to assist and promote the activities of the four
Cali~o:nia Research Lodges. They have done a magnificent job of
prov1dmg speakers, preparing papers and circulating materials to
every Lodge which has requested any. Too many M asters, however,
are. not yet awa re of the opportunities available to them through the
assistance of the Res earch Lodges. Your committee has unanimously
endorsed the Grand Lodge resolution removing the restriction on Masters and W ardens of Research Lodges. This resolution will again be
voted upon at this session. The committee recognizes that unless
this resolution is adopted several of the Research Lodges will not be
able to contin ue and the cause of Masonic education in California will
be dealt a serious blow.
This year again the Grand Lodge Masonic Educa tion Committee
spons?red the second annual joint meeting of the four Research Lodges,
held in Fresno. California, June I. J 963. A copy of the program is
made a part of this report. It is most difficult to adequately acknowledge
the ~reat work done in preparation for this seminar by Central California Research Lodge, its Master, Wardens and Secretary. As a result
of the success and need for continuation of this type of Masonic edu-

cation. the Grand Mas ter has approved a third annual Research Lodge
Conference to be held in San Francisco in Jul y. 1964. which the Grand
Lodges of Oregon, Washington and Arizona have been invited to
attend or participate. All Master Masons are invited to be present.
The theme of the conference will be: Let Freedom Ring.
Again, this year, your committee will continue one of the most popular portions of Grand Lodge Week: the Tuesday evening Masonic
Education Seminar, beginning at 7 P .M. at the California Masonic
Memorial Temple a t 1111 California Street. There will be a special
added event this year. The nationally famous Northern California DeMolay Show and Band will perform in the main auditorium just prior
to the opening of the joint session. The complete program for the
seminar is attached.
Your Education Committee has also provided during the year a
small Masonic article on the Apron, suitable for reading in the Lodge or
reprinting in the Lodge Bulletin . This was so used by many of the
Lodges. The outstanding publication of the committee was the pamphlet
titled : " What C an A Mason Tell A Non-Mason About Freemasonry"
by Elbert W. Davis. Past Grand Lecturer. This pamphlet has been reprinted several times as many Lodges are now purchasing the pamphlet
for distribution to each member of the Lodge. Copies can be ordered
directly from Grand Lodge at 5 cents each.
The committee has been actively engaged in completing a question
and answer booklet which it hopes to publish this coming year. This
booklet will provide answers to many of the questions about Masonry
which are frequently a s ked.
Because of the considerable interest aroused by the televised Masonic interview with our Grand Secretary Edward H. Siems. a 16 mm.
motion picture film has been made from the original video tape. This
film is available for showing in Lodges and at open Masonic meetings.
The running time is 6 minutes. A special subcommittee of the M asonic
Education Committee is studying the question of the preparation of
additional Masonic films. tapes, etc. for general circulation to the California Lodges. A further report on this subject will be made during the
coming year.
The committee wishes to acknowledge the encouragement and support of our Grand M aster M. W. Ira W. Coburn, always willing to
lend of his time and energies in the cause of Masonic education.
Many details of our work could not have been accomplished without
the invaluable aid and assistance of our Grand Secretary, Assistant
Grand Secretary and their staffs.
In attempting to summarize the benefit of the va·s t expenditures of
time, energy and money on behalf of Masonic education, your committee would like to quote from the Illinois Intender Handbook: "In

recent decades the emphasis has been changing from merely producing
'bright' Masons, i.e .. those proficient in the rituals, to that of producing
;nte/ligent Masons - Masons who not only love their ritual and know
how to present it effectively, but who also have an ample knowledge of
the background. the aims. and the purposes of the Fraternity." If your
Committee on M osonic Education has been able to contribute to this
changing emphasis, then it is confident it has merited its existence.
Respectfully submitted.

GRAND ORATION
"WE ARE BUILDERS. YET"
CHARLES BECKER, Grand Orator
M o;,t Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished Guests. My Brethren:
We belong to the great fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons.
The implements of our Craft, however, are no longer for operative toil.
We do not now. as part of our covenant, set fast the Doric pillar nor
release from marble the ornament of the Corinthian capit;:il. We no
longer sketch the complications of Gothic piles, and cement buttresses
of haughty towers, and carry up, course by course, the aspiring stones
of pinnacles. The tools of the Craft are representative now of speculative
truth and speak to the inward eye of laws and duties that make life
noble and character symetrical and strong. Yet, though we build no
structures such as our ancient brethren reared, though the temples in
which we meet are not the monuments of our own proficiency in the
art whose instruments we cherish, we are builders and preservers in a
richer sense, for our Order itself grows stronger and more precious
with years, and its uses are more varied and beautiful with the lapse
of time.
"The Masonic organization is far more remarkable and wonderful
than the noblest edifice it ever added to the landscape of history.
"Let us pause, brethren, on the word 'organization'. Man can arrange, manufacture, weave, forge, adjust, refine. but he cannot organize
as nature does. He can make machines through which the forces of
nature will play for cunning ends, but he cannot conjure the principle of
life into any mould of his making. He can start shuttles that will weave
a carpet for the reception room of a palace in one loom .... He can tell
how sugar is secreted in the veins of a clover blossom but he cannot make
a clover seed and you might well ask the wisest scientific man to fashion
a world, as to create one of the green needles which a pine tree produces
by the million, or one of the innumerable blades of grass.
"But the great glory of organization is when it is revealed in human
life.
"In savage life men are slightly organized. A savage tribe is like a
heap of sand, the atoms are distinct, they are aggregated, not combined;
no beautiful product springs from them; and the first wind of disaster
blows them away. A half civilized nation is but slightly organized, so
far as noble purposes and high sentiments are concerned. Progress is
marked by wider. higher, finer developments, issuing from the combination and co-partnership of souls. There can be no such thing as justice
until men, in la rge masses. are rightly related to each other. There can
be no prosperity in a community until the majority of its people are so

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

213

organized that their minds receive training, and their energies are unfettered. There can be no happiness, except as the result of proper
relations permanently established between the different classes or strata
of the social world.
"No man liveth to himself. Whether one member suffer, all members
suffer with it; or one member be honored , all the members rejoice with it.
... When a compacted unity of living beings is seen one of the most
precious objects for which the world was built is attained. A large and
well ordered family is such a jewel. A neighborhood at peace and free
from scandal is, - or rather I should say, would be - a still more precious jewel of the same quality. A state, a nation. so constructed that the
forces of all ranks of its inhabitants should be brought into play, and
rights of all ranks should be saved from pressure, would be a more
marvelous and a more inspiring structure than the material order and
harmony of our solid globe.
"It is in the light of this principle that the value and nobleness of
Masonry appear.
"This is the most remar kable social organization in the world. None
on the globe. with half so many elements in its composition, is so old .
. , . We delight to feel. brethren . that the past, measured by as many
ages, is under us; but it is not beneath us in broken symmetry, and a
dead grandeur as (the ruins) under Jerusalem . It is ra ther beneath us
as the roots are beneath the tree, and as the central rings are hidden in
the trunk. They give power ... to the structure still. They are parts
of its present majesty, sources of its living vigor, prophecies of its future
strength.
"We should take satisfaction. brethren, nay, a noble pride, in the
consciousness o.f the age and vastness of our organization. Shall we not
feel that there is dignity. that there is privilege, in being living :flber·s of
an organization which has passed from one era of the world to another
... which has on its roll names that sparkle in history like sovereign
stars, and which exists. not for purposes of private aggrandizement, or
the selfish joy of its members, but to give deeper root to good principles
in the world. and to diffuse the spirit of peace and order? If a Mason
is not grateful and glad over his fellowship, it is because he does not
appreciate the value in the world of the organization of good ....
"Society is struggling to reach the order which nature thus indicates.
Civilization is ye t in its infancy. There is no town, no village, yet where
the bounty of nature to all the needy is fulfilled. Let us be grateful.
brethren. that within our fellowship charity is organized, as well as law
and peace . ..•
"How good and how precious it is for brethren to dwell in such
unity!"

are the words of Thomas Staiir King spoken one hundred years ago, on

At the unveiling ceremonie s in Washingt on, Senator Samuel Shortridge said of this man:
"I would have you kno~ him. as we knew him. He was frail of body,
but transcendent~y great m mind. Gentle, affectiona te, unassumin g,
happy when serving, and endowed with a marvelous gift of speech, he
quickly won the love and admiration of our people ... .
. "It c~n b~ said in very truth that Thomas Starr King fell in love
with California and that California fell in love with him. No pen , no
ton~ue , has more vividly or more eloquently described the physical
glories of that State than did pen and tongue of this reverend man.
. ".But you ask me why we loved him; w hy we exalt him; why we place
him m bro~ze here in the Capitol of the Republic. Soon a fter his coming
to California the battle of the brothers, the Civil War, broke out. Thomas
Starr King hated no man, no State. but oh how he reverenced the Constitution and loved the Republic. He flung himself in a spirit of loyalty
t~ the defense of the fl ag of Washingt on a nd Jefferson and Jackson and
~mcoln .. By da y and night, across va lleys and through mountain passes,
m sunshme and storm. he traveled and appealed in behalf of the Union.
Nobler or more eloquent appeals were never made in behalf of the Republic. Wearied, he never faltered; and though warned by his friends,
he ~.ever rested during those dark and doubtful days.
A~~ the?· like Moses in sight of the promised land-in sight of the
Republi.c s triumphan t flag- in sight of the Union he saved-in sight of

4th. 1864. ~hus from the cradle to the grave he traveled but forty years.
H e passed mto the nobler life with a smile on his lips. repeating in a

wept, the Nation wept.
"Though dead, he speaks to us a nd enjoins upon us to be faithful to

Such was the tribute to a man who was a Mason!
And now, my brothers, as we meet here one hundred years later, let
us examine our craft; let us exa mine our orga nization to see if we are
builders and preservers yet; whether our O rder itself has grown stonger
and more precious with years and whether its uses have become more
varied and beautiful with the lapse of time. Let us look at the business
in which we are engaged.
1

It is obvious at the outset that our methods, policies, procedures and
practices are the same; that our ideals. principles and tenets are the
same; that our avowed purposes are the same; that Free M asonr y is
today the same as it has always been and always shall be. Certainly our
business has expanded in volume but do our records , a t the same time.
show that we have increased or expanded in either achieveme nt or activitiy? Do our records show that we a re builders yet, not of material buildings which decay and waste away by the lapse of time itself; but rather
builders of edifices with materials of integrity, ethics, mora ls, and virtues
which last forever ? Or have we stopped building?
The physical structures in many instances which housed the meeting
places of our brethren one hundred years ago no longer stand or exist
because they were made of pedshable physical. material things. But the
institution s which Free M asons build and establish wherever needed, any
place in the world, can never be affected by the lapse of time but continue
forever, so lon g as man exists. These structures are made not with stones
and bricks. They are built with truth, honesty, respect and justice for
all men-inde structible materials. Such constructi on may be, from time
to time, interrupte d by forces foreign to these truths; whose very existence is dependent upon suppressin g truth. suppressin g knowledg e, subjugating the wills of men , and where freedom. liberty and justice is
unknown . But as we have seen in each instance where such building was
interrupte d, it was only for a temporary period of time. because even
though the builders of such forces, systems or governme nts deny the
existence of. or necessity for our divine laws of human nature. freedom,
honesty and justice, their mere denial does not abolish these human laws.
which though spiritual in form are as much a part of nature as the physical laws themselves.
In evaluating the business in which we are engaged further, it a ppears to some perhaps that the Free M ason today is more speculatin g
than speculative; that h e has reached a point in his evolution, that he has
so progressed in his profession from the operative M ason to the speculative one, it is reasonabl e for him, in view of the great number of men
similarly occupied . to merely make his investmen t in the organizati on and
then leave it to the others to do all the necessary work, and hope that all
things will turn out well.
It appears, my brethren, that today we are perhaps more speculatin g
than speculativ e. While we have thousands upon thousands of men
employed in our craft, there are no signs, no obvious signs, of construction of worth while human structures . The greatest number of our craftsmen stand ready and willing at all times to expend their greatest effort
in doing whatever may be necessary of them to insure tha t the structures ,
the foundation s of which their ancient brothers built. remain strong and
sound at all times. Some cra ftsmen , of course, may be more technically

218

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

skilled than others but each is capable of doing hi s part a nd his share of
the necessary work. We must agree that the edifices our ancient
brethren reared, while they stand as beautiful and sturdy as when first
erected, they are today in need of some repair. S uch a structure, no
matter where built, is built to serve the world and the building cannot be
restored to its entire beauty and glory if there is need of repair any place
in the world.
We say that Masonry is universal and that in every age and every
clime are Masons to be found. Masons, yes, but masonry. no. We
have seen in our own time the disbanding of masonry by government al
decree, but we need only to look at the form of the government to understand the true basis for this infamous action. They would have their
people believe that such action is necessary because Free Masonry is a
secret organization and as such is a threat to their government . How
smug we would be to believe this. How powerful we would believe we
were, to be able to keep hidden any secrets whatver they may be, when
these same forces are able to acquire some of the most closely guarded
security information of a nation. If then there is work to be done. and
at the same time there is no apparent activity, if this be true, then in
evaluating the business in which we are engaged we must endeavor to
learn the reasons.
We know tha t when our brethren in this country had work to do at
the time of the Revolutiona ry W ar, they did it. We know that when
there was work to be done respecting h uman righ ts. as well as freedom,
that there should be no taxation without representation, our brethren
did it. And, we know tha t when a republic was to be formed by the
people, there were M asons there and they did it, and we gave support
to the public school at a time when it was most needed.
Can it be, my brethren. that our craftsmen, to some extent, are not
working today because they have no know ledge of what is expected of
them beyond attaining their certificate, or that they are unaware as to
where their efforts and energies might be usefully employed? H ave we
so impressed our craftsmen at the outset of their membership that they
believe all things Masonic are secret and confidential; or if this be not
so, then they do not even know what is to be, and should be revealed
and that which should not be revealed.
What a shame it is for any Mason when asked by a non-Mason,
" What is this masonry to which you belong? What does it do? What
does it stand for? " and tha t M ason replies, "I cannot tell you because it
is a secret." What a pity it is for any Mason w ho has just been initiated,
when on returning home, his family is patiently waiting for him and
asks, "What kind of organization did you join? What are you supposed
to do? and what is masonry all about?" and he replies, " Don't ask me
because I cannot tell you. " What a tragedy it is that we do not draw

clear. plain and understanda ble designs upon the trestle board so that
our craftsmen may know what is expected of them and where and when
and how it is to be performed.
It is not that we are unable to draw these proper designs but perha ps
it is that we have become so busy in bringing the workmen through their
apprenticesh ip to their positions as master craftsmen, we have little time
left to then set the master craftsmen to work. What the craftsmen have
been taught they have been taug ht well, and all that a Mason should
know is contained within his training while becoming a master mason;
but thou gh he has been taught well, and though he has passed his necessary examination s and has been found proficient, it appears in many
instances that he has not learned that which h e has been taught.
This situation, however, is not of recent origin. It has existed for
many years. The only observation which is worth y, however, is that we
have been derelict over the years in making the necessary and proper
adjustments , and have been content to let business go on as us ual. My
brethren, let me read to you from the Masonic Mirror, "Devo ted to the
in terest of Masonry on the Pacific Coast." This is Volume 1, Bulletin
No. 2, and I quote:
" Every well informed Mason will agree with us in the assertion, that
there is a strange lack of Masonic knowledge in Lodges. and among
Masons generally. This ignorance even extends to the officers of the
Lodges, who ought, at least. to be posted in the ordinary governmen t of
a Lodge, if not in Masonic jurisprudence. We make Masons of good
men and true, but w hen thus made, the work has just commenced ." That
was said in October, 1869.
It has been said with some degree of sincerity, that we raise a brother
and then bury him, and very little if anything occurs in between.
We are concerned. my brethren , and ri ghtfu lly so, in learning about
our so-called public image. What does the community think o f us; what
does anyone know of us; how are we regarded individually and collectively? My brethren . we can have no public image, nor can we merit the
respect of the uninformed community so long as so many of our bre thren
are unable to give any account or even an excuse. for the existence of
the organization itself or of the purposes for which they have banded
themselves together by an indissoluble chain. We are concerned when
others fear us, we are disturbed when others are suspicious of us. and
we are confused when others d istrust us, but it is really not their fault.
We have no right to the respect of anyone when all they can learn about
us, even those w ho are interested, is nothing except that all we stand
for and all we hope to do is not for them to know. It is perfectly natural
to fear the darkness . but w hat we actually fear is not the absence of
light, but the insecurity in not knowing what might be lurking there.
How ridiculous we must appear when we expect worthy men to join with
us without any knowledge of what their application might be leading

them into. We have been instructed and properly so. that the ritualistic
work of our ceremonies is confidential. known only to Masons, and is
the means by which we may identify one another. Therefore, the Mason
who says that Masonry is a secret organiza tion , is in fact saying that
there is nothing more to Masonry than ritual. Perhaps he is right.
We say that Masonry is a progressive moral science, but our progress
instead of being forward as progress should be, appears to be circular,
going round and round from one degree to another and then back to the
beginning again. What a shock it must have been to some, to see a fourpage spread in a nationally distributed magazine on "Free and Accepted
Masons," including pictures and symbols. There were many I know who
resented this article because they felt it was too revealing, however, the
artic:le concluded with this paragraph:
"While the ritual of Free Masonry remains secret from the world,
the fraternity has for hundreds of years taught its members that Masons
must share in the cons truction of the temple of brotherhood for all races,
religions, tongues and nationalities."
There for ten cents, my brethren, more good was done in explaining
Masonry for all to know than it appears we have been able to do regardless of the amount of our investment.
You may be wondering why I am belaboring this point. It is only
because such conditions do actually exist and any evaluation which did
not recognize them would be incomplete. What utter nonsense it is to
say that Masonry is secret when there is more information published
about this organization than any other, and you need only to go the any
encyclopedia to find page after page of the history, background, principles and obligations of a Mason. I have said many times that Masonry
by its very nature is not and cannot be secret. because if there is any
thought, any deed, any act contemplated or done by a Mason or a group
of Masons which cannot stand the gaze of public inspection then for
sure any such thought. deed or act is not Masonic.
How then does our business appear to you as we look at our situation today-one hundred yea rs later? There are many who say that our
principles today are just as pure and righteous as they always have been,
therefore, we should do nothing which might in the slightest affect the
purity of these principles. Certainly if we belie\'e that Masonry is a state
of mind , a philosophy, a .get of moral virtues which requ ires no doing, but
just believing. then we have made of Masonry an impotent source for
good and need expect nothing to result from it. On the other hand, there
are those who because of lack of knowledge, lack of understanding and
lack of true Masonic interest believe that our way of doing business is
archaic and old fashioned: therefore, we should change our methods and
become more competitive with other modern organizations. There then
is the conflict, not an unsurmountable one, but a conflict between those
who believe that any activity, regardless of how well intended, on the

part of Masons, might possibly be disapproved or misinterpreted by
others. thus causing a controversy. a nd rather than risk such a situation,
it is perhaps best not to do anything, or say anything or become involved
in anything at all . and those who say we should "do like the other
folks do."
The business of Masonry cannot progress nor can Masonry continue to be the progressive moral science we say it is under either theory
of this conflict. Masonry. though pure, and virtuous and righteous was
never intended to be so noble that it was not practical and unattainable:
nor was Masonry intended merely because it espoused the cause of the
common man, and requires that Masons respect and have a wholesome
concern for the welfare of all men that it should be reduced in its operations to the catering only to the whims and pleasures of man.
The real business of Masonry is serious and active and the action of
the Mason in his work is huma n and exemplary. It may be likened to
some extent to that of a non-profit corporation in that it was organized
to render public service for the good of all without any profit inuring to
any of the stockholders. This, therefore, means that for Masonry to be
progressive, it must be active and vital, current and living. The greatest
of literary manuscripts has no significance whatever, if it is not read.
The most sensitive of musical compositions gives no pleasure unless it
is played, and the mos t beautiful objects of art reflect no beauty unless
they are seen; so it is true with Free Masonry. The noblest of our tenets, the most virtuous of our principles are meaningless and as of naught
unless and not until they a re actively practiced by the craftsmen.
Knowledge that is not experienced is valueless and unfulfilled intentions
are worthless. •
We repeat with great and justifiable pride at every opportunity the
history of our early American brethren and the important feats which
they accomplished. We are proud of these accomplishments and we
are proud of these Masons because they portray Masons in action. As
we review our organization one hundred years later, I believe it is fair
for each of us to ask ourselves, "What have I done-what am I doing?"
How many times since becoming a Mason have we reminded ourselves
and proved to others by our actions that in us as Masons, hypocrisy
and deceit are unknown, that we. as Masons. are distinguished by our
sincerity and plain dealing , and that with heart and tongue, as Masons,
we join in promoting the welfare and happiness of others?
We require that a Mason's actions be efficient and proficient, that
they be uniform and conform, that they be traditional and customary
but, my brethren , what about brotherly love, relief and truth; temperance, fortitude. prudence and justice; charity. fraternity and good will
toward all men. We measure the success of our action not by any
power, position or possessions, but rather by the closeness of performance of our ideals. As Masons we have not only the duty to conscien-

tiously believe in the principles and tenets of Free Masonry but we
also have the duty and obligation to act at every opportunity and on
every occasion in their performance. We have the duty and responsibility to resist actively that which is wrong, unjust and untrue-it is not
enough just to say that we are against it. We must all realize that the
more we have the more we owe to others, and, my brothers. it takes a
big man to champion a small cause.
We must realize, and teach the others, that the Lodge Room is only
where Masons meet to be enlightened, but the real work of the Mason
is done ou~side the Lodge, wherever the need may be.
Our duty is then clear. If we are to prosper during the next century,
we must convince the world by our actions that on becoming Masons we
have become better men; and that we are engaged in the industry of
spreading useful knowledge, practicing unceasing and unostentatious
charity and inculcating fraternity and good will among all men.
By your actions outside the Lodge shall ye be judged, by your
actions outside the Lodge shall Masonry be judged: thus shall the image
of Free Masonry be born. On that day every Mason shall stand in the
pathway or at his doorway and all who pass him shall know, that he is
one to whom the burdened heart may pour its sorrows, one to whom
distress may prefer its suit, one whose hand is guided by justice and
whose heart is expanded by benevolence. We are builders, yet. On that
day, all Masons will say to all who are in need, to all who are in fear,
to all who are enslaved and to all who are not free, I am a Mason, try me.
The Grand Oration was received with a standing ovation.
The Grand Ma·s ter directed the Grand Secretary to have the printed
copies of the oration made available to the members of Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
At the 1962 Communication of Grand Lodge the dispensation of
Triad Lodge U.D. was continued for an additional year. It has no w
petitioned for a charter.
At the same Communication the Committee on Charters recorded
the fact that Old West Lodge U.D. had been instituted October 2.
1962, by authority of a dispensation dated the same day. The dispensation being dated and institution occurring during the month of the
1962 Communication, no action by Grand Lodge was called for, a nd
the Lodge continued under dispensation until October l, 1963. T his
Lodge has now petitioned for a charter.
Four more Lodges have been instituted since the close of the 1962
Communication and the Opening of the 1963 Communication. Of these
four, two have petitioned for charters, and two are not yet in a position
to do so for reasons which will be explained.
The two which have petitioned for charters are Mount Baldy U .D.
and Plaza de Los Angeles U.D.
We thus have a total of four Lodge~ seeking charters. They submitted their records and sent delegates who appeared before the Committee on Charters. We will treat our recommendations as to these in
two sections:
First, in the cases of Triad. Old West. and Plaza de Los Angeles.
we found some errors or omissions in their records. but these were not
sufficiently material to detract from the over-all favorable picture. The
Inspectors accompanied the delegates in their appearances before the
Committee, and as a result of constructive exchange of views, the errors
and omissions either were corrected or assurance given that this would
be done.
Therefore. we are able to report that the work and proceedings of
these three Lodges prove satisfactory; they have produced certificates
that their respective proposed Masters and Wardens are each thoroughly skilled in the work and lectures, and they have shown that they
are clear of all indebtedness.
The Committee on Charters, therefore, unanimously recommends
that charters be granted and numbers assigned as follows:
Triad Lodge No. 812 at Montebello, in the County of Los Angeles;
Old West Lodge No. 813 at Newhall, in the County of Los Angeles;
Plaza de Los Angeles Lodge No. 814 at Los Angeles, in the County
of Los Angeles.
Second, in the case of Mount Baldy Lodge U .D., this Lodge was
instituted on November 24, 1962, in the City of Ontario and as previously noted has presented a petition for a charter. In considering this

224

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

petition , the Committee finds many factors in their favor. The Lodge
has grown from 49 charter members to a present membership of 64 and
has been diligent in carrying out Grand Lodge activities.
The purpose of a Lodge being carried under a dispensation is to provide a period in which the Lodge can establish its ability to conduct its
affairs and prove to this Grand Lodge that it has a sound basis for
future growth and stability. The burden of proof is upon the Lodge and
the dispensation granted by the Grand Master charges the M aster and
W ardens with this responsibility : "To return the dispensation with
their Books of Records, an a ttested copy of their By-Laws. and a full
report of the doings of their said Lodge to our Grand Lodge ... for
examination and for su ch further action in the premises as sh~ll then be
deemed wise and proper."
In the present instance it proved inconvenient for the Master or
Wardens to be present so the Master appointed the Secretary. the
Senior and Junior Deacons to represent the Lodge before the Committee. It should be pointed out that these three Brethren had been very
active in the format ion of the Lodge and obviously had the interests of
the Lodge at heart. however, the Committee on Charters was unable
to confer with those officers directly responsible for past and immediate
future conduct of the Lodge.
The records submitted reflected very little gain in financial strength
during a year of operation. The Lodge had purchased equipment
amounting to about $600.00 and had dropped behind about this amount
in its cash position . In other words, had the purchases not been necessary, the Lodge would have about broken even. A projection of somewhat higher expenses reasonably to be expected in the future creates
doubt about the Lodge's ability to break even with present revenues.
The Lodge has been operating on minimum dues and fees and has considered increasing them but has taken no action to date.
We do not see any serious difficulties ahead for this Lodge that
cannot be remedied by proper action: however, we feel that the Lodge
will be strengthened by having their dispensation continued for another
year so that they \\'ill have an opportunity to put into effect such revisions in their operations as will tend to remove any possibility of
financial deficiency. We do not intend to overemphasize the question
of finances but set it forth here as merely one of the fa ctors needing
remedial action.
Another factor which cannot be overlooked, even though it is not
determinative on the question. is the apparent belief on the part of
those responsible for governing the Lodge. including their Inspector,
that the obtaining of a charter was routine and perfunctory. These
Brethren ha,·e in good faith. but erroneously, overlooked ( 1) the fact
that the Grand Lodge holds absolute determination of whether a c~ar­
ter will be granted. and ( 2) that it is mandatory for the Lodge to satisfy
Grand Lodge that its work and proceedings have been satisfactory

It is the opinion of this Committee that Grand Lodge has no other
Cemetery obligations than the three named in this report and t?at when
they are cleaned up and put in a respectable condition, the maintenance
for the combined three should not be over $1,500.00 or $2,000.00 per
year. It is felt, however, that some consideration _and study be made as
to the possibility and cost of placing the Columbia Cemetery under endowed care. If there is no objection from this Grand Lodge, the Committee will proceed to make such a study.
The neglected state of the cemetery in Grass V alley, owned by
Madison Lodge No. 23 has been corrected by that Lodge.
During the year a representative of this Committee visited a num~er
of cemeteries in the southern part of California. particularly those which
have set aside sections for the burial of Masons and their families. Included in such visits were: Rose Hills Memorial Park. Whittier; Forest
Lawn, Glendale; Valhalla, Burbank, and Memory Garden Memorial
Park, Brea. Each of these, as well as many others in the area, are operated by private corporations under State law providing for perpetual
care and reflect no discredit upon the Fraternity.
Specific assignments were as follows :
Hueneme Masonic Cemetery Association: This is a California corporation , originally started around the turn of the century by. members
of the now extinct Hueneme Lodge No. 311. The cemetery 1s located
in a remote but growing section between Oxnard and Port Hueneme
and is in a neglected condition. The whereabouts of many of the stockholders are unknown; however. some local Masons are on the Board of
Directors. For several years, this Committee has urged that the corporation take steps to eliminate the word "Masonic" from its corporate
title, without success. It is therefore recommended that the matter be
referred to the Committee on Commercialism, which has power to act
under Section 332-A CMC.
Memory Garden Memorial Park, Brea: This cemetery, a relatively
new operation, serves a large area in which there are seven Lodges of
the 628 and 629th Districts. It is tastefuUy laid out a nd well manag~d
by high grade people. A section has been set aside, known as Acacia

229

Lawn. upon which the corporation has contracted for the erection of a
marble altar with a replica of the open Holy Bible. It is desired, upon
completion of the altar, to dedicate the same with appropriate Grand
Lodge ceremony. This Committee recommends that ·s uch dedication be
approved with the proviso that the inscription on the Bible be biblical
rather than Masonic. The cemetery corporation has already gone on
record that it will not take advantage of the M asonic name in selling
lots in this section.
This Committee, operating under Section 204 CMC, would be
greatly aided in its efforts if the Inspectors of the several Masonic Districts in the State would request Lodges under their jurisdiction owning
cemeteries or sections thereof, to see that such properties are creditably
maintained.
We wish to express our sincere thanks to the Grand Master, Most
Worshipful Ira W. Coburn, who has given us much encouragement and
sound advice, to the Grand Secretary and his gracious staff for all their
help, and to the Inspectors of the several Districts, who have always
been most helpful in lining up proper men for the various jobs that
had to be done. Our thanks also to those, who. while not members of
the Fraternity. have taken the time to phone or write letters expressing
their appreciation to the Grand Lodge for their efforts in restoring
the Columbia Cemetery.
Respectfully submitted.

REPORT OF BOARD OF
LIBRARY COMMISSIONERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Y our Board of Library Commissioners is glad to report a continued
interest in and usage of the facilities of the Library throughout the Jurisdiction. In this respect, the Lending Library has extended its operations
to include California Master Masons sojourning outside the confines of
this State. The expressions of appreciation that have been received from
those who have availed themselves of the facilities of the Library, 'both
inside a nd outside this Jurisdiction. demonstrate the fact that the Library
is successfully filling a long-felt need.
One new direction in which the Library has been performing a service is in the assistance it has been able to furnish to those wishing to
write papers for presentation in Lodge, as part of the program fostered

230

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

by the C ommittee on Masonic Education. One such paper, on the subject of " Elizabeth St. Leger, the Lady Freemason," by Brother Ford
E. S amuel. the Historian of Oak Grove Lodge N o. 215, was presented
at the Stated Meeting of the Lodge for April. and is indicative of the
type of activity our California Lodges might undertake. Masters and
Wardens of Lodges are urged to encourage similar activity in the future. as a means toward heightening interest in Masonry among their
members.
In this connection, it might be observed that requests for Masonic
information have come in even from hiHh school students desirous of
writing term papers on some aspect of Masonic history. These requests
have not only b een cheerfully met but have been encouraged wherever
possible.
In oddition to the lending activities of the Library. our Reference
Library has a lso been used by those able to come in and do research
work on materials that it is not deemed advisable to send out by mail.
The resources of both the Reference and the Lending Library have
been augmented this year, as in years past. by the addition of useful
and valuable Masonic works by standard authors. In this manner. 200
works have been added by gift. and 50 by purchase. At the present
writing. our stock of books stands at 2.415 volumes.
By gift, we have acquired a remarkable collection of ma terial that
has been accumula ted during a lifetime of Masonic endeavour by the
Most Worshipful Past Grand Master Leon Whitsell ( 1938). for many
years Chairman of the Committee on History, and who has given us
his voluminous notebooks. <Scrapbooks. papers and albums, all having
to do with the early history and development of California Freemasonry
and the numerous personalities involved therein, all of which will prove
more and more valuable as the years roll by. By gift, also. from the
estate of our late-lamented Brother 0. J. Wohlgemuth - "Wally," as
he was affectionately known by all. the first Chairman of the Committee
on Research (now the Committee on Masonic Education), and a past
Chairman also of the Committee on History. and a long-time collaborator with Brother Whitsell - we have acquired his equally remarkable collection of color slides of old California Masonic Temples and
their colorful interiors, with descriptive notes, and numerous memorabilia having to do with early California Masonic his tory.
One curious article that has come to us from out of this collection
of Wally Wohlgemu th's is a cylindrically -shaped object about five
inches in diameter and seven inches long, with a w ooden handle. that
looks very much like an operative stonemason's setting maul. except that
it is padded and soft. Just what practical use this curious object could
have served, we are at a loss to imagine; however, it will be preserved
in our Museum Cabinet as a relic out of the past, and perhaps some
imaginative archaeologist in the distant future may come up with some

fanciful theory as to its possible origin and purpose.
By purchase. the Museum has acquired an interesting German
M a rtin Luther Bible, first published about 1535 A.O . It is the first of
the Bibles translated from the original Hebrew into one of the languages
of Western Europe to use the name Hiram Abiff. Earlier translations.
and many of the later ones. leave out the Abiff. This collector's item
therefore has obvious Masonic interest and significance.
The continued purchase of books for the Library has been found
necessnry beca use of the fact that the acquisition of books by gift alone
has not been found to be adequate. The more s ubstantial works. that
give permanent and unusual value to any Masonic Library, are hard
to come by, and are generally not in the hands of the average Mason.
They must consequently be purchased, if our collection is to be rounded
out. and must be sought out. mostly in second-hand bookstores. in different parts of the world, since these valuable works are generally out
of print. A request has accordingly been made for an adequate appropriation for that purpose in the Budget we are submitting for your
approval. While the space available for our books helves is necessarily
limited . there is still plenty of room for expansion for years to come.
and it is planned that the Library will remain within its present confines
for the foreseeable future, and certanly within the limits of the Temple
building.
In addition to the acquistion of books by purchase. the continuous
donation of Masonic books and articles of related interest to your
Grand Lodge Library and Museum , by individual members and by
Lodges who may not have adequate facilities for storing them, is to be
encouraged. and is therefore brought to your attention once again. One
such article, recently donated to us by Thousand Oaks Lodge No. 478
of Berkeley - a beautiful bust in Wedgewood China of a nineteenth
century Past Grand Master of the United Grand Lodge of England the Earl of Zetland - now proudly stands on a suitable pedestal in
your Grand Lodge Library.
We urge that the facilities the Library offers to California Masons
be br~ught to the attention of Lodge members regularly, throurih Lodge
bulletins. Unfortunately, too many Master Masons throughout the
Jurisdiction are still unaware that a Lending Library exists for their
benefit and is willing and anxious to be of service.
For the benefit of visitors to the Masonic Temple, the Library has
been kept open two days a week, on Mondays and Wednesdays, and
our gratitude goes out to those devoted brethren whose services have
ma~e _it _possible to keep the Library open to visitors not only of this
J unsd1ct1on but from Jurisdictions around the world. During the last
twelve-month period, as many as 1.215 signatures from su~h visitors
have been counted in our Registry Book, some from countries half-way
around the world. In this connection. thanks are due to Brother William

From the above figures one can easily perceive where th~ most effective action has taken place. It is true that it is easier to secure
sojourners in a small, growing residential community than in a more
static big city. Nevertheless, Los Angeles No. 42 and Hollywood No.
355. which a re situated in the midst of a city, had considerable success. It is the continued belief of this committee that success will attend
only the most diligent of effort by the Lodge Officers who may. or may
not. feel that it is worth this effort.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON COLUMBIA TEMPLE

May I now take this opportunity to thank all of the members of this
committee, the custodian of the Temple and particularly the various
Blue Lodges that have made the pilgrimage to this grand replica .
Respectfully submitted.
CHESTER M . SMITH

240

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
May we the Committee for Columbia Temple, report that the building now meets with the approval of the State Park Fire & Safety Marshal. that approved type fire extinguishers and proper exit signs have
been installed.
The exterior of the building is being treated with a waterproofing
in preparation for the protection from the elements during the next
three years. The heating and cooling equipment have been inspected
and reported to be in good order.
The station emblems that were presented to Grand Lodge at the
1962 Communication have been installed. to the pleasure of all who
have attended Columbia Temple.
On November 15th, the committee received a letter from the Grand
Master with a copy of a report he received showing that the Jurisprudence and Finance Committees had concurred on the matter presented to them by Past Grand Master Guy Mize with regard to the
University of Pacific using the ground floor of the Columbia Temple
for a Museum of Early California H istory. In response to the Grand
Master's letter. the Committee on Columbia Temple met February 9,
1963. with representatives from University of Pacific in Columbia
to discuss the matter of a museum at Columbia Temple. The meeting
was well represented with members of the State Parks and Beaches,
Univel'sity of P acific and Columbia Temple Committee. The matter of the museum was discussed pro and con with the final result that
all were favorable to the museum but with the provision that Grand
Lodge should maintain control of its policy as well as exhibitions in
the museum proper. This matter was reported back to the Grand
Master a nd in turn the Grand Secretary was to contact the Depart.men t of State Parks and Beaches in regard to ·c onditions of lease, etc.
A meeting was held on this matter with the Grand Master and Grand
Secretary, members of California State Parks and Beaches, University
members, members o f Columbia State Park and California State Park
Historians. Many and various conditions were discussed at this rneet-ing with the final result that the State Parks and Beaches highly approves the proposed museum with the provision that Grand Lodge
maintain full and complete control.
On August 1st, Grand Lodge published a list of resolutions presented for 1963 Communication in which a resolution is printed with
regard to Columbia Temple and a Masonic Museum.
Your committee now stands ready and eager to fulfill the wishes
of Grand Lodge in the establishment of a museum on the ground Boor
of the Columbia Temple.

REPORT OF CODE COMMISSION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Code Commission reports that, as the brethren are aware, a
cumula tive supplement for the California Masonic Code, covering the
decisions approved and changes made in our law between 1957 and
1962. was compiled and published following the close of the last Communication. It is regretted that there w<1s a delay in delivery due to
some unfortunate circumstances. and plans have been made to expedite
the publication of the next supplement covering the changes m<1de
this year so that the brethren may have those changes as soon as
possible a fter the close of this Communication.
In order to cover possible travel and other expenses of your commission, it is requested that an appropriation of $150 be made.
Respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM NANKERVIS, JR.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
Since filing our repor t for 1962, there have been no changes in the
payroll ta x laws or the Federal Admission Tax which apply to our
various Masonic organizations.
As has been our custom in past years , we present, for reference
purposes, the usual schedule of tax rates and wage bases for the variious payroll ta xes which will be in effect during the calendar year
1961 and thereafter. We again present in our report a section on
Federa l Admissions Tax.
FEDERAL WITHHOLDING (IN COM E) TAX

All wages paid to employees of a Masonic Lodge are s ubject to
Federal income tax w ithholding. In order to determine the amou nt of
income tax which is to be withheld from wages paid to its employees.
the Lodge should ask each employee to complete and file with the Secretary of the Lodge <l Federal Form W -1, Employee's Withholding
Exemption Certificate. Reference to withholding tax tables furn ished
by the Treasury Department will enable the Secretary to determine the
amount to be withheld.
FEDERAL I NSURANCE CONTRIBUTIONS (SOCIAL SECURITY) ..

An employee of a Masonic Lodge is subject to tax for each calendar quarter during which he earns $50, or more. The tax ra tes shown
below are applicable to the first $1,800 of wages paid to each employee
during the calendar year. These rates are to be paid by both the employer and the employee.
Calendar Year
Percent
1964 th rough 1965
3%
1966 through 1967
1 Ys
1968 and thereafter
1%
There is a possibility that changes may be made by the Congress
in the wage base and/or percentage rate applicable to the year 1964.
FEDERAL UNEMPLOYMENT TAX

Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if they employ fo ur or
more individuals who are paid $50 or more per calendar quarter, providing they have first qualified as an "employer" by employing four
or more employees on at least one day in each of twenty or more
weeks during the calendar year. For this purpose, all paid employees
of the Lodge, including the Secretary and those who are performing
ritualistic services (Tiler, Organist. Soloist), should be counted if they
recei ve $50 or more per calendar quarter.
Federal Unemployme nt Ta x at the rates shown below will be applicable to the first $3,000 of wages paid to each employee during the
calendar year. However, Lodges which are subject to the California

TRIAL RECORDS NOS. 1145, 1235, 1559, 1574, 1580,
1628, 1630, 1646 AND 1651
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Petitions for restoration have been received from the accused in
the following trial records:
No. 1145-A member of Whittier Lodge No. 323.
No. 1235-A member of Mountain View Lodge No. 194.
No. 1559-A member of Poinsettia Lodge No. 633.
No. 1574-A member of Belvedere Lodge No. 539.
No. 1580-A member of Hollenbeck Lodge No. 319.
No. l 628-A member of Ashlar Lodge No. 306.
No. 1630-A member of Fresno Lodge No, 247,
No. 1646-A member of Foothill Lodge No. 564.
No. 1651-A member of The Gardens Lodg e No. 621.
ln determining whether or not a petition for restoration should be
granted. your committee takes into consideration many facts such as
the seri~usness. of the Masonic offense of which the accused is charged,
the period which has elapsed from the date of expulsion by Grand

251

Lodge to the date of the petition for restoration, whether or not the
accused has sufficiently rehabilitated himself, letters of recommendation submitted on behalf of the accused , if any, and the feeling of
the accused's former Lodge as to whether he should be restore~ .
.
It should be pointed out that when a petition for restoration 1s
approved by Grand Lodge the accused becomes a member at large,
and consequently must petition his former Lodge or another Lodge
for affiliation.
Your committee has given full consideration to all th e petitions
submitted and, based upon facts of each individual record, offers the
following resolution:
.
.
RESOLVED: That the petitions for restorat10n m the following
trial records be granted:
No. 1235-A member of Mountain View Lodge No. 194.
No. 1559-A member of Poinsettia Lodge No. 633.
No. 1574-A member of Belvedere Lodge No. 539.
No. 1580-A member of Hollenbeck Lodge No. 319,
No. 1630-A member of Fresno Lodge No. 247.
No. 1646-A member of Foothill Lodge No. 564,
No. 1651-A member of The Gardens Lodge No. 621,
and that the petitions for restoration in the following trial records be
denied:
No. 1145-A member of Whittier Lodge No. 323,
No. 1628-A member of Ashla r Lodge No. 306.
Adopted.

• TRIAL RECORD NO. 1797
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Accused member of Marin Lodge No. 191 was charged with moles ting a minor of which he had been found guilty in th~ state_ courts: H e
was given notice of the charges, which notice required him to file a
plea within five days. He filed no plea and eve~tually the Tr~al Master
reported to the Lodge, making a finding of guilty and ordermg expulsion.
There is no authority for a five-day notice. If the accused is in the
same county as the Lodge, ten days notice is required: if elsewhere,
thirty days.
Although the finding of guilt in this case is true and correct, th_e
lack of proper notice is jurisdictional. When we expel a Mason it
should be done properly, no matter how bad he may be.
We, therefore, off er the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That the expulsion in Trial Record No. 1797 be re~
versed and the matter remanded to Marin Lodge No. 191 fo.r proper
proceedings.
Adopted.
