Also among the deceased is the name of Assistant Grand Lecturer
Ralph W. Collins. Brother Donald G. Campbell. the Grand Lecturer,
will give the eulogy for Brother Collins. Our Grand Master, Most
Worshipful Ira W. Coburn, wjJl give the eulogy for his close friend,
Brother 0. ]. Wohlgemuth, the Chairman of the Special Commission
on Masonic Practices, who passed away on April 1, 1963.
In addition to these just mentioned your committee is confronted
with a long list of those who have served this Grand Lodge as officers,
committeemen, or inspectors, and of others who have rendered outstanding service to Masonry and their fellowmen. Because of the
large number who have merited mention in this report the tribute
to individuals will have to be brief.
EARL LEE KELLY of Sacramento died at Fresno on November
1st after a brief illness. He was 70 years of age. Brother Kelly was
well known in banking and civic circles. Since 1939, until his retirement, he was a Vice President of the Bank of America. Prior to 1939
he had served as State Director of Public Works for seven years,
and for two years as Chairman of the California State Highway Commission. For some time he was President of the California State Fair
Board. Earl L. Kelly was raised in Reading Lodge No. 254 on February 27. 1920, and served as Master of that Lodge in l 923. He served
this Grand Lodge as Grand Standard Bearer for two years, in 1928
and 1929. Throughout the years he has been faithful in service. California public life and California Masonry have been enriched by the
faithful service of Brother Earl Lee KeJJy.
MAX ALARIC PLUMB. A Masonic veteran of over sixty years
left us when Max A. Plumb died on November 3, 1962, at the age of
92 years. Max was raised a Mason on April 19, 1902, in Oxnard
Lodge. He became a charter member of Charter Rock Lodge No. 11 O
in February, 1910, and was Master of this Lodge in 1913. He became
Secretary of Charter Rock Lodge in 1914 and served for forty-three
yea.rs in that office. He was a co-founder of the East Bay Masters and
Wardens Association. His service in Grand Lodge was long and
varied. In 1923-24 he was Executive Secretary, Grand Lodge Committee on Education. and published a booklet and bulletins which have
been used extensively. He was a member of the Necrology Committee
1925 to 1929; served as Inspector of Berkeley District No. 30 (now
No. 316) from 1916 to 1923; <Served as Senior Grand Steward in
1919-when Edward H. Siems was Grand Master. He also served and
wa.5 honored in York and Scottish Rite Commandery. Born and educated in Connecticut, he came to the west coast in 1899 and taught in
San Francisco high schools from 1907 until the time of his retirement.
He is survived by his widow and a son and daJJghter, all residing in
the East Bay. His was an abundant life, rich in service. He lived

CYRIL WESLEY McCLEAN. Brother Cyril W. McC!ean entered into rest on April 20, 1963. He was 70 years of age. He was a
native of Waitsburg, Washington, a graduate of the University of
California, and served in the Navy in World War I. He received his
law degree in 1923 from George Washington University and about
1926 moved to Oakland and established his law practice. He served as
Chairman of Alameda County Republican Central Committee and held
important positions in the Bar Association. Brother Mac was raised a
Master Mason on February 20, 1917, and served as Master of Sequoia
Lodge No. 349 in 1935. The follcYwing year he served as Junior Grand
Deacon of this Grand Lodge. In 1936 he assumed the duties of Secretary of Sequoia Lodge and continued in that office until l 957. The
loss of this loyal Mason is felt in his own Lodge and also in this Grand
Lodge. He is survived by his widow, a son, three daughters. and I 0
grandchildren. to whom we extend sincerest sympathy.
JOHN THOMAS BOND. On June 3, 1963, John T. Bond of
Hollywood, passed away on his sixty-seventh birthday. He was raised
in Hollywood Lodge No. 355 on November 12. 1936, and later served
as Master of that Lodge. Throughout Masonic circles he was affectionately known as "Mr. Hollywood Lodge." He also served as Master of Southern California Research Lodge. In 1958 he was the competent Grand Marshal of this Grand Lodge. He held many offices and
served with distinction in many Masonic organizations.
Born in Tacoma, Brother Bond received his formal education at the
University of Washington. For 43 years he had been in the confectionery business, operating his own firm, John T. Bond & Son. A member of his own Lodge says "he will be remembered as 'Johnny-CandyBond' who made life's rough and rugged road smoother and easier by
dispensing so many kinds of much-needed sweetness along the way."
Our sympathy goes out to the widow and family of this dynamic.
warm-hearted man.
HORACE WELLS RICE. Born in San Francisco on April 11,
1892, Brother Rice passed away on June 29, 1963. Moving to San
Rafael in his early youth he had spent practically all his life in that
city. He served in World War I. Since 1927 he had been engaged in
the insurance business, retiring in 1961. Being very fond of travel he
had visited Europe and the Orient twice. He died the morning a.fter
he and his wife had returned home from a Mediterranean cruise.
Brother Rice was raised a Master Mason in Marin Lodge No. 191
on April 1, 1914 and was Master of that Lodge in 1920. It was during
his year as Master that P.G.M., and P.G.S. Lloyd E. Wilson was

Section 700a
As a part of Resolution No. 31, the Grand Secretary s~ggests that
Section 700a. being a decision of Grand Master Patton m 1900, be
repealed.
This decision held that a Master who directs the Junior Warden to
prefer charges against a member cannot preside at the trial. nor should
the charges so preferred be presented to such Master.
We believe it should be proper for the Master who orders a charge
of unmasonic conduct filed agains t a member should be authorized to
receive such charge. preside <it the mee ting for election of. ~omm.is­
sioners, and issue summons to the accused and other admm1stra t1ve
duties connected with such proceedings, but that such Master should
not preside at the trial. To repeal the e.ntire s ubsec~ion would remove
the in hibition that such Master not preside at the tnal. In order to accomplish what we believe to be proper. we offer. with the consent of
the Grand Secretary, the following resolution in two parts:
RESO LVED: That subsection 7000 be repealed, and tha t it
BE FURTHER RESOLVED : That Section 700 be amended and
that there be added thereto the words, "and provided further that a
Master who has ordered the Junior Warden to file a charge of unmasonic conduct against a member is disqualified to preside at the trial of
such member."
We move the adoption of the resolution and recommend a yes vote.
Adopted 5 / 6 vote.

RESEARCH LoDGE OFFICERS
1962 RESOLUTION ( 11 )
( P. 61 - 1962 PROCEEDINGS)
The resolution relative to Research Lodges was before Grand Lodge
at its last Communi cation and received a majority vote of approval. Because it did not receive the required 5/ 6th vote. it must now come
before Grand Lodge for reconsider ation.
This resolution would eliminate Section 385 CMC which requires
that only a Past Master of a California Lodge is eligible for election as
Master or Warden of a Research Lodge and provides that if such Master or Warden is not a Past Master of a California Lodge, he must
posse&s a certificate of proficiency in the opening and closing cere~
monies. Tt would also amend paragraph 10 to clarify the distinction
between a Past Master of a Research Lodge and a Past Master of other
constituen t Lodges.
Section 385 makes it clear that it was never intended that Research
Lodges were to be governed by the s ame regulation s as other constituen t
Lodges, wherein it is stated that "A special classification of constituen t
Lodges is hereby establishe d."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

If we are to preser ve those Research Lodges that find it difficult, if
not impossible, to interest Past Masters to serve as M asters or Wardens
of the Research Lodges, we feel tha t this resolution should be adopted.
We therefore move the resolution and your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a yes vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence recommends a no vote.
The resolution was adopted by a 2/3 vote.

As required by California Masonic Code 554w. the F lag of our

to this Committee, however, that flying the Flag on or in front of the
California Masonic Memorial T emple. not only whe n the Grand Lodge

would be necessary to employ an additional building custodian to fully

ATTENDANCE CHURCH SERVICE MAU NDY THURSDAY
(23)
This resolution would require all Lodges to be dark on the Thursday preceding Easter , except for Stated Meetings.
Masonry unites men of every faith, sect and creed and it has done
so successfully in the past because of the inflexible rule that discussion
and contention are excluded as objects of Masonic concern . In 1875 it
was said ( CMC I 6j) '' Masonry has its own proper objects and purposes, and those must be considered by us to the absolute exclusion
of all others and particularly of such as would aro use contention and
confusion."
M aundy Thursday is strictly a Christian . secta rian observance. Our
many members of other faiths would be offended if such observance
were mandatory and they would be fully justified in aski ng for similar
treatment concerning their sectarian holidays.
We think that favoring one religion. as proposed in this Resolution
23, would arouse conten tion and con fusion and lead to disharmony
within the C ra ft.
The correct M asonic reply to all requests for such sectar ian observances is a firm denial. Thus will we continue to unify those of differing
creeds and promote the great objects of Freemasonry in California.
We move the adoption of the resolution and urge a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

LIMITING SIZE OP LODGES
(27)
Resolution No. 27 proposes that the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee to prepare legislation governing the size of our
Lodges for action of this Gra nd Lodge in 1964. Smaller Lodges are
desirable but no jurisdiction has been able to achieve this result by stat~
utory ac tion. Insurmountable diffic ulties arise from any ri gid rules of
limitation. Lodges with members hip over the maximum provided would
have to cease their Masonic work. Lodges would be in the same dilemma
when their membership reached the max imum. Larger Lodges would
have to look forwa rd to many funerals for certainly there could be no
legislation forcing a certain nu mber of Brothers to withdraw from a
Lodge, by lot or otherwise. On the other hand voluntary action can be
most effective. In one city in our jurisdiction the old established Lodge
assisted in the formation of an additional Lodge, even to the extent of
giving some of its officers to the new group. The results were spectacular and soon led to the formation of still another Lodge. The mother
Lodge has prospered and Freemasonry in the communi ty has been
strengthened. This could not have been accomplished by legislation.
W e move the adoption of the resolution but urge a no vote.
A majority voted against the r esolution.

RECOMM ENDATIO NS

The Grand Lodge Committ ee on Masonic Informat ion conclude d
their report with four recomme ndations which have been referred to
your Committ ee on Policy and General Purposes, for consider ation
and report.
The first three recomme ndations have to do with generally encouraging Masters of constitue nt Lodges to dissemin ate informat ion through

with the Grand Lodge Committ ee on Masonic Informat ion and the two
M asonic Press Clubs now existing in our jurisdicti on in order to "con-

tribute to the optimum public recogniti on and understa nding of the true
purposes of Freemas onry."
Your Committ ee sees no harm in the approval of these recomme nda tions as they are permissiv e matters only and bind no one to specific
action.
The fourth recomme ndation is that the "Handbo ok for Masonic

therefore , recomme nd approval of a publicati on about which we know
nothing.
We recomme nd approval of this report.

AMEND CMC SECTION 17(0)-AccELERATE PRINTING SUPPLEMENT
( 1)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Polky and General Purposes. to which was
referred Resolution No. I, reports as follows:
The resolution does not propose to amend the language of a section of the California Masonic Code, but proposes to amend one of
the annotations to Section 17-an annotation which merely summarizes
a report of the Grievance Committee of 1889, which was adopted by
Grand Lodge that same year. This, of course, cannot be done: the
report of the 1889 Grievance Committee could not be amended in 1963
74 years after it was adopted .
.
However, apparently the purpose of the authors of this resolution
is; to require the Grand Secretary's office to distribute to the constituent
Lodges the text of any changes in the Masonic Code "immediately following the moment action is had in the Grand Lodge." In our opinion
the procedure by which copies of our Annual Proceedings are now
distributed to the constituent Lodges is prompt, efficient and expeditious, nor are we aware of any situation in which the slight delay
necessitated by the processing and printing of the Proceedings has
result in any serious difficulties in the constituent Lodges. The representatives from each constituent Lodge should be able to report back
to their brethren concerning any subs tantial changes which will affect
the functioning of the Lodge. The resolution is neither necessary nor
desirable.
We. therefore. present the resolution for action and recommend a
no vote.
The Committee on jurisprudence:
This resolution is faulty and should not be adopted for the following reasons:
1. An edict or a decision, that is the letter annotations under numbered sections, may be repealed but cannot be amended. The reason
is that a decision or edict is based upon a special sta te of facts and a
decision is an interpretation of the meaning of the code section relating
to the set of facts. This is known as judicial or case law. Every year it
seems that resolutions come in to amend an annotation and our com-

289

CREATE OFFICE OF PAST INSPECTOR
(2)
THE COMMITTEE ON POLICY AND GENERAL PURPOSES
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which has
been referred Resolution No. 2, calling for the creation of the office of
P ast Inspector together with a special certificate, reports as follows :
We respectfully call attention to the fact that the premise upon
which this resolution is based is erroneous. We quote from that portion of the preamble of the resolution which reads, "Grand Lodge Officers retain their titles after their elected or appointed service, i. e ..
P ast Grand Master. Past Grand Sword Bearer, etc." This is not
correct.
Section No. 4 CMC specifically defines a Past Grand Officer as
"one of the seven elective Grand Lodge Officers who has been regularly elected and installed and who has ser ved his term as such in
this Grand Lodge.''
We agree w hole-heartedly with one section of the resolution's preamble which s tates that "ex-Inspector" is not a proper or dignified title.
Appointed Grand Lodge Officers, however, should always be referred
to as former Grand Lodge Officers, and of course, this applies to Inspectors also. Such a title is every bit as dignified as "Past Inspector"
and carries the same connotation.
W e wonder if the proposers of this resolution realize that every
Inspector, as well as Grand Lodge Officer. is presented with a pocket

290

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

parchmen t certificate with his name handsome ly inscribed and signed
by the Grand Master and Grand Secreta ry with the seal of the Grand
Lodge, naming his office and the date of his appointme nt. This seems
to comply substantia lly with the spirit of that portion of the resolution
recommen ding a certificate and we see no reason for any change.
This in no way should be construed as any slight to the office of
Inspector. We recognize Inspectors as devoted officers of Grand Lodge
but feel that presently they are receiving equal considerat ion with every
other Grand Lodge Officer. and that they are the last ones who would
want to be singled out for special considerat ion.
We move the adoption of the resolution but urge a no vote.
The Committe e on Jurisprudence:
To effect the purpose of this resolution we present the following:
RESOLV ED: That Sec. 160 CMC be amended by adding at the
end thereof the following :
Each Inspector, retiring with at least one year of service and each
retired Inspector, who served at least one year. shall receive a certificate signed by the Grand Master specifying his term of service conferring upon him the title of Past Inspector.
This resolution should not be enacted for the following reasons:
I. The only ex service members of Grand Lodge entitled to bear
the word Past are the seven elected Grand Lodge Officers (Sec. 40
CMC) and Masters (Sec. 490 CMC).
2. It would be unfair to all other former officers of Grand Lodge
and committee men to single out Inspectors for this dubious honor.
3. Inspectors do not desire such title.
We move adoption of the resolution but urge a no vote.

PERMIT GRAND LoDGE To INVEST FUNDS W1TH
INSURED SAVINGS & LoAN AssN.

( 3)

The Committe e on Finance:
There has been referred to the Committe e on Finance Resolution
No. 3 which seeks to amend Section 246, Subsection 3, of the Code by
authorizin g the investmen t of Grand Lodge, Homes and Endowme nt
funds in certificate s and/ or shares of savings and loan associatio ns.
In considerin g this resolution your Finance Committe e held extensive discussion s with the Grand Treasurer and the individual members
of the Investmen t Committe e and we find that they do not favor the
adoption of this amendme nt to our Grand Lodge investmen t law.
It should be pointed out that the Investmen t Committe e is charged
with the responsibi lity of deciding how all these funds shall be invested,
subject at all times to the restriction s and provisions of our law. This
responsibi lity covers the whole field of investmen ts - demand and term

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

291

deposits in banks : governme nt. municipal and corporate bonds; preferred and common stocks of corporatio ns. Endless research and analysis of financial reports is just one phase of the problem the Inves.tmen t
Committe e faces in making its decisions. Fortunate ly, such finanetal reports in detail and exhaustive backgroun d informatio n are readily available at all times when the Committee takes a look at a corporatio n with
the idea of investing Grand Lodge funds .
In considerin g certificate s and / or shares of savings and loan a ssociations as an investmen t medium. it must be remember ed that. a lthough
these institution s perform a necessary function in the mortgage loan
field. the vast majority of their assets are represente d by long term real
estate loans. Without attempting to weigh the quality of these loans.
the fact remains that the Investmen t Committe e could not, in good conscience, recommen d the purchase of the certificate s and/ or ,s hares of any
savings and loan without substantia l knowledg e of the type and size of
its outstandin g loans, the character and credit rating of the borrower,
and the location and sound value of the property against which the
loans are made. Such informatio n is rarely, if ever, made public; nor is
it readily available. Neither Grand Lodge nor the Investmen t Committe e
has the facilities to make the investigati on which would be necessary to
obtain all these fa cts upon which a judgment could be based.
The situation with the Lodge which wishes to invest in local savings
and loan association s, which it may do under our law, is different. Here
the Officers and Trustees of the Lodge are on the ground. The officen
of the savings and loan are probably known to them. Assuming that tht
Lodge would follow the sound procedure of any prudent investor. they
have the time and are in a position to obtain the facts upon which they
can make a w ise decision.
It is not enough for Grand Lodge or the constituen t Lodge to say,
'This mus t be okay because it is insured by a n agency of the United
States Governme nt." As valuable a safeguard as that may be, something
more is needed when one prepares to invest in the shares of any corporation, particular ly one which derives its earnings from and holds its
assets in long term real estate mortgages .
For all the above reasons, your Committe e on Finance is authorizeci
to report to you that neither the Grand Treasurer nor the Investment
Committe e seeks the privilege of investing in savings and loan certificates, and they oppose the adoption of this resolution .
The Committe e on Finance is also opposed and recommen ds a no
vote.
The Committe es on Policy and G~neral Purposes, and on Investment indicated their concurren ce in th~ recommen dation of the Committee on Finance.

CONTRIBUTIONS LEVIED UPON LODGES- REVOLVING BUILDING FUND
(4)
The Committee on Finance:
There has been referred to the Committee on Finance Resolution
No. 4 which seeks to levy n per capita tax of $1.00 on all Master Mason
members of Lodges for the purpose of creating a Masonic Lodge Temple Building Fund to be administered by the Grand Lodge Committee
on Lodge Financing in the form of loans to Lodges.
Your Committee believes that it would be unwise for Grand Lodge
to incorporate such a plan into our regulations.
Recognizing the good motive behind the proposal. we are of the
opinion nevertheless that it is outside the scope of Grand Lodge to go
into the loan business. It should be noted that in cases of emergency
and, at times. distress, Grand Lodge has not been unsympathetic to
the needs of constituent Lodges. and in a number of cases has voted
financial assistance.
The Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Financing is of considerable
assistance to Lodges in working out financial plans for new Mnsonic
Halls and for their repair and improvement.
If a proposed Lodge building project is sound. the combined knowledge and experience of this Committee and the Lodge members should
make it possible to arrange a financial program from the resources of
the Lodge itself. If not, we doubt the wisdom of asking all Lodges of
this jurisdiction to t<1x themselves to underwrite such a building project.
For the above reasons the Committee on Finnnce opposes the adoption of this resolution and recommends a no vote.

(6)
WEARING OF MASONIC CLOTHING- PUBLIC PROCESSION

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered
Resolutions numbered 6, 7 and 8. These have a com mon purpose and

294

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the first two of them have several common signers. Only one. however ,
No. 7, offers any specific amendm ent to the law.
Each of these resolutio ns assumes that it is in the interest of the
Fraterni ty to improve the "public image" of Masonry and seeks to
improve it by encourag ing Masons to participa te in civic affairs by
wearing Masonic clothing at public affairs without the present restrictions of our law, now embodie d in Section 328 of the CMC. That
Section forbids any Lodge or Mason to appear in Masonic clothing in
any public processio n or at any public meeting or place except for the
burial of a brother or for the performa nce of some strictly Masonic duty
or ceremon y or in accordan ce with a dispensa tion of the Grand Master.
We fail to sec just how the image of Masonry can be in any way
improved or enhanced by the wearing of aprons and other Masonic
regalia. things which the public does not understa nd. The image of
Masonry depends upon the characte r and reputatio n of the Masons
who as individua ls participa te in civic affairs and public life.
There are no public or civic affairs in which Masons, as such. do
or should participa te. If Masons were permitte d to appear in public
processio ns or parades wearing Masonic regalia, they could find themselves parading in public in the company of clandesti nes likewise wearing Masonic regalia. Such organiza tions are equally entitled to a place
in the public processio ns because the civic authoriti es cannot lawfully
discrimin ate against them. The image of Masonry could and would
be seriously damaged .
It is the opinion of your Committ ee that the public appearan ce of
Masons should be s trictly limited a s it is by our present law and that
the discretio n of the Grand Master should not be removed.
We, therefore , move the adoption of the resolutio ns, but urge a
no vote.

The effect of this resolutio n would be to solicit members hip. The
creation of a public image has never been one of the precepts of

TITLE OF PAST MASTER
(12)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 12 proposes that Section 490 CMC be amended to
provide for the designation of Past Master for all Masters of Lodges
under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California, who were regularly elected or named in a charter and installed as Master, and who
died during their term of office - provided the Lodge of which each
was Master, by resolution, designates him as a Past Master of said
Lodge.
Section 490 CMC was amended in 1961 to provide a means for the
bestowing of the title of Past Master on Mas ters who died during their
term of office subsequent to the close of the Annual Communication in
September. 1961. but no provision was made for such action for Masters
who had died before the enactment of the 1961 amendment.
The resolution which is now before us merely expands Section 490
CMC to provide for the bestowing of the title of Past Master on any
Master of any Lodge in this jurisdiction who died during his term
of office since the inception of this Grand Lodge, should his Lodge
so desire.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes feels that the legislation proposed in this resolution is equitable, moves its adoption, and
recommends a yes vote.

IN CONSOLIDATION CONFER TITLE PAST MASTER
(14)
This resolution proposes that in consolidation of Lodges, "the unreelected Master of a consolidated Lodge shall become a Past Master
of the consolidated Lodge, providing he has served more than half the
term for which he was originally elected."
The paramount issues in the consolidation of Lodges are the benefits
to be derived by Masonry in general and the Lodges in particular.
Undoubtedly. each Lodge where consolidations are involved, has
officers worthy of continuance in office. It is within the power of the
surviving Lodge to select former officers of a Lodge which has passed
out of existence and decisions to consolidate should not necessarily be
influenced by the fact that a Master canno t be continued in his office
at the moment of consolidation or receive the title of Past Master
without being re-elected to office in a succeeding year.
It is a reasonable assumption tha t the Lodge which becomes the
surviving Lodge will utilize all available officer material in the years
following a consolidation.
It is the opinion of your Committee on Policy and Genera l Purposes. that this resolution should not be adopted and in moving its
adoption we recommend a no vote.

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS

(15)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes. to which was
referred Resolution No. 15. proposing elimination of the requirements
of physical qualification, have carefully considered these proposals. We
have considered them without emotion and only from the standpoint of
what, in our opinion. would be good for Masonry.
Masonry selects its candidates and admits them only after careful
investigation and a unanimous ballot. No one has a right to become a
Mason. It is a privilege granted to a comparatively small number.
To begin with. we exclude half of the human race. No woman ca n
become a Mason. Half of the remainder of the population is likew ise
excluded, namel y any one under the required age o f 21 years. In California. for more than one hundred years. we have adhered to the regulation that no one having a maim or defect in his body that may render
him incapable of learning the art and physically unable to conform to
what the several degrees respectively require o f him. can become a
Mason.
The physical requirements for qualification of candidates for the
degrees of M asonry are probably as old as Masonry itself. They are a
survival of Operative Masonry and are peculiar to the Masonic insti-

299

If these proposals were adopted, it would require a different r itual
fo r each cas_e of physical defect. depending upon the nature and severity
of th_e p_arttcula~ deformity. This would completely destroy any unifor~1ty m the_.ntuaL Under our law, the conferring of a degree mus t
be m conformity with the established ritual taught by the Grand Lecturer. and the con ferring of a degree in a merely symbolic manner is
out of the q~estio~. (C_MC Section 512-j.) Unless we are prepared
to do away _with uniformity of the r itual. carefully built up for a century,
and prescnbed by Sections 554 and 555 of the CMC. we cannot
change the rule as to physical qualifications. This proposed legislation
does not purport to change Sections 554 or 555 of the Code.
The most appallin.g thing about the elimination of physical requirements. would be that 1t would s ubject a man who may have suffered a
repulsive physical injury to the required unanimous ballot with the
g~eat proba bility that some one or more of the members w~uld reject
him. Th~ res ulting damage to an already damaged personality would
be both 1~calculable and irreparable. It would be fa r kinder to reject
such candidates on purely legal grounds. w hich they can understand.
In ou~ opinio.n, this Grand Lodge has already gone as far in meeting

require of him.

sufferance only. All good men cannot be Masons but the ones we take
must meet our requirements. Yes, Masonry is a peculiar organization
and it is comforting, after the fires and cares of the day. to repair to
a Lodge and there enjoy the harmony and fellowship of the brethren
on the level. M ay we ever keep it that way.
This Resolution No. 15 is frightening and is practically the same
as Resolutions Nos. 7 and 8 ( 1961 Proc. pp. 291-293) which were
defeated. and Resolution No. 5 which was presented and rejected in
1962. We there fore take the same position in our report as we did
last year.
In refusing to present this resolution we raise a nd rely upon a point
of order, as follows:
In addition to numerous Regulations and a part of our Constitution
this resolution would wipe out and destroy Landmark Eighteenth "The qualification of candidates for initiation."
Landmark Twenty-fifth reads:
"The last and crowning landmark of all is. that these landmarks can never be changed." (Page 343 CMC.)
Authority:
"If it shall appear to the Grand Master that any proposed resolution contains anything contrary to the ancient Landmarks of the
Order. he may refuse to permit the sa me to be discussed." (Rule 55
p. 45 Eng. Constitutions.)
We urge the Grand Master to reject this resolution on the ground
that it is out of order.
The Grand Master ruled to reject this request and invited open
discussion.
The Committee on Ritual indicated their concurrence in the recommendation made by the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
By secret ballot a majority voted against the resolution.

LIMIT PROMISE QUESTION

303

15 TO 5 YEARS

(17)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had referred
to it Resolution No. 17. which proposes to add a new section to the
Californ ia Masonic Code. regarding a waiver after a period of 5 years
of that portion of question 15 as stated in Section 527 and under which
an applicant for the degrees promises that he will not apply for or
receive any degree or be initiated in any Lodge, order or organization,
the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a Master
Mason. until he has given satisfactory evidence. by strict examination
in open Lodge. that he is entirely proficient and well qualified in the
Candidate's Lecture of the Degree of Master Mason.
While this Committee appreciates the possible benefits which would
be derived by other bodies. the prerequisite of which demands tha t an
applicant be a Master Mason we feel that just because a man has
neglected to obtain his proficiency certificate in the Candidate's Lecture
~f the Master Mason degree, he should not be released from the promise he made when he applied for the degrees of Masonry. It is the
considered opinion of your Committee that it is the obligation of a
brother to endeavor to receive his proficiency certificate and that by
complying with this promise he will not only gain self satisfaction but
will also be stimulated in his Lodge attendance. which we as Masons
recognize as a fundamental duty necessary for our existence.
We move the adoption of the resolution , but your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes recommends a no vote.
The Committee on Jurispruden ce:
This resolution limits the period of the promise contained in question
15 of the application for degrees.
W e move adoption and urge a yes vote.
A majority voted agai ns t the resolution.
FORM OF APPLICATION

( 18)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred Resolution No. 18. reports as follows:
The resolution proposes to include in the form of Applica tion for
Degrees an additional question reading: " Do you believe in the separation of Church and State?" The reason for proposing the resolu tion
may be summar ized as follows: In order that a candidate may understand the position of California Blue Lodge Masons with regard to the
separation of church and state and to avoid future misunderstanding.

304

PROCEED INGS OF THE

It seems to this Committ ee desirable that every candidat e for our
degrees be reminded of the "separat ion" doctrine and that he understand at the outset the position of Free Masonry in giving our wholehearted support to the doctrine. That objective can be accompli shed,
we believe. by including the ques tion in the Applicat ion for Degrees.
An affirmative answer to the question will in no way bind or commit
the candidat e to the applicati on of the principle to any particula r situation. The asking of the question cannot be construe d as an attack on
any creed or as slanted for or against any denomin ation. since the
principle of the separatio n of church and state is firmly embedde d in
the United States Constitu tion and the Constitu tion of almost every
State in the Union.
We. therefore , recomme nd that Resolutio n No. 18 be adopted and
approved , and that it be referred to the Committ ee on Jurisprud ence
for drafting as an amendm ent to Section 527 of the Californ ia Masonic
Code.
The Committ ee on Jurisprudence:
RESOL VED : That another question be added to Section 527 CMC
reading as follows:
Do you believe in separatio n of Church and State?
Our Constitu tion of the United States comman ds this separatio n.
So the question is a valid one.
We move adoption and urge a yes vote.
A simple majority voted for the resolutio n. Failing a 5 / 6 vote. the
matter was held over until the 1964 Annual Commun ication as a
"Propose d Amendm ent to the Constitu tion" (Sec. 78 CMC). Resolution printed page 80 of these Proceedi ngs.
PROFI CIENCY EXAMINA TION

( 19)
The Committ ee on Ritual:
The Committ ee on Ritual to which Resoluti on No. 19 was referred
reports as follows:
Section 554 provides that all lectures mus t be in conform ity with
the r itual now taught by the Grand Lecturer to " ... require conformity with the adopted ritual and work."
We do not believe that the introduc tion of such latitude in one section of the work as to place the candidat e anywher e in the Lodge room
can lead to anything but confusio n. This is illustrate d by the sole condition imposed by the resolutio n, that "Such examina tion shall be held
with the Candida te facing the East." This would permit the Candida te
to be placed beside the altar. between the pillars, or elsewher e, as long
as he faced the East.
We must also point out that the average lodge room, at time of
examinat ion, has many vacant seats in the east section of the side lines.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORN IA

305

H ere those Brethren who cannot hear in the West are able to sit in
close proximit y to both Candida te and Coach. Addition ally, Candida tes
are not all of sufficien dy strong voice to sit at the W est and be heard
in the East by the one man who must judge their proficiency. the
M aster of the Lodge. The present position was chosen that the Candidate might be near his coach and receive from him the needed encouragement of a proficien t craftsma n and near the Worship ful Master
who is to wisely judge and, with justice, determin e upon the Candidate's proficiency.
In order to conform to the required procedur e, we move the adoption of the resolutio n and recomme nd a no vote.
The Committ ee on Jurisprudence:
This resolutio n relates to the position of the candidat e during proficiency examinat ion.
We move adoption of the resolutio n as presente d and urge a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

sometim es required in regard to the notificati on of delinque nt members .

as such by the Lodge. and it should be presume d that it was delivered
or forwarde d to the member concerne d.
We move the resolutio n be adopted and your Committ ee on Poliq
and General Purposes recomme nds a yes vote.

Strike the words in line four reading " ... deliverable to addressef.
only . . . "

vote.

CALIFORNIA FREEMA SO N RECOMMENDATION

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
That portion of the Grand Master's Message in which he recommends that Grand Lodge establish a policy of sending the California
Freemason, at Grand Lodge expense. to every California member, has
been referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes .
The Grand Master cites as his reason for the recommendation that
·'the cost is relatively small for the advantage which would result and
that its receipt by all our members might inspire them to return to active
membership, re-develop their interest in Lodge activities. and thus aid
in meeting the· problem of membership apathy which is of so much
concern to all of us."
We agree with the Grand Master's reasoning and are convinced
that renewed interest in the Lodges might be engendered in the minds
of many of our members by receiving this official communication from
the Grand Lodge. Too many members do not attend Lodge meetings
and are entirely out of touch with the Fraternity. It is our opinion that
the reading of the California Freemason would do much to overcome
this sad condition .
We. therefore. move approval of the recommendation and your
Committee recommends a yes vote.
Committee on Finance:
There has been referred to the Committee on Finance that portion
of the Grand Master's Message in which he recommends that our
magazine. California Freemason. be distributed free by Grand Lodge
to all regular members of Lodges in this jurisdiction. This matter has
been before Grand Lodge on numerous occasions in the past and
Grand Lodge has consistently voted it down.

IDENTIFY BANK AND BANK BALAN CE IN ANNUAL AUDIT

( 22)
There has been referred to the Committe e on Finance Resolution
No. 22 which would require that the names and location of all banks
and the a mount of monies on deposit in each be set forth in detail
in the annual report of the Investmen t Committe e of Grand Lodge
and the auditor's report of investmen ts of the Grand Lodge , the Masonic Homes of California , the Endowme nt Fund. the Memorial Temple. and any and all other funds under the control of Grand Lodge.
Your Committe e on Finance is opposed to the adoption of this
resolution because we feel that it is impractica l. serves no useful purpose. and is contrary to the auditing and reporting procedure s of
every corporatio n of any size in this country with which we are familiar.
Our regulation s place upon the Grand Treasurer full and complete
responsibi lity for the funds of Grand Lodge. Investmen ts in securities
are listed because they are more or less fixed. Ca·s h on hand held in
banks is an entirely different matter. These funds are fluid and fluctuate according to our banking and investmen t needs. We carry only

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

315

working balances in our commercia l accounts. Obviously . these balances change from day to day. Savi ngs deposits are maintaine d primarily to provide funds for a short term fixed need. such as a Homes
building program or as a part of a balanced investmen t program. These
are all subject to chan ge from month to month. The figures which
might be reported to you by Grand Lodge could be, and very likely
would be. quite different in the following thirty days.
These are the reasons why no audit or corporate report with which
we are familiar publishes these details of cash on hand in banks for
the use of its stockhold ers or the general public- because it is impractical and serves no useful purpose.
Our accounts are regularly audited by a firm of national and international standing. The audits follow procedure s consistent with practices approved by the American Institute of Accountan ts. The details
are at all times on hand in the Grand Lodge office and a re available
for inspection by any member of Grand Lodge.
In making this report your committee has consulted the Grand
Treasurer , the Assistant Grand Treasurer . the Grand Secretary. the
auditors. and the individual members of the Investmen t Committee .
We might add that each of these brethren unconditio nally supports
the position of this committee in opposing the adoption of this resolution. We recommen d a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution .

REPORT OF COMMI TTEE ON RITUAL
To the Mo st Worshipfu l Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M . of California:
WEARING MASONIC APRON S

(26)
The Committe e on Ritual. to which was referred Resolu tion No.
26, reports as follows :
This resolution would. in effect. destroy the uniformity of the
work and practice in those Lodges which have officers' aprons inscribed or embroider ed with insignia designatin g the office of the acting appointee at the time of degree work. It has been brought to the
floor of Grand Lodge before and each time the representa tives of
the Lodges have voted against the proposal.
We wish to point out several things:
F irst. no officer of any Lodge has ever been invested with his
apron. It is Lodge paraphern alia. If he is Master and if he surrender s
his office for a degree, he thinks nothin g of surrenderi ng the jewel
with which he was invested ; the gavel, which is the emblem of power;
or the hat, the symbol of authority. So, too, we believe he should .
with grace. surrender his embroider ed apron.
Secondly. degrees are conferred upon a candidate. The visual effect

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

is for the candidate. If a number of officers have vacated. a nd their
places are taken by side-line members. are we to greet the candidate,
half with white apron s. the rest with embroidered: and these , bea ring
no relationship to the office being occupied?
Those officers who have witnessed the opening of Grand Lodge
for one of its many ceremonies have seen these officers, both elective
and appointive, wearing the regalia indicative of the office of the day.
We suggest for any Lodge the sen sible and rational solution of
wearing white aprons in all stations at all conferrals of degrees. If
the Master then is to sit out. he may do so in the embroidered apron
without destroying the uniformity which is essential to the work. M a ny
Lodges use this custom of clothing all degree participants in the symbolic lambskin and enthusiastically report not only an absence of confusion in the Temple but better preservation of the embellished aprons
by use only at Stated Meetings.
Since our law requires, under Section 55-f. that each degree conferred must be in conformity with the ritual now taught by the Grand
Lecturer and recognized by the Grand Lodge. and, further, since this
resolution would destroy the uniformity required by this section. we
suggest that it purports to amend this section and would require a fivesixths vote of Grand Lodge.
In order to conform to the required procedure. we move the adoption of the resolution and recommend a no vote.
A majority voted a gainst the resolution.

material to be used by the coaches in their important work with the
Candidate.
This program, however, is a Lodge program, with help and supervision by the District Inspector. The Lodge already knows which of
its candidates becomes proficient. Each Inspector can, with little effort.
obtain up-to-date reports from the Lodges of his District. The Inspector
and the Masters and Wardens can lead the program and obtain real

the educational aspects of the program .
The resolution would place a tas k upon the Grand Lecturer which
cannot be successfully accomplished and add materially to the work
load of the Grand Secretary's office, through which all reports would.
of necessity, clear. No useful result would be accomplished and, like
other efforts to s hift responsibility from the local level. the Lodge would
end up getting less.
In order to conform to the required procedure, we move the adoption
of the report and recommend a no vote.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes indicated their
concurrence in this recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolution.

OPENING PRAYERS
Monday Morning
Almighty God. Great Architect and Creator of all. we place ourselves and what we are about to undertake, in Thy hands. Guide, direct and prosper us. we beseech Thee. Grant that this undertaking
will be a good success. and for Thy glory.
Make us feel that unless Thy blessing is with us, we cannot succeed. and that except the Lord build the house, their labour is lost that
build it. Direct us. then, in this and all our doings with Thy most gracious favor, and further us with Thy continual help. that in all our
works begun. continued and ended in Thee. we may magnify Thy
Holy Name. Amen.
Monday Afternoon
Let Thy peace come down. 0 God. upon our unquiet souls; still
the tumult of our stormy selves; close the gates against the disorder
and confusion of our time, until within us we may find a place to steady

321

our hands for prayer, and prepare our hearts for praise of Thee. If
we turn from the world. it is not to disdain it; if we shut it out. it is not
to forsake it; if we turn toward Thee, it is not to deny it.
We need Thy strength to meet it, Thy truth to understand it. Thy
grace to forgive it, Thy love to redeem it.

if in the wonder of the world. or in the goodness of our fellow men.
or in the faith of hard pressed people, we do not see Thy grace showing itself: if in the hour of unexpected delight or in the time of sudde~
adversity we have no hea rt to welcome Thee. then let Thy Holy Spmt
stab us wide awake. until we are alive-living souls in the kingdom of
Thy power and peace. and live with Thee the life of eternity in the

Tuesday Morning
Almighty God. who hast given us this good land for our heritage,
we humbly beseech Thee that we may always prove ourselves a people
mindful of Thy favor , and glad to do Thy will. Bless our land with
honorable industry, sound learning and pure manners. Save us from
violence. discord and confusion. from pride and arrogance. and from
every evil way. Defend our liberties. and fashion into one united people the multitude brought hither out of many kindreds and tongues.
Endue with the spirit of wisdom those to whom in Thy name we entrust the authority of government, that there may be justice and peace
at home. and that through obedience to Thy law we may show forth
Thy praise among the nations of the earth.
In the time of pros perity. fill our hearts with thankfulness. and in
the day of trouble. suffer not our trust in Thee to fail.

midst of time.

Tuesday Afternoon
Almighty God. who art King of Kings and Lord of Lords, ruler of
all the people of the earth. forgive. we beseech Thee, our shortcomings.
Purify our hearts to see and love the truth. Give wisdom to our counsellors. and steadfastness to our people. and bring us at last to that
Fair City of Peace. whose foundations are mercy. justice and good
will. whose Builder and Maker Thou art. that the earth may be filled
with the knowledge and love of God. as the waters cover the sea.
Wednesday Morning
May we never be so much occupied with our own affairs that we
have no concern about the needs of others.
Bless all works of charity, that the hearts and souls and bodies of
those in need may be comforted and enriched. Watch over all sick and
aged folk . over little children. widows and distressed worthy brothers.
May all Masonic institutions be places of contentment and peace.
Bless in particular our Homes at Decato a nd Covina, and so enkindle
fervent charities among us all that we be evermore kindly affectioned
with brotherly love. that Thy will may be done on earth as it is in
heaven. Amen.
Thursday Morning
Eternal God. whose days are without end, Who art the center
of life's fire and peace, deliver us from coldness of heart and complacency of soul, in this time of prayer. 1£. in strength of body or in
understanding of mind. or in joy of spirit we do not feel Thee present.

Thursday Afternoon
Creator a nd Redeemer of all mankind, we have labored. each in his
own place. trying to share in the work of the world. We have known
the anguish of incompetence, and we have tasted the bitterness of defeat. We have dreamed dreams and seen visions·--Our brains and our
ha nds have longed to lift our labor to such creative skill that it would
show our joy in Thy goodness.
Grant us patience to endure our failures. and humility to outgrow
our successes. and wisdom to follow the light as Thou givest us to see
the light. that step by step we. may travel toward the blessed land that
Thou hast prepared for them that love and serve Thee.
Friday Morning
Great Architect. Creator and Sustainer of all. we thank Thee for
every common thing that serves and supports our life. For the bread
we eat. the air we breathe. the roof that s helters us, for the earth on
which we live. and the air through which we fly.
Deeper than the things themselves. we see Thy providence moving
with loving kindness and mercy to bless us in a thousand. wa_ys. . .
Through fellowship with one another, through the souls high v1s10n.
the mind's deep truth, we follow paths wherein Thou hast led us to
greater and larger life. Continue to be with us as we return homestir us from our lethargy. enlighten our darkness. and encourage our
hope. that we may ascend from glory to glory, from s trength to stre~1gth
-in all things rejoicing in Thee, our Creator, Redeemer and Fnend.

fields.
It was a life that our Freemason ry seemed destined to touch and to
guide. from birth to passing. So. as we pause this afternoon briefly and
pay our last public tribute. we are reminded that it was Dr. Benjamin
Cory. fourth Master of San Jose Lodge N o. I 0. who ushered our brother
into this world at San Jose on F ebruary 17. 1877.
The historian who comes after us will record the events of this long
and illustrious career and will linger in admiration over the success
story of a strong American. It \Vas a noble example of the rise and
progress of an humble citi:en to grea tness. Blessed with a magnetic
and dynamic personalit y. and with a powerful and luminous mind. his
achieveme nts were outstandin g in the fields of the law, the military. the
civic. the fraternal. and the financial. Few have risen to such towering
heights in even one of these: and yet. as his many friends frequently
remarked, whatever he undertook he carried through to completion and
did well.
He attended. the public schools of San Jose and received his Bachelor
of Arts degree from Stanford University . 1898.
At Stanford he had been First Pres ident of his class; Editor-inChief of the Stanford Quad Campus Year Book. baseball manager in
1898. member of Sigma Nu Fraternity . Phi D elta Phi Legal Fraternity .
S kull and Sna kes Honor Soc iety . and the Press Club. He was Regent
or national head of Sig ma Nu. 1906-08.
On graduation from S ta nford in 1898 he studied law and after being
admitted to the Bar. distinguis hed him self in a civil and corporate
practice. For many years he was associated in the practice of law at
San Francisco with his good friends . George and Thomas Crothers.
and later also with his sons , Frank. Jr .. and William. and with whom
I also was privileged to be associated . following World War II. He
became nationally recognized as ex pert in law apperta ining to life insur ance. He was a member o f the American Bar Associatio n . the State Bar.
and the San Francisco Bar Associatio n; on the Board of Governor s
of the State Bar. 1929-1930: a Governor of the San Francisco Bar Association . 1928-1929 ; President of the Associatio n of Life Ins urance
Counsel. 193 1-1933: and P resident of the Stanford Law Society. 1932-

328

329

PROCEEDJr>;GS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

1933. H e was twice President of the Stanford Alumni Association. in
1919 and again ten years la ter.
As a civic leader, he worked to make sure the "winds o f freedom "
wo uld continue to blow over San Francisco. California , and the nation.
As early as 191 0. when he was still a young lawyer, a news story spoke
of him:
" F ew men have accomplished as much good for the community in
which they live as Francis V . Keesling . the well-known at torn ey. whose
life . . . has been filled with a multitude of good deeds. Stanford owes
him a debt of gratitude second only to that for the founde rs . ... "
He had organized, soon a fter his graduation. and fought through
virtually single-handed to adoption by the voters. a constitutional
amendm ent exempting such foundation trusts as Stanford from taxation.
This made possible financial stability for building that great university.
His achievements in the military reached epic heights during the
San Francisco earthquake and fire. Having enlisted in 1901 as a private
in the Nationa l Guard . Battery D. First Artillery, by 1906 he was a
major commanding the First Battalion. Trained in joint maneuvers of
the United Sta tes Army and the National Guard at West Point.
Kentucky, the San Francisco crisis tested his efficiency as a military
officer. California a rchives and elsewhere contain official reports praising
his heroic work in protecting lives and property. in feeding a nd housing
the displaced . a nd resc uing victims who had been trapped in the ruins.
As he took the fina l salute of his battalion when they ma rched in review
on completion of thei r mission. his eyes were moist for his men were
disbanding after having earned the commendations of the low and the
mighty. These included those expressed by Governor Pardee to the
extra session of the Legisla ture, June 2, 1906. and that of E . H . H arriman, the r ai lroad magnate of his day. who sa id:
"These men left their private affairs and their homes at a critical
tim e, many laboring under the distress of personal loss, and gave their
service to their Sta te in her hour of need. Praise, a nd only praise, is
due the N a tional Guard of California for its ser vice in this crisis."
He was a lways a s taunch advocate of clea n government. Active
in politics. he aligned himself with the Republican party, becoming
Chairman of the Rep ublican State Central Committee, 1914- 1916. He
was a can dida te for Lieutenant Governor in I 910 a nd for Governor in
1914. In 1942 he w«s na med to the Council of the Na tiona l Municipal
League. His political philosophy was well expressed by himself as
.
follo ws:
" I believe that the desirable political objective is good and efficien t
government and that this can be attained only by the election of reputable officials who possess integrity and ability. I proceed with definite
conviction that this end can be achieved by politica l parties of the right
kind."

One thing of which he was most proud. a nd deservedly so, was the
part tha t his a ssistance, advice and energy played in the building of the
Golden Gate Bridge. He was a Director o f the Golden Gate Bridge and
Highway D istrict from 1929-1937; also Chairman of its Building Committee a nd the confidant of Joseph B. Strauss, the chief engineer. On
more than one occasion Strauss s tated to me, his a ttorney during the
construction litigation, that if it had not been for Brother Keesling's
help. freely a nd frequently given him, the task would have been impossible.
In view of his great contribution, he was given the honor of making
the dedication speech at the dedication of the bridge May 28, 1937.
Another testimonial to his civic-mindedness was his chairmanship
o f the Committee of the Board of Freeholders elected to prepare the
San Francisco Charter of 1931. Said o ne member of the Board:
" The good nature and sincerity of Frank Keesling were of immeasurable help in reconciling differences. The zeal that he felt for his
task and the ambition promptly to complete the draft of the Charter
were rapidly shared by his colleagues purely by the force of example.
If o ne gave an hour of time. Keesling gave two ho urs: and when the
Committee adjo urned. Keesling bent to the task of preparing more
matter for the next meeting. "
From 1936 to 1940. he was also Chairman of the Interim Committee
of twenty-five of the California Conference on Government and Taxation. As such . he presented to the Governor the Committee's report
which. in relation to the State government, was similar to the now
famo us Hoover report in relation to the national government. He was
also a member of the Board of Directors of the Better Bu siness Bureau
of San Francisco, and he served for seven y ears as President of an
orga nization close to his heart for its great humanitarian work for
youth without regard to race, color or creed, the San Francisco
Y .M .C.A.
In financial affairs, he was one of those lawyers who might be said
to ha ve a "business mind." He there fore ha d been called to high positions in the financial circles of o ur nation. His notable executive services
include being President of West Coast Life Ins urance Company, 19381949, and Chairman of its Board of D irectors, 1949- 1953. In 1933-1934.
he was President of the American Life Convention. an association of
U . S. an d Canadian life insurance companies writing over 95 % of the
ins urance written in these two countries. For many years since 1942 he
had been President of the California Ins urance Federation. Also, he
was Cha irman of the Board of Directors. Blair Holdings Corporation.
with offices in New York C ity.
His attention was drawn to Masonry by outstanding men he knew
during his boyhood in San Jose. Through them, he form ed a "favorable
opinion of the Fraternity." Accordingly, when old enough, he presented

PRO CEEDINGS OF THE

GRAN D LODGE O F CALIFORNIA

his Petition to CaliforniC1 Lodge No. I, and was made a Mason of that
Lodge in 1900. H e chose this Lodge in o rder to be with his frien ds
George a nd Thomas Crothers. who already were members.
In Masonry . as in everything else. he qu ickly rose to the top. Starting through the chairs of his Lodge as Junior Steward in 1902. he
served as its Master in 1907. He then became active in the affairs of
Grand Lodge and. in 1913. commencing as Junior Grand Warden he
progressed regularly to his election as Grand Master in 191 6. In 1942.
because of his fin ancia l ability. he was elected Grand Treasurer and
served for years with great distinction in that capacity.
As Deputy Grand Master. he laid the cornerstone of the Masonic
H ome for Children at Covina in 1916. The following year . when he
was Grand Master, he dedicated the H ome. And. though many other
demands were made upon his time, he never ceased to concern himself
with its welfare. He had been credited also with persuading Charles
M . Wollenberg. later Grand Master. to take a place on the Board of
Trustees of Masonic Homes - first in an advisory capacity. then as
Chairman. He championed the "Pennsylvania Plan." a system of individual contributions. modified to suit conditions peculiar to California
Lodges. as a means of meeting the need for increased financing. It was
he ""' ho presented specific legislation for obtaining from the fee of each
petitioner for degrees sums to go toward s upport of the Homes.
Clearly. his services to California Blue Lodge Masonry were enough
to keep him more than busy. Yet he found time to take an active part
in the vario us concordant bodies. He became a membe r of all York and
Scottish Rite Bodies. was Potentate of the San Francisco Shrine. and.
in 1913. received the J3rd Degree in the Scottish Rite and also served
for a time as Deputy in California of the Scottish Rite Supreme
Council.
He belonged to the Pacific Union. University. Union League. Commonwealth. San Fra ncisco Golf and Menlo Country Clubs.
Yes. our brother was a great American . Pro bono publico was his
credo. He was a citizen's citizen. He was a maker of history. He was
a lawyer's lawyer. He was a symbol of clean government. He was truly
a Master Mason. He has left a lasting mark for good upon the men and
the events of his time. Free men of his City. of his native State. and
of his country today give him the benediction of their heartfelt prayers.
Now his dynamic spirit mingles with those who died that this nation
might be born. that our flag might float freely in the sunlight of liberty.
H is wife . Haidee. having preceded him in passing . we express to his
survivors ou r deep sympa thy. They include his four children of whom
he always spoke with such paternal pride. Mrs. Jacqueline K. Sesnon of
Beverly Hills and Mrs. Thomas B. Laird of San Francisco: two sons.
Francis. Jr .. now President of the West Coast Life Insurance Company .
and William H .. prominent attorney of San Francisco; a brot her. Roy

Keesling of H ealdsburg; seven grandch ild ren and two great grandchildren .
Ma y his spirit ever guide them and us. a s he - mentor to ma ny _
did in life. toward a truer and nobler courage to stand as .soldiers s hould
stand in life's battle. and to fight as citizens shou ld figh t for the preservation of those things we hold dear.
In the sublim e words of Vergil. in his Aenid . let us say:
